award.abstractText:
This award is funded in whole or in part under the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 (Public Law 117-2).

PART 1:   NON-TECHNICAL SUMMARY

Living organisms build skeletal elements that serve a variety of functions, ranging from mechanical support to protective armor. An intriguing phenomenon in biomineralization is the incorporation of organic molecules into a growing crystal, which profoundly alters the mineral’s macroscopic properties and function. Proteins are known to play a critical role in controlling mineral formation, while the impact of sugars is yet poorly understood. By using well-defined model systems, this research will advance our fundamental understanding of polysaccharide-mineral interactions. Transferring biological construction principles to industrial processes has the potential to benefit practical applications, such as the environmentally friendly synthesis of fracture-resistant ceramics that emulate mineralized structures in nature. Progress in this area will benefit diverse disciplines, including but not limited to materials science, polymer chemistry, nanotechnology, geosciences, or biomedical engineering. Specific examples include the mineral-catalyzed sugar synthesis on meteorites or pathological mineralization processes in the human body. The principal investigator aims at broadening the participation of under-represented minorities, women and K-12 students in STEM through educational outreach activities. Early research engagement of students from minority-serving institutions is intended to create a pipeline for STEM talent.


PART 2:   TECHNICAL SUMMARY

An intriguing phenomenon in biogenic minerals is the inclusion of organic matter into a growing crystal, which has important implications for the material’s macroscopic properties. Prior investigations have revealed that intracrystalline proteins play a critical role in controlling mineral formation. However, the role of polysaccharides in regulating biomineralization is not well established at present, although they occur frequently in biologically produced crystals and often constitute a large portion of the organic-mineral interphase. The main objective of the proposed research is to address this knowledge gap by investigating the role that carbohydrates play in mineralization. The proposed work will focus on in vitro model systems based on naturally occurring minerals and polysaccharides, which closely mimic fundamental interactions of the organic matrix in living organisms, while eliminating the complexity and heterogeneity associated with living systems. Single crystals with polysaccharide inclusions will be prepared by a slow diffusion method and analyzed for their hierarchical structure and chemical composition using a combination of electron microscopy, vibrational spectroscopy, and X-ray scattering. The study will give insights into the mechanism of polysaccharide incorporation into crystals, and the relationship between chemical composition, structural organization, and crystallographic orientation. This research further seeks to develop sustainable synthesis protocols that emulate carbohydrate-mineralized structures in the biosphere. This project intends to broaden the participation of underrepresented minorities, women and K-12 students through outreach activities. Specifically, the PI intends to develop a new course and online learning module on Biomineralization for integrating STEM education and research. The PI is planning to organize a crystal summer school for middle school students from minority-serving institutions. High school and undergraduate students will be offered learning opportunities through faculty-mentored academic and summer research projects on bioinspired mineralization.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Intellectual Merit: An intriguing phenomenon in biogenic minerals is the inclusion of organic matter into a growing crystal, which has important implications for the material’s macroscopic properties. Prior investigations have revealed that intracrystalline proteins play a critical role in controlling mineral formation. Previously, the role of polysaccharides (sugars) in regulating biomineralization was unclear, although they occur frequently in biologically produced crystals and often constitute a large portion of the organic-mineral interphase. Our research addressed this knowledge gap by investigating the role that carbohydrates play in mineralization.

  • The work focused on artificial mineral model systems based on naturally occurring minerals and common polysaccharides, such as pectin, heparin, hyaluronic acid and chitosan. Our research on model systems closely mimicked fundamental interactions in the skeletons of living organisms, while eliminating the complexity and heterogeneity associated with living systems. Our data confirmed the entrapment of various organic molecules inside inorganic crystals. The inclusion of biological molecules inside an inorganic crystal was found to influence the crystal shape, crystallographic orientation and microstructure across length scales.
  • We systematically examined the mesoscale crystalline architecture of strontium sulfate model systems, specifically crystallographic orientation and local strain resulting from polysaccharide inclusions using synchrotron X-ray powder diffraction, wide-angle X-ray scattering and Transmission Electron Microscopy.
  • We pioneered the use of nanoscale vibrational spectroscopy in the electron microscope for the identification of intracrystalline biomolecules in collaboration with the Center for Nanophase Materials Science (CNMS), Oak Ridge National Laboratory.
  • We discovered a previously unknown transient amorphous strontium sulfate (ASS) precursor phase stabilized by the negatively charged polysaccharide heparin.
  • The polysaccharide chitin is one of the most abundant natural polysaccharides. We developed a technology to derive three-dimensional chitin scaffolds from edible mushrooms though a series of chemical extraction methods. We created hybrid chitin/mineral composite materials and characterized their chemical composition, morphology, and mechanical properties. Inorganic minerals, such as calcium carbonate or hydroxyapatite, were deposited within the oriented chitin fiber structure to achieve structural reinforcement.
  • We investigated strontium sulfate biomineralization in the Acantharia (Acantharea), widespread marine protozoa. Our research resolved the complex internal morphology of Acantharian endoskeletons using synchrotron-based X-ray nanotomography.
  • Sulfated polysaccharides are abundant in many biologically grown minerals, such as corals. Stony coral tissue loss disease (SCTLD) is a devastating coral disease that first emerged off the southeast coast of Florida in 2014. We explored how SCTLD affects the skeletal minerology and composition of the organic matrix, as well as the multiscale hierarchical organization of the biomineral down to the crystallographic orientation of aragonite.
  • Our lab applied and advanced state-of-the-art methods for the characterization of biominerals and their model systems. Synchrotron X-ray nano- and microtomography was coupled with deep-learning segmentation strategies to study mineralized structures in a quantitative manner.
  • We investigated the amount of organo-mineral content in shark vertebral cartilage (including glucosaminoglycans), its structure and orientation on the micro- and nanoscale, and how it influences the biomechanical properties of shark vertebrae and overall swimming efficiency. Raman spectromicroscopic data showed a relative increase of glucosaminoglycans (GAGs) with respect to collagen and a decreased abundance of GAGs in mineral-rich zones of shark cartilage, highlighting a crucial role of sugars, specifically proteogylcans, in biomineralization.

Broader Impacts: Florida Atlantic University is designated as Hispanic-Serving Institution and R1 Opportunity College and University, providing invaluable educational opportunities and fostering student success.

  • Our biomineral model systems were designed to mimic biological interfaces. A better understanding of carbohydrate-mineral interactions is poised to benefit materials science, polymer chemistry, nanotechnology, geosciences, and biomedical engineering.
  • This project developed sustainable synthesis protocols that emulate carbohydrate-mineralized structures in the biosphere. Progress in this area will benefit diverse disciplines, for example by advancing our understanding of the mineral-catalyzed sugar synthesis on meteorites or pathological mineralization processes involved in osteoarthritis.
  • The project supported BS, MS and PhD students who received hands-on training in wet chemistry and multimodal materials characterization. Undergraduate students were offered learning opportunities through faculty-mentored academic and summer research projects on biomineralization.
  • The PI organized a one-week “Crystal Summer School” for up to 20 K6-10 students in 2023, 2024, and 2025, combining short lectures, STEM career panels, lab tours, instrument demos, and laboratory experiments on abiotic crystallization, biomineralization, nanotechnology, and nanoscale microscopy.
  • The PI mentored middle and high school students engaged in science fair projects related to biomineralization, for instance calcium oxalate model systems that mimic kidney stones.
  • The PI’s public outreach to society encompassed public lectures, instrument demonstrations, and lab tours for people of all ages, ranging from K-12 to learning in retirement.

award.abstractText:
Telehealth is greatly affecting our nation’s healthcare system, economy, and workforce, including the training of healthcare professionals (i.e., physicians, residents). This project advances health, psychological, educational, medical, engineering, and computing sciences related to human-machine AI collaboration in delivering high-quality patient care and augmenting medical training and expertise development in telehealth. An interdisciplinary team of researchers from the University of Central Florida (UCF), along with hospital and educational partners from UCF’s College of Medicine, Orlando VA Medical Center, Nemours Children’s Hospital, and AdventHealth University, will augment healthcare-professional training, expertise development, and diagnostic reasoning using AI-based immersive technologies in telehealth. Given the transformative and disruptive impact of telehealth across all societal facets (e.g., racial disparities, economic burden on patients, organizational disruptions, lack of medical training in telehealth), this project assembles, connects, engages, and addresses current local, state, and national disparities by involving academics across disciplines and leveraging evidence-based research with a variety of stakeholders, including government officials, hospital administrators, healthcare professionals and patients, employers, and industry partners. The interdisciplinary research team and collaborating stakeholders work together in the design of a paper-based prototype intelligent collaborative immersive telehealth system for training healthcare professionals and interacting with real human patients, transforming current medical training, fostering expertise development, and significantly enhancing patient outcomes.

This planning grant has three goals. (1) To secure, engage, collaborate, and develop a network with stakeholders, academics, and industry partners across multiple sectors to advance understanding of workforce, health, economic, organizational, AI, technological, and social issues related to telehealth. (2) To test the effectiveness of existing telehealth technologies used by healthcare professionals to understand their impact on diagnostic reasoning by collecting multiple sources of data from healthcare professionals and patients to examine physiological-cognitive-affective-metacognitive-social processes during telehealth interactions. And (3) to design an intelligent collaborative virtual telehealth system prototype that supports healthcare professionals’ diagnostic reasoning, expertise development, and training that can be used in various healthcare scenarios. Intelligent collaborative immersive telehealth systems will augment and transform healthcare professionals’ education, training, and delivery of high-quality medical care. Such systems are key to addressing major societal, health, educational, technological, economic, organizational, and human challenges (e.g., quality of medical care, lack of quality telehealth education and training). The project’s immediate impact will be broadening participation across local, state, and national stakeholders in addressing major issues related to telehealth and how it will transform and disrupt society. Various data types collected from this project will provide evidence of the issues related to medical expertise, diagnostic reasoning, medical errors, and organizational disruptions, and new metrics for measuring the impacts of telehealth. Additionally, hundreds of community members from all sectors will participate in workshops, data collection, and design sessions where they explore current telehealth environments and design a paper-based prototype intelligent collaborative telehealth system to enhance medical education and training to accelerate expertise development, minimize medical errors, and deliver high-quality medical care while fostering the workforce pipeline in healthcare professions and AI in medicine. Additionally, these findings will be broadly applicable to training middle-schoolers and high-schoolers interested in STEM and healthcare professions.

Overview:

Telehealth—using video calls and digital tools to deliver healthcare remotely—has been transforming the U.S. healthcare system. It impacted how care was provided, how much it cost, and how future healthcare professionals like doctors and nurses were trained. A team of researchers at the University of Central Florida (UCF), along with partners from the Orlando VA Medical Center, Nemours Children’s Hospital, and UCF’s College of Medicine, Nursing, and Health Sciences and Professions and industry partners, worked together to assess the impact of various AI- and non-AI-based technologies impacted healthcare training and decision-making within several clinical settings.

Throughout the project, we achieved three main goals:

Build a collaborative network of researchers, educators, healthcare professionals, industry leaders, and government stakeholders to explore the challenges and opportunities telehealth brings to the workforce, healthcare systems, and medical training.

Study how current telehealth and other innovative clinical tools (e.g., holographic simulations, human digital twins) were used by doctors and other professionals, and collect performance and multimodal trace data (e.g., verbalizations, eye movements, facial expressions) on their decision-making during patient interactions to better understand how they made decisions.

Design an intelligent virtual telehealth system prototype that supports better training, diagnostic reasoning, and clinical expertise, which could be applied across many different healthcare situations.

Why This Mattered (Intellectual Merit):

This project brought together experts in medicine, nursing, and other allied healthcare fields, psychology, education, engineering, and computer science to push the boundaries of how AI and immersive technology could improve medical care and training. As telehealth became more common, especially after the pandemic, the team recognized the urgent need to train healthcare providers effectively for this new mode of care, sparking a wave of innovation in the healthcare industry.

The project made significant strides in addressing some of the most pressing problems in healthcare, such as unequal access to care, the high cost of services, and the lack of consistent telehealth training in medical schools. By involving a wide range of participants—university researchers, doctors, patients, hospital leaders, and tech companies—the research team aimed to build a training system that would reduce medical errors, augment decision-making skills, and prepare providers for the realities of remote care.

The outcome was several scholarly publications and presentations, including a chapter on a prototype intelligent, collaborative telehealth system that showed promise in transforming how medical training was delivered. It also led to the submission of a NSF grant and engagement with new collaborators at UCF and elsewhere. It laid the groundwork for more innovative, safer, and more efficient telehealth practices that prioritize both healthcare professionals’ growth and patients’ well-being.

How This Helped Society (Broader Impacts):

This project supported the future of the healthcare workforce by helping professionals gain the knowledge and confidence they needed to care for patients remotely. It addressed the challenge of delivering high-quality virtual care and explored new ways of teaching doctors and nurses using cutting-edge tools.

The team involved dozens of people—students, healthcare workers, and experts from different fields—in collaborative meetings, focus groups, workshops, testing sessions, and co-design activities. These participants shared their experiences, provided feedback, and helped design a system to meet the real needs of those working and being treated in telehealth environments.

The project also helped identify key issues, such as when and why medical errors occurred in across clinical settings, and how organizational systems could better support providers. The data collected offered new ways to measure the quality of telehealth care and informed how future training programs could be improved.

Finally, the work extended beyond current healthcare professionals. It inspired current clinicians, clinicians-in-training (e.g., undergraduate students in clinical sciences), high school students, and other medical professionals (e.g., occupational health physicians) by showing them how healthcare and AI could come together in exciting and meaningful ways. The project sparked interest in STEM and health careers, laying a foundation for future generations to enter the healthcare system better prepared for the digital age.

award.abstractText:
Disease-causing bacterial microorganisms associated with food can cause various infectious diseases with significant health impacts.  Food manufacturing and processing facilities are a rich place for these foodborne pathogens to spread; thus, it is important to have efficient detection systems that can be used to quickly monitor foodborne bacterial pathogens in food manufacturing facilities.  Current technologies that are available for detecting pathogens can be expensive and/or take a long time to get results, so they are not suitable for routine application in fast-paced food manufacturing sites where products are developed continuously.  New and improved technologies are needed for rapid detection of foodborne pathogens in order to avoid health impacts and economic losses due to food product recalls.  This project will develop a novel technology that will accurately detect foodborne bacterial pathogens using a unique artificial molecule called ‘aptamer’ that is designed to act as a true test for the desired pathogen with the result detected in multiple ways to enhance precision.  The technology will use computational methods and mobile devices, such as smartphones, to enable rapid detection and wireless data transmission for remote access to the results.  The technology can be developed to detect various types of foodborne bacterial pathogens in real-time, a significant step towards improving food safety in food manufacturing and processing facilities.  The project will provide students with hands-on training in the development of the technology to build the related skillset in the United States workforce.  The project will also facilitate K-12 outreach programs on food safety as well as promote STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math) education amongst women and underrepresented minorities. 

The food industry needs “fit-for-purpose” pathogen detection technologies that can be easily integrated into manufacturing process systems to rapidly deliver precise identification and quantification of bacterial pathogens in real-time.  Leveraging an interdisciplinary research team that will exploit structural bioinformatics, data analytics, and aptamer-based biosensing, the proposed project will develop a wireless multimodal aptasensor with mobile integration to precisely detect foodborne bacterial pathogens via an integrated electrochemical and optical monitoring.  The technology will deliver the following performance characteristics: (i) a high-precision method for flow-through monitoring; (ii) a portable device that can be moved to different process locations; (iii) an ability to detect target pathogens in complex food micro environments; (iv) capacity for real-time remote monitoring and integration into SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) systems; and (v) multimodal sensing capability to enhance precision.  These represent significant improvements over existing foodborne pathogen detection systems used in food manufacturing facilities.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Food safety is a critical issue in the food industry, where harmful bacteria can easily contaminate products during processing and manufacturing. To help address this problem, our project focused on developing a simple yet highly accurate method to detect Staphylococcus aureus, a common foodborne pathogen. Detecting this bacterium quickly and reliably is essential to protecting public health and preventing costly recalls. We chose to study S. aureus because of its prevalence in food contamination events, and we targeted a specific protein on its surface to design biological probes known as aptamers to detect the pathogen rapidly. The development of the aptamer for S. aureus establishes a foundation for a new generation of rapid tests in food safety.

Our team took a multimodal approach to develop and analyze a new sensing device, referred to as an aptasensor, to detect the presence of S. aureus. One part of this approach used a light-based technique to signal when the aptamer binds to the bacterium’s protein. Another part of our system relied on electrochemical detection, which measures changes in electrical signals when the bacteria bind to the sensor surface. This dual strategy provides stronger and more reliable results to confirm the bacterial presence. We detected the presence of the bacteria in actual food samples contaminated with S. aureus at low levels. We used deep learning, which is a type of artificial intelligence that can handle large sets of data and find patterns, to create an approach that can be used to interpret the detection signals. We also combined the sensor into a wireless mobile platform, creating an application that allows users to run tests on-site. The data can then be shared with quality control teams or other decision-makers in real time, potentially saving countless hours and reducing the spread of contamination.

Beyond the lab, we placed a strong emphasis on training and outreach. We provided hands-on research experiences to ten students, including female student in engineering and students from groups traditionally underrepresented in science and technology. We also hosted middle and high school students from various backgrounds, offering them hands-on experiences in food safety. Our research was recognized by the Institution of Chemical Engineers (IChemE), which awarded us the 2023 Biochemical Engineering Award. This honor shows the real-world relevance and innovation of our approach. Our research also showed that it is possible to integrate biology, engineering, and artificial intelligence to create practical tools that address pressing real-world problems.

award.abstractText:
The goal of this project is to develop caregiving robots that can provide long-term assistance with activities of daily living (ADLs) to people with mobility limitations. Despite great strides taken towards sustainable solutions in controlled environments, robots are far from ready for adoption in real home environments as long-term caregiving solutions. Key factors could be the over-reliance on full autonomy in tasks that require dynamic physical and social interactions in unstructured environments as well as the lack of personalized assistance. Based on the central tenet that robots need to optimize both physical and social interactions to provide efficient, safe, and personalized assistance for ADLs, this work will focus on developing robot-assisted feeding as a long-term caregiving solution for a person with upper-extremity disability in an unstructured, real-home environment. Successful feeding consists of bite acquisition (i.e., picking up a food item) and bite transfer (i.e., moving it into the mouth). This project develops methods to integrate these activities towards the development of an intelligent and personalized robot-assisted feeding system. The models leverage multimodal feedback to develop human-in-the-loop control policies that adapt to a range of human and environmental factors. Realizing that full autonomy can be challenging in unstructured and dynamic environments, the methods will leverage expert human feedback while minimizing the cognitive load and interweave them intelligently with autonomy to arrive at a long-term caregiving solution. This work will have a direct impact on the lives, health, and comfort of millions of people in the world who live with motor impairments. Developing policies that consider the human in the loop at every step and learn from their feedback through multiple modalities will have an impact on many other human-robot interaction domains including but not limited to assistive teleoperation.

This project will advance the state of the art of robotics from both a technical and algorithmic perspective. First, novel bite acquisition algorithms will be developed that are capable of picking up deformable objects in unstructured settings. Second, bite-transfer algorithms will be developed that learn from physical feedback provided on the robot or on the utensil when transferring food inside of a person's mouth. Finally, the research team will develop active and adaptive algorithms that tap into other sources of data, such as comparisons or language instructions, to intelligently improve the acquisition and transfer algorithms and personalize the feeding experience. This work leverages the idea of learning from multimodal human feedback---specifically by embracing physical interactions rather than trying to avoid them---to better manipulate and transfer food. The assistive acquisition and transfer algorithms will be extensively evaluated through human subject studies. The algorithms will be implemented on multiple high-degree-of-freedom robotic platforms across labs. Planned user studies and low-level implementations will advance the state of robotics outside of assistive feeding, particularly towards other ADLs or Instrumental ADLs (IADLs) in home settings, such as meal-preparation, cooking, and housework.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
For over a million Americans, eating is not a simple act. For every bite, they are completely dependent on a caregiver. Spinal cord injuries, strokes, cerebral palsy, multiple sclerosis, and many other conditions can limit a person's ability to feed themselves, leaving them reliant on others for one of life's most personal activities. This project asked a simple but important question: could a robot help?

Through this collaborative effort funded by NSF at Cornell University, in partnership with the University of Washington and Stanford University, we set out to design robots that can assist with mealtimes safely, comfortably, and in ways that respect individual preferences. We organized our research around three intertwined questions: How should a robot pick up unfamiliar food? How should it safely move that food into a person's mouth? And how can each person personalize the robot to fit their own needs, habits, and dining contexts?

Over the life of the award, the project produced a series of advances on each front. To handle the enormous variety of food a person might want to eat, including soft tofu, firm steak, slippery noodles, mashed potatoes, and many others, we developed systems that can look at a plate, estimate the physical properties of each food item, and choose the right approach, such as skewering, scooping, twirling, or cutting. If the robot's initial strategy fails, for example if a piece of steak turns out to be harder to pierce than expected, it uses touch and visual feedback to adjust on the fly. We also taught robots to plan a full meal rather than just a single bite, deciding which food to pick up next while respecting personal preferences such as bite order, food pairings, or items to avoid.

To bring bites into the mouth safely, we tackled two complementary challenges. For people with severe mobility limitations who cannot lean forward to take a bite, we built a system that can place food directly inside the mouth with precise control and the ability to respond naturally to physical contact. For timing, which means knowing when the person is actually ready for the next bite, we developed a wearable approach using small sensors on a glasses frame and at the throat. The system detects natural signals such as chewing and swallowing to figure out when to proceed, without requiring the person to perform any explicit action. This makes the robot unobtrusive enough to use during conversation or while watching television.

To make these systems genuinely useful for real people in real homes, we focused increasingly on personalization. In partnership with two community researchers, one living with multiple sclerosis and one with a spinal cord injury, we built a complete mealtime assistance system that users can adapt in plain language. For example, they can tell the robot to move faster, use a different ready signal, or feed spaghetti before meatballs. Safeguards ensure that any changes remain safe. We also developed approaches that let the robot learn each person's preferences over time, growing more attuned to them across meals without requiring explicit reprogramming. A separate but related challenge is knowing when the robot should ask for help rather than proceeding on its own. Too many interruptions frustrate users, while too few can lead to failures. We developed methods that let the robot decide when to ask for guidance, and what to ask, while keeping the burden on the user as low as possible.

This work advanced the scientific foundations of assistive robotics by producing new methods for perception, planning, human in the loop interaction, and personalization. The open source tools and simulation environments we released are now used by researchers at universities around the world, and the international robotic caregiving competition we hosted attracted teams from the United States, Europe, South America, and Asia. Teams competed in tasks such as robot assisted dressing and bed bathing.

Beyond advancing science, the project has had direct societal impact. It trained a diverse cohort of graduate and undergraduate students. It engaged high school and college audiences through outreach demonstrations. It established lasting partnerships with care recipients, occupational therapists, and clinical centers, including Columbia University Irving Medical Center and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, helping ensure that the technology we build is grounded in the real needs and experiences of the people who would use it. Most importantly, by designing, deploying, and evaluating our systems in the homes of people with disabilities, not just in labs, the project charts a path toward robotic caregiving that is ready for the world, not just the research community.

award.abstractText:
This award is funded in whole or in part under the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 (Public Law 117-2).

Identifying and labeling important features in medical images such as X-rays and ultrasounds is fundamental to both diagnosis itself and to building libraries of images that support education, training, and auditing of medical quality. This work is time-consuming even for trained experts, making it an impactful and important problem domain to study for researchers in computer vision, machine learning (ML), and natural language processing (NLP). These artificial intelligence (AI)-based techniques have made great progress in object recognition and labeling for everyday camera images; however, medical images pose additional challenges because of the need to account for detail and relationships between substructures in the image, the need to generate captions that apply not just to the whole image but to these important substructures, and the need to handle noise and artifacts created in medical image processing. Further, the tolerance for error is low; interpretations need to be coherent, grammatically, and semantically correct in order to be useful. This project focuses on the intersection of biomedical informatics and imaging science, working to develop high quality datasets of human-annotated visual concepts in images that appear in public collections such as open access biomedical journals, then using those datasets to train novel vision, ML, and NLP algorithms. The work will support multi-institutional research and educational collaborations between three minority-serving institutions, providing advanced research and classroom training in AI, ML, and cloud computing to students from groups historically underrepresented in computing.
 
To improve image interpretation and retrieval effectiveness, this project will (1) create a crowdsourcing-based annotation system to clinically annotate important regions of interest (ROIs) of images; (2) advance object detection models to segment images and map medical image ROIs; (3) advance multilabel concept classification techniques by considering correlations between concepts; and (4) apply contextualized embeddings via deep language models to generate the captions. The proposed approaches will be evaluated through comparison with current methods in benchmark datasets, including the ones constructed for this project.  The end goal is the development of an AI-based prototype that helps physicians focus on interesting image regions, find relevant comparison images, and describe findings in correct and standard ways, all of which can reduce medical errors and benefit both medical departments and society by reducing the cost per exam. In addition to the research objectives, the project will implement a research-education medical AI training program including cloud-enabled classrooms, cross-institutional mentoring, and partnering with an existing industry internship “pathway to success” initiative to build the science and technology workforce of the future.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Medical imaging plays a critical role in modern healthcare, enabling clinicians to diagnose diseases, plan treatments, and monitor patient outcomes. The rapid growth of imaging data across multiple modalities has created a pressing need for automated tools to support interpretation and reporting. This project addressed these challenges through the development of advanced medical image captioning systems that generate clinically meaningful textual descriptions from medical images.

The project advanced the state of the art in biomedical informatics by integrating computer vision, natural language processing, and machine learning for multimodal medical image understanding. A key contribution is the development of a unified, resource-efficient vision-language framework applicable across radiology, dermatology, and neurology domains. This framework emphasizes semantic accuracy, clinical grounding, and fairness in generated outputs, enabling scalable deployment in diverse clinical settings.

A central research contribution is the systematic benchmarking of vision-language models (VLMs) for medical image captioning using parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques, particularly Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). This work provides a comprehensive comparison across models of varying scales and adaptation strategies, demonstrating that efficient tuning of a small fraction of parameters can achieve strong performance while significantly reducing computational cost. By establishing a unified evaluation framework, the project fills a critical gap in prior research and provides a reference benchmark for future studies.

To address the lack of descriptive supervision in dermatology, the project developed a novel medical image captioning dataset by integrating skin lesion images with curated clinical knowledge from external sources. Automated text mining and embedding-based methods were used to extract clinically relevant concepts, improving both the interpretability and quality of generated captions. In addition, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework was developed to incorporate domain-specific knowledge into caption generation. This approach enhances factual consistency and reduces hallucination by grounding outputs in clinically relevant evidence.

For neurological imaging, the project introduced CausalRAG-AD, a unified MRI-based framework for Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis and reporting. This system combines calibrated transformer-based classification with structured, evidence-grounded report generation aligned with AT(N) and NIA-AA clinical criteria. Key innovations include: (i) the CausalRAG-ViViT model with ROI-guided attention and fold-safe temperature scaling for reliable probability calibration; (ii) a retrieval-based reporting pipeline that generates auditable reports with explicit numeric grounding from imaging and clinical biomarkers; (iii) counterfactual explanation mechanisms that quantify minimal changes required to alter diagnostic outcomes; and (iv) integration of longitudinal survival modeling for disease progression prediction. Together, these components enable a clinically interpretable, reproducible, and decision-support-oriented AI system.

The project also demonstrated strong performance in international benchmarking efforts, with successful participation in the ImageCLEFmedical Caption challenge from 2022 through 2025. These contributions highlight the robustness and competitiveness of the developed methods in standardized evaluation settings.

Beyond research, the project had substantial impact on workforce development, education, and diversity in AI and biomedical computing. Through collaboration between Morgan State University and Dillard University, the project provided hands-on research training to students from underrepresented groups. Six undergraduate students participated in summer research programs focused on machine learning for biomedical applications. Eight graduate students completed thesis research in advanced computing areas, and six graduate research assistants progressed to PhD programs in AI/ML-related fields.

The project also facilitated high-impact professional development opportunities. Four graduate students were awarded IBM Master's Fellowships (2022-2025), and three students were selected for the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) PREP program, where they contributed as Guest Researchers on machine learning projects.

Significant contributions were made to curriculum and institutional capacity building. The project enhanced an undergraduate machine learning course at Dillard University and led to the development of two graduate courses at Morgan State University: Image Understanding and Computer Vision and Explainability and Fairness in Machine Learning. These efforts strengthened academic programs and expanded access to advanced AI training. In addition, the project supported the development and approval of a PhD program in Advanced and Equitable Computing at Morgan State University (approved in 2025), creating new pathways for doctoral-level research and workforce development.

Research outcomes were widely disseminated through publications and presentations at leading venues, including IEEE-EMBS BHI, IEEE ICMI (2025,2026), SPIE Medical Imaging (2025),  CLEF, ABRCMS 2025, etc. Publications appeared in journals such as MDPI Bioengineering, Algorithms, Machine Learning and Knowledge Extraction, and IEEE Access.

The broader impact of this work lies in advancing AI-driven medical image interpretation for applications such as clinical decision support, digital health systems, and medical image retrieval. The project delivers scalable, efficient, and clinically grounded AI methodologies, along with new datasets and benchmarking frameworks that will support future research. Equally important, it strengthens workforce diversity and capacity by training students from underrepresented groups and fostering collaborative, interdisciplinary research environments.

Overall, this project establishes a strong foundation for the development of trustworthy, efficient, and equitable AI systems in healthcare, with lasting impact on both scientific innovation and workforce development.

award.abstractText:
The goal of this project is to develop caregiving robots that can provide long-term assistance with activities of daily living (ADLs) to people with mobility limitations. Despite great strides taken towards sustainable solutions in controlled environments, robots are far from ready for adoption in real home environments as long-term caregiving solutions. Key factors could be the over-reliance on full autonomy in tasks that require dynamic physical and social interactions in unstructured environments as well as the lack of personalized assistance. Based on the central tenet that robots need to optimize both physical and social interactions to provide efficient, safe, and personalized assistance for ADLs, this work will focus on developing robot-assisted feeding as a long-term caregiving solution for a person with upper-extremity disability in an unstructured, real-home environment. Successful feeding consists of bite acquisition (i.e., picking up a food item) and bite transfer (i.e., moving it into the mouth). This project develops methods to integrate these activities towards the development of an intelligent and personalized robot-assisted feeding system. The models leverage multimodal feedback to develop human-in-the-loop control policies that adapt to a range of human and environmental factors. Realizing that full autonomy can be challenging in unstructured and dynamic environments, the methods will leverage expert human feedback while minimizing the cognitive load and interweave them intelligently with autonomy to arrive at a long-term caregiving solution. This work will have a direct impact on the lives, health, and comfort of millions of people in the world who live with motor impairments. Developing policies that consider the human in the loop at every step and learn from their feedback through multiple modalities will have an impact on many other human-robot interaction domains including but not limited to assistive teleoperation.

This project will advance the state of the art of robotics from both a technical and algorithmic perspective. First, novel bite acquisition algorithms will be developed that are capable of picking up deformable objects in unstructured settings. Second, bite-transfer algorithms will be developed that learn from physical feedback provided on the robot or on the utensil when transferring food inside of a person's mouth. Finally, the research team will develop active and adaptive algorithms that tap into other sources of data, such as comparisons or language instructions, to intelligently improve the acquisition and transfer algorithms and personalize the feeding experience. This work leverages the idea of learning from multimodal human feedback---specifically by embracing physical interactions rather than trying to avoid them---to better manipulate and transfer food. The assistive acquisition and transfer algorithms will be extensively evaluated through human subject studies. The algorithms will be implemented on multiple high-degree-of-freedom robotic platforms across labs. Planned user studies and low-level implementations will advance the state of robotics outside of assistive feeding, particularly towards other ADLs or Instrumental ADLs (IADLs) in home settings, such as meal-preparation, cooking, and housework.

award.abstractText:
Disease-causing bacterial microorganisms associated with food can cause various infectious diseases with significant health impacts. Food manufacturing and processing facilities are a rich place for these foodborne pathogens to spread; thus, it is important to have efficient detection systems that can be used to quickly monitor foodborne bacterial pathogens in food manufacturing facilities. Current technologies that are available for detecting pathogens can be expensive and/or take a long time to get results, so they are not suitable for routine application in fast-paced food manufacturing sites where products are developed continuously. New and improved technologies are needed for rapid detection of foodborne pathogens in order to avoid health impacts and economic losses due to food product recalls. This project will develop a novel technology that will accurately detect foodborne bacterial pathogens using a unique artificial molecule called ‘aptamer’ that is designed to act as a true test for the desired pathogen with the result detected in multiple ways to enhance precision. The technology will use computational methods and mobile devices, such as smartphones, to enable rapid detection and wireless data transmission for remote access to the results. The technology can be developed to detect various types of foodborne bacterial pathogens in real-time, a significant step towards improving food safety in food manufacturing and processing facilities. The project will provide students with hands-on training in the development of the technology to build the related skillset in the United States workforce. The project will also facilitate K-12 outreach programs on food safety as well as promote STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math) education amongst women and underrepresented minorities.

The food industry needs “fit-for-purpose” pathogen detection technologies that can be easily integrated into manufacturing process systems to rapidly deliver precise identification and quantification of bacterial pathogens in real-time.  Leveraging an interdisciplinary research team that will exploit structural bioinformatics, data analytics, and aptamer-based biosensing, the proposed project will develop a wireless multimodal aptasensor with mobile integration to precisely detect foodborne bacterial pathogens via an integrated electrochemical and optical monitoring.  The technology will deliver the following performance characteristics: (i) a high-precision method for flow-through monitoring; (ii) a portable device that can be moved to different process locations; (iii) an ability to detect target pathogens in complex food micro environments; (iv) capacity for real-time remote monitoring and integration into SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) systems; and (v) multimodal sensing capability to enhance precision.  These represent significant improvements over existing foodborne pathogen detection systems used in food manufacturing facilities.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Food safety is a critical issue in the food industry, where harmful bacteria can easily contaminate products during processing and manufacturing. To help address this problem, our project focused on developing a simple yet highly accurate method to detect Staphylococcus aureus, a common foodborne pathogen. Detecting this bacterium quickly and reliably is essential to protecting public health and preventing costly recalls. We chose to study S. aureus because of its prevalence in food contamination events, and we targeted a specific protein on its surface to design biological probes known as aptamers to detect the pathogen rapidly. The development of the aptamer for S. aureus establishes a foundation for a new generation of rapid tests in food safety.

Our team took a multimodal approach to develop and analyze a new sensing device, referred to as an aptasensor, to detect the presence of S. aureus. One part of this approach used a light-based technique to signal when the aptamer binds to the bacterium's protein. Another part of our system relied on electrochemical detection, which measures changes in electrical signals when the bacteria bind to the sensor surface. This dual strategy provides stronger and more reliable results to confirm the bacterial presence. We detected the presence of the bacteria in actual food samples contaminated with S. aureus at low levels. We used deep learning, which is a type of artificial intelligence that can handle large sets of data and find patterns, to create an approach that can be used to interpret the detection signals. We also combined the sensor into a wireless mobile platform, creating an application that allows users to run tests on-site. The data can then be shared with quality control teams or other decision-makers in real time, potentially saving countless hours and reducing the spread of contamination.

Beyond the lab, we placed a strong emphasis on training and outreach. We provided hands-on research experiences to ten students, including women in engineering and students from groups traditionally underrepresented in science and technology. We also hosted middle and high school students from various backgrounds, offering them hands-on experiences in food safety. Our research was recognized by the Institution of Chemical Engineers (IChemE), which awarded us the 2023 Biochemical Engineering Award. This honor underscores the real-world relevance and innovation of our approach. Our research also showed that it is possible to integrate biology, engineering, and artificial intelligence to create practical tools that address pressing real-world problems.

Mobile devices are an integral part of our lives, but can pose serious security and privacy threats, such unauthorized access to security-sensitive user data and services. This project explores human physiology to discover new biometrics of the human speech production system to enhance user authentication on mobile devices. These novel biometrics are captured and inferred using a variety of sensors that are present on mobile devices. The project also investigates the feasibility to deploy the discovered biometrics on mobile devices to improve security. The work leads to a new type of practically deployable biometric traits for mobile authentication. The outcomes of this project can be adopted by industry and could have a societal impact on facilitating a variety of security-sensitive mobile services and applications. The research activities are integrated into the Florida State University's Computer Science education program and include curriculum development, involvement of underrepresented minorities in computing, and K-12 educational outreach.

This project explores the sensing capabilities of mobile devices to capture new biometrics of users for enhanced mobile authentication. The work innovates by targeting physiological and behavioral characteristics of the human speech production system, such as bone-conducted vibration and articulatory gestures, for mobile device user authentication. The project develops novel sensing techniques to capture the discovered biometrics, and systematically investigates the practicalities of implementing the novel biometrics on mobile devices in terms of hardware and context variability. Understanding the impact of device hardware and context variability helps strengthen the discovered biometric traits, by adapting them to drifts in contexts and behaviors. The discovered biometrics are evaluated and integrated with existing mobile authentication methods under a multimodal and multifactor authentication framework. The outcomes of this research can deepen our understanding of mobile devices authentication by considering human speech signals and the sensing capabilities of mobile devices.

This project builds the mathematical and scientific foundations of deep learning by characterizing the fundamental quantities and general laws that govern the empirical phenomena observed by applied scientists and engineers.  Deep learning is a paradigm in machine learning and artificial intelligence where statistical models are learned from data by designing networks of parameterized modules and training them on big datasets using optimization algorithms.  It has widespread effects on science and society, from autonomous vehicles to online commerce and social media. Scientific research increasingly relies on deep learning for data-driven scientific discovery.  This project brings together a multidisciplinary team of statisticians, mathematicians, computer scientists, and electrical engineers.  Research outcomes affect many core academic disciplines and intelligence augmentation technologies by providing scientific guidelines for practical applications of deep learning.

The research program addresses the concept of scaling laws. On the practical side, scaling laws greatly simplify parameter setting for large experiments and model transfer to new domains. On the theoretical side, scaling laws shed light on empirical phenomena and unify them with mathematical concision. The team builds upon recent advances in optimal transport, empirical processes, nonparametric statistics, information theory, and complexity theory, and grounds its work in empirical observations made in large experiments in natural language processing and computer vision, among other applied domains. The research outcomes provide practical guidelines for scientists and engineers who employ deep learning to tackle challenging problems, and also constitute fundamental advances in the core areas of mathematical, statistical, and computer sciences.

This project studied how and why large artificial intelligence (AI) systems improve in performance as they scale in model size, data, and computing power. The work combined advanced mathematical and statistical analysis with large-scale controlled experiments to elucidate how training algorithms, data choices, and evaluation measures affect the accuracy and trustworthiness of modern AI systems. The research produced new methods for quantifying the similarity between AI-generated and human-generated text and images, novel theoretical frameworks for understanding stochastic algorithms, and reliable techniques for identifying biased patterns that lead to misalignment in AI models.

The project translated these findings into methods, algorithms, and tools that the broader AI community can adopt and extend. The team released open-source experimental testbeds for benchmarking modern AI systems, open-source software packages for detecting and tracking overly influential training examples, and large, publicly available datasets for unimodal and multimodal AI foundation-model research. These research products are already widely used by researchers and engineers across academia and industry to design and improve machine learning based and frontier-level AI systems.

The award also generated substantial training and educational outcomes. The project supported multiple PhD students and postdoctoral researchers, who coauthored award-winning articles in leading machine learning, language modeling, and AI conferences and journals and subsequently moved on to tenure-track faculty positions in academia and research roles in industry. The investigators developed and taught advanced courses on deep learning, language modeling, and data-centric AI; organized workshops and summer schools; contributed to programs that broaden participation in AI; and delivered widely attended research talks and media interviews that informed broad audiences about both the promises and the limitations of contemporary AI systems.

award.abstractText:
Robots made of metals, hard plastics, or similarly high stiffness materials are restricted in range of motion and shape changes. It would be extremely beneficial if a robot could be reconfigured on-the-fly to generate on-demand shapes and motions required for various tasks such as walking, crawling, and jumping. This award supports fundamental research on how to leverage mechanical modules with elastic instabilities, e.g., bistable modules that can rapidly switch between two stable states, to spontaneously reconfigure a robot’s shape and motion. The research will also develop novel robots with multi-modal locomotion capabilities that can adapt to environments without modifying their mechanical structure. The resulting knowledge will advance the national health and benefit the society in unprecedented ways ranging from search-and-rescue in disasters (e.g., earthquakes) to monitoring in hazardous environments (e.g., nuclear plants). Additionally, this award will offer a unique opportunity to integrate insights from robotics, mechanics, design, and fabrication into intellectually intriguing and visually appealing broadening participation activities to inspire, engage, and educate students and the public alike, with the science and technology of reconfigurable robots. Examples of activities include senior design projects, summer program for high school students, and science and engineering festival.

The objective of this research is to gain a fundamental understanding of a new class of soft robots made from soft/flexible modules with elastic instabilities. The goal is to enable soft robots with reconfigurable body shapes and leg motions for multimodal locomotion that can adapt to various complex environments. The strategy is to construct the robots using bistable modules connected in a closed loop for the body and an open loop for the legs, and then actively tune the energy landscape of each module on-the-fly to generate desired body shapes and leg motions for multimodal locomotion. Three research thrusts will be explored: 1) achievement of reconfigurable body shapes through an in-depth understanding of the energy landscapes of bistable modules via the use of quasi-static mechanics; 2) achievement of programmable motions through physics-based dynamics modeling using Cosserat rod theory and model-based reinforcement learning; and 3) validation of the models with the development of a robot with multimodal locomotion capabilities, such as walking, crawling, jumping, and climbing. The knowledge generated from this project will provide guidelines on how to systematically exploit elastic instabilities to generate programmable shapes and dynamic motions. 

This project is supported by the cross-directorate Foundational Research in Robotics program, jointly managed and funded by the Directorates for Engineering (ENG) and Computer and Information Science and Engineering (CISE).

award.projectOutComesReport:
Intellectual Merit: Under the support of this grant, Yin and his team have explored leveraging elastic instabilities for creating multifunctional high-performance soft robots in fast swimming and adaptive locomotion in unstructured environments. It remains grand challenges to achieve fast, high-efficient, and maneuverable aqueous soft robots with high performance comparable to their biological counterparts, due to the compliance of their soft body. To address the challenges, the team has developed two generations of flapping-wing-based soft robotic swimmers by leveraging elastic instabilities. In generation 1 of the soft swimmer, it has a bi-directional soft bending actuator and bi-stable flapping wing. The surface swimmer shows a butterfly stroke–like gait, achieving a fast speed of 3.74 body length/s, high power efficiency, and low energy consumption cost via snapping in the wing. To overcome the limitation of surface swimming, the generation 2 of the soft swimmer utilizes a monostable flapping wing to reduce the actuation inputs from 2 to 1 by spontaneously stroking up via elastic restoring force-driven snapping back. This largely simplifies designs, actuation, and control for achieving a record-high speed of 6.8 body length per second, high energy efficiency, and high maneuverability and collision resilience in navigating through underwater unstructured environments with obstacles by simply tuning single-input actuation frequencies.

The team also demonstrated leveraging elastic instabilities for creating autonomous and intelligent soft robots, especially in unstructured environments with obstacles. It remains challenging to create autonomous soft robots that can intelligently interact with and adapt to changing environments without external controls. To address the challenge, the team developed a twisted ribbon-based autonomous soft robot embodied with decision-making capabilities. It can self-avoid obstacles via adaptive soft body-environment interaction-induced snap-through instability for redirecting its self-rolling direction. It shows self-escaping capabilities from various challenging mazes, including mazes on granular terrains, mazes with narrow gaps, and even mazes with in situ changing layouts, without integrated sensing and external controls.

Overall, 11 journal publications have been published including papers in Nature Communications, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Science Advances, and Advanced Materials.   

Broad Impacts: Under the support of the grant, the research results from this grant have enriched the curriculum of two undergraduate and graduate classes in applied finite element analysis and materials by design by integrating them as part of the course lectures and/or course projects. This grant has fully or partially supported five Ph.D. students and 1 postdoctoral associate with three Ph.D. students who have been graduated. The research results from this grant has been disseminated through SES and RoboSoft conferences, invited talks in US universities, and journal publications, as well as media tools such as LinkedIn, twitter, and Youtube videos and media news report. Nine publications in Advanced Materials, PNAS, Science Advances, and Nature Communications have received over 300 media reports from US, UK, India, Germany, France, Japan, Spain, Mexico, and China etc., as well as over 95,000 views on Youtube since May 2022.

award.abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of a device to treat chronic lymphatic system failure (lymphedema). An estimated 10 million Americans are affected by lymphedema while two-thirds of all cases are cancer-related. Lymphedema is a chronic condition that prevails throughout the patient’s lifetime, and passive treatment methods, such as compression devices, are routinely used to treat the condition. However, currently patient compliance is a problem.  The proposed device is intended only to be worn for a short period of time unlike compression stockings and is expected to improve patient compliance and satisfaction. Current sequential compression devices are reported to be uncomfortable, which also results in reduced patient compliance. The ergonomic design of the proposed device may be more comfortable, which is expected to result in increased patient compliance.

This I-Corps project is based on the development of a technology to treat lymphedema. The proposed device is designed to create 20,000 compressions per minute, whereas the currently marketed sequential compression device only creates 1 compression per minute. The core technology produces sound waves in a novel pattern of microcurrents to move fluid. The sound wave technology may be used to treat lymphedema, edema, fibrosis, fibromyalgia, and venous insufficiency in various tissues that include lymph, nervous, connective, and muscular tissue. This device has been tested in silico and data support the proposed mechanism of action, and the therapeutic effects have proven successful in a human model.   The goal is improved lymphatic return to reduce the girth of the limb and improve function thereby alleviating symptoms of lymphedema.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This NSF I-Corps Nationals grant supported a clear understanding of product market fit for unmet needs within the lymphedema treatment space. With the funds our team completed over 230 customer discovery interviews to have a clear understanding of each box on the business model canvas as evidence through customer discovery. 

Through customer discovery our team found that effective lymphedema treatment is multimodal and encompasses a variety of different treatment therapies which include nutrition, exercise, physical Therapy, massage therapy, static compression devices, and active sequential compression devices. While the use of all therapies provides the best therapeutic outcomes, we found that not all patients take advantage of all modalities. Severity of the underlying pathology that is causing lymphedema was one factor that influenced this decision.

Understanding we have product market fit for several subsegments of the overall lymphedema market, we stepped back and took a broader look at the business model canvas and our ecosystem to understand the pathway to bring a product to patients. Over 60 customer discovery interviews were focused on these segments of the business model canvas.


To gain an understanding of necessary partnerships for a startup company and what is required for manufacturing design and production, our team did customer discovery interviews with experts in Chicago. We toured their facility and got the background of what is required for a startup company to thrive through the transition of a patented research project with preliminary data and designs to a revenue generating startup company. This exploration continued both at the NWA Tech Summit and at BioMED Silicon Valley. At each of event over 40 customer discovery interviews were performed to get insight into the left side of the business model canvas. There is a plethora of specialty companies that provide support for medical device startups to have components that meet regulatory approval requirements. One of the key insights is to specialize at the core of novelty and expertise and use of the shelf solutions and experts well versed in adjacent areas where the startup cannot hold a competitive advantage. Through the collective of these customer discovery interviews we saw value in the using some of the customer discovery funds to develop a market ready prototype. This prototype will provide understanding for continued customer discovery. It will also be beneficial in conversation we hope to have funding groups in the future, who value seeing a physical, market ready device.

The minimum viable product (MVP) provided a physical platform to enhance the understanding of the device to aid conversations regarding the left side of the business model canvas. Specifically, the MVP provided the opportunity to understand the supply chain and partners required to scale up manufacturing. Having the components in place with an MVP provided insight for those involved in manufacturing to comment on what is required to create a go to market plan. There were a number of valuable customer discovery interviews with organization that considered using the device in practice. This MVP also provided insight for a deeper conversation during the customer discovery interviews with clinicians regarding the physiology of patients and how the proposed therapeutic mechanism compares to traditional treatment mechanisms. 

Not having a keen understanding of the FDA approval process, the NSF I-Corps team met with a number of FDA experts to understand the regulatory landscape. We performed customer discovery interviews with a number of business professionals, FDA regulatory consultants and physicians to gain more insight into this area. We found that we can seek FDA approval or elect for an exemption. As a first step we will seek an exemption. We also grasped the complexity of the FDA approval and exemption process and have a clear understanding of the need for help to successfully make it through the process. 

We spent time understanding the supply chain and the total cost to develop a product to bring it to market. We understand that there is a computer chip paneling wiring, and pneumatic devices which are embedded inside of the soft fabric. Each of these components has different manufacturing sources and requirements. 

We spent time exploring the complexity of sequential compression devices on the market today and the overall cost for manufactures to produce these devices. Through this process we found that these large manufacturers who hold large shares in the market also have a keen understanding of the unmet needs of the patients. They are seeking to acquire novel solutions to address these needs. 

Overall, we found there is an unmet need within the lymphedema treatment market that merits continued research and exploration to bring a new product to market to solve unmet patient needs. Our team looks forward to seeking more funding to uncover a solution for these patients.

award.abstractText:
Robots made of metals, hard plastics, or similarly high stiffness materials are restricted in range of motion and shape changes. It would be extremely beneficial if a robot could be reconfigured on-the-fly to generate on-demand shapes and motions required for various tasks such as walking, crawling, and jumping. This award supports fundamental research on how to leverage mechanical modules with elastic instabilities, e.g., bistable modules that can rapidly switch between two stable states, to spontaneously reconfigure a robot’s shape and motion. The research will also develop novel robots with multi-modal locomotion capabilities that can adapt to environments without modifying their mechanical structure. The resulting knowledge will advance the national health and benefit the society in unprecedented ways ranging from search-and-rescue in disasters (e.g., earthquakes) to monitoring in hazardous environments (e.g., nuclear plants). Additionally, this award will offer a unique opportunity to integrate insights from robotics, mechanics, design, and fabrication into intellectually intriguing and visually appealing broadening participation activities to inspire, engage, and educate students and the public alike, with the science and technology of reconfigurable robots. Examples of activities include senior design projects, summer program for high school students, and science and engineering festival.

The objective of this research is to gain a fundamental understanding of a new class of soft robots made from soft/flexible modules with elastic instabilities. The goal is to enable soft robots with reconfigurable body shapes and leg motions for multimodal locomotion that can adapt to various complex environments. The strategy is to construct the robots using bistable modules connected in a closed loop for the body and an open loop for the legs, and then actively tune the energy landscape of each module on-the-fly to generate desired body shapes and leg motions for multimodal locomotion. Three research thrusts will be explored: 1) achievement of reconfigurable body shapes through an in-depth understanding of the energy landscapes of bistable modules via the use of quasi-static mechanics; 2) achievement of programmable motions through physics-based dynamics modeling using Cosserat rod theory and model-based reinforcement learning; and 3) validation of the models with the development of a robot with multimodal locomotion capabilities, such as walking, crawling, jumping, and climbing. The knowledge generated from this project will provide guidelines on how to systematically exploit elastic instabilities to generate programmable shapes and dynamic motions. 

This project is supported by the cross-directorate Foundational Research in Robotics program, jointly managed and funded by the Directorates for Engineering (ENG) and Computer and Information Science and Engineering (CISE).

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Most robots today are rigid, fixed in form, and built for a single purpose. Nature offers a different model: animals routinely change their body shape and movement strategy to navigate complex, changing environments. This project asks whether we could build soft robots that similarly reconfigure their bodies and behaviors on the fly to accomplish multiple tasks across diverse conditions.

The key idea underlying our approach is bistability --- a physical phenomenon in which a flexible module has two distinct stable shapes, much like a light switch that stays reliably in either position without continuous energy input. By snapping rapidly between these two states, a bistable module can release stored elastic energy to produce fast, powerful motions. More importantly, by tuning the module's physical properties, we can reprogram which two shapes it prefers and how much energy is required to switch between them to effectively change the robot's mechanical behavior on demand.

A central intellectual contribution of this project is to develop a comprehensive theoretical and experimental framework for actively tuning bistable modules. We addressed both the forward problem to predict how a module behaves given its physical parameters, and the harder inverse problem: given a desired shape or motion, what parameters should we set? We derived analytical solutions for the inverse problem for single modules and validated them experimentally across dozens of parameter configurations, confirming close agreement between theory and physical prototypes. To tune the energy landscape in practice, we demonstrated multiple strategies: adjusting the initial bending angle of a flexible spine using heat-activated shape-morphing beams, and controlling the stiffness of an artificial muscle called twisted-and-coiled actuators to serve as active springs.

Grounded in this theoretical foundation, we built a series of robotic systems that demonstrate the real-world versatility of bistable and shape-morphing design. A quadruped robot morphed its body to walk, crawl, and climb horizontally across different terrains. An amphibious robot reconfigured its limbs to both swim and walk on land. A multimodal robot combining tensegrity wheels for ground travel with a bistable snapping mechanism for jumping to achieve rapid, energetic motions that conventional soft robots cannot produce. These demonstrations established that programmable bistability is a practical and versatile design principle for multifunctional robotic systems.

A deeper challenge this project tackled is that a robot's physical configuration and its control strategy are typically designed separately, yet they are fundamentally interdependent. In the final phase of the project, we developed a co-optimization framework that simultaneously optimizes a robot's physical properties and its movement strategy using reinforcement learning. Applied to a reconfigurable robotic manipulator, we demonstrated that certain tasks are simply impossible when control alone is optimized --- the robot's body must also adapt. Solutions learned entirely in simulation transferred successfully to a real physical prototype, confirming reliable, repeatable performance. This framework provides a general and principled pathway toward robots that are both physically and behaviorally adaptive, which are directly applicable to bistable and variable-stiffness robotic systems.

This project made substantial contributions in human resource development across multiple levels. At the graduate level, the project trained multiple PhD and master's students, providing mentorship through the full research cycle from theoretical analysis and experimental validation to conference presentations and scientific writing. Multiple undergraduate and REU students gained hands-on research experience in fabrication, experimental testing, and data-driven methods, with several continuing on to graduate study. Research findings from this project have also been integrated into a graduate-level course on biologically inspired robotics at Colorado State University, directly enriching classroom instruction and exposing students to cutting-edge problems at the intersection of mechanics and intelligent systems.

Beyond the university, the project pursued sustained and broad public outreach. The team participated in numerous public events, including multiple years of the Little Shop of Physics Open House, which in 2025 alone reached approximately 10,000 attendees, predominantly K12 students, through hands-on bistable and shape-morphing robot demonstrations. Additional outreach events engaged high school students in pre-collegiate engineering programs, FIRST Robotics competitors, CSU alumni, university donors, and the broader front range community. Research results were also covered by popular science outlets including Popular Science, IEEE Spectrum, and TechXplore.

To summarize, this project has laid a strong theoretical, experimental, and computational foundation for a new class of soft robots that can reconfigure their bodies, reprogram their mechanical behavior, and adapt their strategies across tasks and environments --- bringing robotics meaningfully closer to the multifunctional versatility we observe in living systems.
