award.abstractText:
Ribonucleic acids (RNA) are biopolymers with substantial amounts of negative electrical charge, and the surfaces of proteins that bind them often contain amino acid residues with electrical charge that can help attract, direct, and bind their targets. Importantly, these are large and flexible molecules so fluctuations in their structure and local environment play a significant role in their function. This project seeks to understand how the process of molecular recognition between RNA and proteins is influenced by their electrostatic interactions and by the dynamic environment in which binding occurs by developing a multimodal instrumentation that combines a variety of spectroscopic techniques. This research will train students in a multidisciplinary skillset at the interface of physical chemistry and biophysics, with broader impacts that include the development of transferrable methods for quantitative characterization of biomolecular interactions. In this project, scalable and quantitative experiment kits for remote learning will be designed and implemented with the goal of expanding hands-on, experience-based education beyond typical teaching laboratory settings.

Interactions between proteins and RNA show significant diversity – proteins can recognize their RNA targets in ways that are specific to their sequence, to their structure, to both, or to neither. To uncover the molecular-scale mechanisms that tune substrate recruitment, complex stability, and cooperative target recognition by multiple protein domains, this project integrates electrochemical and spectroscopic tools to measure the dynamic signatures of protein-RNA binding, their conformational fluctuations, and their response to non-equilibrium perturbations – all under the effects of a controlled electrostatic environment. RNA substrates will be localized at an electrode surface to tune their electrostatic interactions with proteins in solution, and the resulting protein-RNA complexes will be probed with a multimodal instrument that combines electrochemistry with mid-infrared plasmonics, ultrafast multi-channel fluorescence, and pump-probe spectroscopies. The outcomes of this research will reveal the way electrostatic interactions and fast dynamics of biomolecular structure and solvation affect the thermodynamics and kinetics of formation, stability, and dissociation of protein-RNA complexes. This project is supported by the Molecular Biophysics Cluster of the Division of Molecular and Cellular Biosciences.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This award supported work to uncover how electrostatics and local dynamics control the binding of ribonucleic acid (RNA) by proteins that incorporate ordered and disordered regions. We paired this research with efforts to increase the availability of hands-on learning with portable experiment kits.

To study the behavior of biomolecules in controlled environments, we developed sensitive laser spectroscopies to probe biomolecules at an electrode surface, which allowed us to detect signatures from a mixture of local environments and distinguish between the effects of multiple, simultaneously applied stimuli (pH, voltage). We identified a two-stage binding process for loqs-PD, a protein that binds double-stranded RNA to facilitate gene expression and antiviral response in fruit flies. We found that initial binding is efficient and stable, the formation of complexes with high protein density is disfavored, and that their equilibrium and kinetics are affected by substrate conformation and electrostatics. Because loqs-PD binds double-stranded RNA using two well-ordered domains connected by a flexible linker and flanked by large intrinsically disordered regions, local dynamics play an important role in its molecular recognition properties. To understand how local dynamics and heterogeneity connect with experimental observations of molecular recognition, we used computer simulations to construct a model of loqs-PD that captures its well-ordered domains and the inherent flexibility of its disordered regions. We extended this work to other RNA-binding proteins, using computational models, spectroscopy, and structure determination to examine how conformation affects the molecular recognition properties of PABPC1 -- a key player in mRNA degradation with multiple ordered and disordered domains that exists as a dimer before binding its target.

A longstanding challenge to understanding the role of local environment in biomolecular interactions is probing them in biologically-relevant conditions. A promising avenue uses photochemically-active biomolecules in imaging. In work inspired by this project, we reassessed the long-accepted paradigm for the function of these biomolecular probes -- replacing a model based in singlet oxygen generation with one that realized electron transfer is the primary pathway for their reactivity.

To capitalize on the spectroscopy and biomolecular aspects of this project, experiment kits were designed to (1) measure optical spectra and discuss light absorption, emission, and scattering; and (2) measure the kinetics of enzymatic starch hydrolysis. These kits have an easily adjustable quantitative component that makes them valuable assets for introductory discussions of optics and enzymes at a variety of educational levels. Testing with 9th grade students identified strategies that enhance their usability, such as stocking pre-loaded samples of shelf-stable materials, including a guided analysis template, and providing pre-assembled components. These kits can be used during classroom visits paired with small research presentations, but also as loan equipment for incorporation into existing lesson plans as in-class activity or even as homework. Their flexible design, along with the fact that the kits are easily re-stocked and reused, was intended to support long-term use and maximize their impact over time.

Finally, this award supported the interdisciplinary training of junior scientists in a wide variety of experimental and computational tools, and its results have been disseminated through peer-reviewed journals, conference presentations, and seminars at institutions across the country.

award.abstractText:
With support from the Chemical Measurement and Imaging Program in the Division of Chemistry, Professor Richard Vachet, Professor Vincent Rotello, and their groups at the University of Massachusetts-Amherst are developing new methods to measure nanomaterials in biological samples. Nanomaterials are important in a growing number of technologies, ranging from consumer goods and industrial applications to biomedicine. To properly understand the consequences of such nanomaterials in each application, new measurement methods are needed that can report on their distributions and biochemical effects. Professors Vachet and Rotello are developing new imaging tools that can simultaneously provide both sets of information for nanomaterials in tissues. The proposed imaging methods rely on sophisticated laser-based mass spectrometry that can also provide fundamental information about the interactions of light with nanomaterials. The new methods developed in this grant are also leading to new ways to computationally combine data obtained from these new imaging methods and more traditional microscopy methods, thereby deepening the insight that can be extracted from these imaging methods. A diverse group of undergraduate and graduate students will be involved in the project, and these students will obtain training in cutting-edge mass spectrometry and nanotechnology, two areas of broad importance.

The Vachet/Rotello group is developing new imaging approaches that combine laser ablation inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICP MS) and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization MS (MALDI MS) to simultaneously track nanomaterials and biomolecules (e.g. metabolites, lipids) in tissues. They are exploring new multi-modal image segmentation approaches to more easily identify sub-organ specific molecular markers. They are also developing new computational methods to fuse images from LA-ICP-MS imaging, MALDI-MS imaging, and microscopy. Combining images from these modalities will improve spatial resolution and enhance the chemical information present in the images. They are also synthesizing new mass tags that can be conjugated to any nanomaterial to improve multi-modal imaging. New software that is developed in this project is made freely available to the research community.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Intellectual Merit: During this project, we successfully combined laser ablation inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) imaging, matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry imaging, and optical microscopy to enhance the detection and localization of nanomaterials in tissues. When combined in the appropriate manner, these imaging methods work synergistically to provide deeper insight into how nanomaterials affect tissue biology. Using LA-ICP-MS, we have also created a straightforward new method for quantitatively imaging polymeric nanomaterials, which are inherently difficult to detect in biological samples. In addition, we have proof-of-principle data that shows we can computationally fuse LA-ICP-MS and microscopy images to create higher resolution LA-ICP-MS images, paving the way to image the biodistributions of elements with close to cellular resolution without additional experimental time or equipment. Upon applying our new multimodal imaging approaches, we have obtained mechanistic information about how new cancer-targeting nanozymes and antimicrobial nanomaterials work to reduce tumor size and destroy biofilms, respectively.

 

Broader Impacts: Nanomaterials are attractive for therapeutic and industrial applications. They are also increasingly used in consumer products. Our new imaging methods afford unprecedented insight into nanomaterial distributions and their biological effects in organisms. The information that is provided by these new methods will improve the design of nanomaterials to maximize their desired functions while minimizing any negative biological consequences. Already, these methods have yielded important insight into how novel cancer-targeting nanozymes and antimicrobial nanomaterials work. As our methods are adopted and used by other researchers, we expect them to have an impact in industrial, diagnostic, and medical applications. Our research has also positively influenced the training of a new batch of scientists, including six PhD and six BS students. Each was trained in the areas of nanotechnology and mass spectrometry, which are research areas that are having a broad impact in many fields of science and technology. Moreover, 50% of the students who received training as part of this project are women, who are underrepresented in the chemical sciences.

award.abstractText:
Cancer remains the second leading cause of death in the US. Immunotherapy is a cancer treatment that aims to help the body’s immune system fight cancer. While excellent responses have been observed for a large number of patients with varying disease types, a considerably larger number of patients have received little to no benefit from immunotherapy. This varied outcome has been attributed to the highly heterogeneous physical and physiological profile within and around  tumors that suppress the immune system’s response. Various physical, chemical, and biological treatment modalities are under investigation for altering the tumor environment from a state where immune effects are suppressed, to one supportive of an anti-tumor immune response. However, these approaches are hampered by the lack of techniques for monitoring the tumor state in response to candidate treatments. Technologies that enable continuous monitoring of the tumor’s immune state, and thereby guide precise delivery of interventions to drive tumors to an immunostimulatory state, offer the promise of unlocking the full potential of immunotherapies. A cyber-physical systems (CPS) perspective is uniquely suited to addressing this challenge, treating the tumor as an “in body CPS” with the development of sensors and analytical techniques for longitudinal assessment of the tumor, coupled with co-located methods for delivering physical/chemical treatments for modulating the environment within the tumor towards an immunostimulatory state. If successfully developed and translated, the CPS framework for immunomodulation investigated in this project may ultimately guide selection and optimal delivery of priming interventions prior to immunotherapy delivery, determine when priming interventions have successfully modulated the tumor to an immunogenically favorable state, and for assessing treatment response. The investigator team will develop a graduate-level course on biomedical cyber-physical systems along with modules on implantable biomedical sensors for undergraduate courses. Further, this project will provide summer research opportunities for students from under-represented groups via the Pathways to STEM program. 

This project will investigate a CPS framework for immunomodulation of the tumor microenvironment (TME), integrating: (1) a unique 3D micro-array sensor and treatment (MIST) device consisting of a sensing/actuation platform for longitudinal sensing and control of physical and physiological parameters within the TME; (2) novel model-informed machine learning techniques for determining tumor immune state from TME physical/physiologic characteristics; and (3) model-guided therapy via the MIST device for driving the TME to an immunostimulatory state. award.projectOutComesReport:
This project developed and evaluated a Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) framework to improve cancer treatment by enabling real-time sensing and modulation of the tumor microenvironment (TME), aiming to enhance immunotherapy effectiveness. At the core of this work is the Multi-modal Integrated Sensing and Therapeutic (MIST) device, a minimally invasive, microneedle-based platform capable of monitoring key physiological parameters (pH, oxygen, electrical conductivity) within tumors while also delivering localized therapeutic interventions such as mild hyperthermia. This work integrated advanced microfabrication, machine learning frameworks, heating-based TME modulation, and in vivo validation to demonstrate how CPS can inform and guide targeted cancer treatment, offering a pathway to more personalized and adaptive therapeutic strategies. 

  

Intellectual Merit: 

This project established a new class of in-body CPS for cancer treatment, advancing interdisciplinary research at the intersection of biomedical engineering, materials science, and data-driven control. The MIST device, fabricated using advanced diffraction lithography and metallization processes, achieved stable, high-resolution sensing of tumor pH, oxygenation, and electrical conductivity in vivo, enabling continuous monitoring of tumor physiology. The device consistently captured data indicative of the TME’s known physiological characteristics—such as mild acidity (pH ~6.5–6.9), reduced oxygenation levels (partial pressure <30 mmHg), and elevated electrical conductivity compared to normal tissues—which are associated with tumor progression and immunosuppressive conditions. These real-time data streams were incorporated into physics-informed machine learning frameworks, allowing prediction of unmeasured states within the TME and enabling informed, closed-loop control strategies for interventions. Additionally, we developed computational models linking bioheat transfer and interstitial pressure, illustrating how thermal interventions can modulate the TME to support immunotherapy. The modeling tools were employed to develop an experimental platform for delivering controlled radiofrequency hyperthermia to small-animal tumor targets. Collectively, this project demonstrated how CPS can transform cancer monitoring and treatment, bridging high-fidelity sensing with actionable therapeutic delivery. 

 

Broader Impacts: 

The project’s outcomes have significant implications for advancing personalized cancer treatment, offering tools for precise monitoring and adaptive therapy, potentially improving patient outcomes while reducing side effects of systemic treatments. By enabling continuous, real-time monitoring of tumors and targeted therapeutic delivery, the technology reduces reliance on invasive biopsies and intermittent imaging, supporting a shift toward proactive and adaptive care models. The project also contributed to STEM workforce development, providing research opportunities for high school, undergraduate, graduate students, and postdoctoral scholars, and engaging the community through hands-on microfabrication and sensing demonstrations. Additionally, the project’s integration of sensing and actuation frameworks lays the groundwork for future smart implantable systems for broader biomedical applications, promoting innovations in healthcare technology. 

 

Products: 

Outputs from this project include peer-reviewed publications and presentations covering topics such as microneedle-based sensor development, uncertainty quantification in machine learning, and multi-physics modeling of tumor heating. These have been submitted to the NSF Public Access Repository and are publicly available. In addition to scholarly outputs, the project produced: 

  • Fabricated microneedle devices with integrated electrochemical sensing: We developed, fabricated, and characterized multi-modal microneedle arrays designed to measure critical parameters of the tumor microenvironment, including pH, oxygen partial pressure, and electrical conductivity. These microneedles were fabricated using advanced microfabrication techniques such as diffraction lithography for high-aspect-ratio structures, precision metal deposition for conductive pathways, and polymer patterning to ensure biocompatibility and structural stability. 

  • Software tools for spatiotemporal data imputation and uncertainty analysis 

  • Computational models simulating hyperthermia delivery within heterogeneous tumor tissues, and an experimental platform for delivery of controlled radiofrequency hyperthermia to small animal tumor targets. 

 

Summary: 

Over the course of this project, this project successfully developed, optimized, and validated the MIST device as a smart CPS platform for tumor monitoring and treatment. The project demonstrated the device’s capabilities in fabricating microneedles with integrated multi-modal sensors, validated its real-time performance in in vivo models, and linked its sensing outputs to machine learning frameworks for enhanced interpretation and control. It established a pathway toward closed-loop cancer therapy, showing how localized sensing can guide thermal interventions to modulate the TME in support of immunotherapy. Through this work, the project advanced the fields of CPS, biomedical sensing, and cancer research, providing a foundation for future translational efforts and contributing to the long-term vision of personalized, adaptive healthcare technologies.

award.abstractText:
Cancer remains the second leading cause of death in the US. Immunotherapy is a cancer treatment that aims to help the body’s immune system fight cancer. While excellent responses have been observed for a large number of patients with varying disease types, a considerably larger number of patients have received little to no benefit from immunotherapy. This varied outcome has been attributed to the highly heterogeneous physical and physiological profile within and around  tumors that suppress the immune system’s response. Various physical, chemical, and biological treatment modalities are under investigation for altering the tumor environment from a state where immune effects are suppressed, to one supportive of an anti-tumor immune response. However, these approaches are hampered by the lack of techniques for monitoring the tumor state in response to candidate treatments. Technologies that enable continuous monitoring of the tumor’s immune state, and thereby guide precise delivery of interventions to drive tumors to an immunostimulatory state, offer the promise of unlocking the full potential of immunotherapies. A cyber-physical systems (CPS) perspective is uniquely suited to addressing this challenge, treating the tumor as an “in body CPS” with the development of sensors and analytical techniques for longitudinal assessment of the tumor, coupled with co-located methods for delivering physical/chemical treatments for modulating the environment within the tumor towards an immunostimulatory state. If successfully developed and translated, the CPS framework for immunomodulation investigated in this project may ultimately guide selection and optimal delivery of priming interventions prior to immunotherapy delivery, determine when priming interventions have successfully modulated the tumor to an immunogenically favorable state, and for assessing treatment response. The investigator team will develop a graduate-level course on biomedical cyber-physical systems along with modules on implantable biomedical sensors for undergraduate courses. award.abstractText:
It is now a national research priority to design and develop novel computer hardware for artificial intelligence as well as smart sensing with capabilities for high-performance and energy-efficient computing. This project proposes a new architecture, PARIS (Phased Array Radar with In-Sensor Computing), that simultaneously senses and processes 3D images in real time. The new architecture mimics the human visual system, which not only detects and senses 3-D visual images but also performs first-stage image processing before the more complex processing in the visual cortex of brain. It is the first in-sensor computing architecture leveraging a phased-array radar system for an energy-efficient, high-performance, low-cost, and compact sensing/computing platform. By combining phased-array radar imaging and neuromorphic computing, PARIS opens up a new avenue for research in in-sensor computing and intelligent image processing. The project has transformative impact on a wide range of industries including medical instruments, autonomous vehicles, machine vision, robotic control, IoT devices, smartphones, and consumer electronics. Research activities of the project are involving female and minority students, strengthening the PIs’ current K-12 outreach activities, and enhancing grand-challenge courses for all majors at the university.

It is well-known in artificial-intelligence systems that moving raw data from sensors to processing elements is very costly in terms of energy, performance, and hardware. The newly proposed architecture starts artificial neural-network computation concurrently while sensors are acquiring data, substantially reducing data movement between sensors and processing elements. Such simultaneous sensing and computation are made possible by several technology breakthroughs. 1) In-sensor dot-product computations with linearly tunable weights allowing in-sensor training and inference of artificial neural network; 2) a novel statistical signal acquisition technique, namely, Jitter-based Analog-to-Probability Conversion, allowing for direct use of digital pins of integrated circuits for high-bandwidth measurement with low-overhead; 3) a compact single-board system supporting very high radio frequency bandwidths and completely removing the radio frequency analog front-end required by conventional microwave imaging systems (e.g. analog-to-digital converter, filter, or amplifier) by leveraging the very short rising/falling edges of the digital waveforms used in today’s I/O interfaces. The theory and design of the in-sensor computing architecture is being established, and a 16-node prototype is being built. A thorough evaluation and comparison is being conducted to demonstrate its performance, energy efficiency, hardware cost, and potential applications to a wide range of industries. Research results are being published in professional conferences and journals and incorporated into undergraduate electrical/computer engineering curricula.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project proposes a new architecture, PARIS (Phased Array Radar with In-Sensor Computing), that simultaneously senses and processes 3D images in real time. PARIS mimics neuro-biological architectures present in the human visual nervous system and aims at fundamentally tackling the grand challenges of high cost, high power consumption, and long latency of conventional machine learning techniques for image processing. Rather than moving a large amount of sensed raw data to processing elements (PE), PARIS starts neural network computation concurrently while sensors acquiring data, substantially reducing data movement between sensors and PEs. Such simultaneous sensing and computation are made possible by several technology breakthroughs. 1) In-sensor dot-product computations with linearly tunable weights allowing in-sensor training and inference of AI computations; 2) A novel statistical signal acquisition technique for high-bandwidth measurement with low-overhead; 3) A novel dataflow architecture that optimize AI inferences on parallel computer architectures.

The project supported several undergrad/grad students working on the research. Numerous technical papers have been published in ACM/IEEE conferences and journals. Two patent applications have been filed. More importantly, a successful technology transfer has been done as based on the outcome of the NSF projects as outline below.

The PARIS technology holds significant potential for adoption by industry, improving the performance/energy efficiency of AI systems. The project has laid the groundwork for transferring this innovative technology to commercial applications.

 

A high tech startup company, FastFlowLM, Inc. was founded on July 21, 2025, entirely based on the NSF-sponsored projects and developed IPs. Our software was released on GitHub: https://github.com/FastFlowLM/FastFlowLM

As soon as the software was released, our software exploded in popularity — thousands of users worldwide now rely on the software. Without outreach from us, AMD discovered the work, contacted us immediately, and began weekly technical and business meetings with us. They described our performance results as “game-changer” for edge AI.

On June 3rd of 2026, FastFlowLM joined AMD's AI team in a transaction that produced strong returns for both University of Rhode Island and Clemson University, and the founders.

This is a perfect example of NSF-funded fundamental research translating directly into U.S. technological leadership in AI and semiconductors.

FastFlowLM’s close alignment and deployment with Lemonade, the AMD open-source inference initiative, has been central to ecosystem adoption, making it easy to bring agentic, retrieval-augmented coding and multimodal experiences to AMD platforms.

The FastFlowLM team joins the AMD Artificial Intelligence Group, where their expertise will accelerate our client and workstation AI software stack and our Day-0 enablement of the latest models. We remain committed to investing in this open  ecosystem, and we’re thrilled to build the future of on-device AI together.

award.abstractText:
Collaborative robots have been widely employed to assist humans in an increasing number of areas. Just as human-human collaboration, the trust in human-robot teams has a property of bidirectional. However, few studies have been conducted on both human-trusting-robot issue and robot-trusting-human issue in a unified framework for human-robot collaboration. The project addresses this challenge by developing a new systematic Bi-Trust framework to integrate humans’ trust in robots and robots’ trust in humans into the human-robot collaboration process. With the established Bi-Trust framework, a trust-level-based computational collaboration model is created to optimize and plan robot actions. The proposed approaches will reduce uncertain failures and improve the collaboration-quality of human-robot shared tasks.

The goal of this project is to develop a systematic Bi-Trust framework for human-robot teams and create new computational models of trust dynamics and trust-level-based collaboration in order to enhance the human-robot partnership. The proposed research activities include: (1) investigating the factors that affect humans’ trust in robots and analyzing humans’ trust using multimodal physical and physiological data; (2) developing a new Bi-Trust framework entailing computational human-trusting-robot model and robot-trusting-human model for human-robot teams and establishing a computational human-robot collaboration model via the trust-local-maximum method; and (3) applying the Bi-Trust framework in real-world human-robot collaborative contexts and assessing its effectiveness. The findings of this project will improve the collaboration-quality for human-robot teams in collaborative contexts such as the new generation of smart manufacturing and potentially benefit the national economic growth by fostering increasing robotics and AI workforce.

This CRII project focuses on developing a systematic bi-trust framework including a robot-human trust model and a human-robot trust model for human-robot teams and applying them in trust-based human-robot collaborative contexts to improve collaboration-quality. The outcomes of this project were shared with both academia and industry through multiple peer-reviewed journal and conference publications, talks and poster presentations by the PI and his team members, seminars and workshops, faculty panels, industry expos, publicly available resources, interactive STEM showcases and tours, media attention featuring this research, and education materials.

The project has led to advanced understandings and new findings on the trust issue in the human-robot collaborative process. The major contributions included the development of (1) a multimodal human-robot trust database with 100 user studies in human-robot collaborative contexts for the field; (2) new characterization approaches for human trust in robots through multimodal physical and physiological biometrics in human-robot partnerships; (3) a human-robot trust model that was effectively used to reveal the correlation between robot performance factors and humans' trust levels and to parameterize humans' trust in robots in real-world human-robot collaborative tasks; (4) a robot-human trust model by which the robot can accurately perceive its trust in the human in real-time during the human-robot collaboration; and (5) a trust-based human-robot collaboration model enabling the robot to actively accommodate and assist its human partner in shared tasks. As human-centered technologies and applications have increasingly impacted everyone everywhere across the world, this project provided original insights for advancing the human factors research in human-robot/machine/AI interaction.

This CRII project resulted in 11 publications in the fields of robotics, automation, artificial intelligence, smart manufacturing, intelligent systems, and data science. The research outcomes led to multiple awards and recognitions including (1) the IEEE STEM Champion Award; (2) the New Jersey Space Grant Consortium Fellowship; (3) the Second Place Best Paper Award at the IEEE MIT URTC Conference; (4) five media reports highlighting the research and educational activities and products enabled by this project; and (5) keynote speech/invited talks at IEEE conferences and seminars.

The project created various training opportunities. It has provided research training for four graduate and four undergraduate students (62.5% of them are from underrepresented groups), which highly widened their career pipelines. This project has upgraded and enriched the PI's robotics courses for both graduate and undergraduate students. New teaching modules on robotics and hands-on projects were developed in the PI's robotics courses that have benefited 241 students (a large portion are female students and underrepresented minorities). During the project period, the PI founded a university-level club Montclair Robotics Club to provide both STEM and non-STEM students with the necessary tools and knowledge to explore the field of robotics and AI. The research outcomes have helped the PI develop a pre-college summer program, establish the IEEE Montclair Student Branch, and organize 19 robotics talks, seminars, workshops, showcases, and open houses that covered over 536 participants including faculty members, college students, parents, teachers, K-12 students, and community partners. These academic opportunities and events have attracted a large number of women and minorities to the STEM field, broadening the participation of groups traditionally underrepresented in CISE.

This award was provided as part of NSF's Social, Behavioral and Economic Sciences Postdoctoral Research Fellowships (SPRF) program. The goal of the SPRF program is to prepare promising, early career doctoral-level scientists for scientific careers in academia, industry or private sector, and government. SPRF awards involve two years of training under the sponsorship of established scientists and encourage Postdoctoral Fellows to perform independent research. NSF seeks to promote the participation of scientists from all segments of the scientific community, including those from underrepresented groups, in its research programs and activities; the postdoctoral period is considered to be an important level of professional development in attaining this goal. Each Postdoctoral Fellow must address important scientific questions that advance their respective disciplinary fields. Under the sponsorship of Drs. Michael F. Bonner, Chaz Firestone, and Barbara Landau at Johns Hopkins University, this postdoctoral fellowship award supports an early career scientist investigating how the human brain represents visual relations. The world is more than a bag of objects: We see not only individual objects and their features (e.g., a fluffy cat or a textured mat) but also how they relate (a cat sitting ON a mat). Relations are a property holding between objects, beyond any properties the objects have on their own. How do we represent such relations? Although relations themselves cast no light onto our eyes, a growing body of work suggests that relations between objects are extracted in rapid and automatic visual processing, much as we automatically perceive an object's shape or color. Despite this, we have surprisingly little understanding of how the human brain represents such relations. For example, does the visual system automatically extract the structure of relations (distinguishing [mat on cat] from [cat on mat])? And might the brain represent relations and the participating objects (e.g., cat, mat, and ON) in an integrated, "compressed" manner (much like a computer might compress the contents of a file or image)? The proposed research aims to provide answers to these and other questions, using a set of physical relations (e.g., containment, support, adhesion, and fit) as a case study. By integrating methods from the fields of vision science and cognitive computational neuroscience, this research will advance our understanding of how the human brain extracts relational information from visual scenes. This research also has broad implications for understanding perceptual processing of physical relations, which are an unexplored but important domain in STEM education and crucial for scientific understanding, e.g., about physical mechanics (such as the movement of gas particles in a container).

The proposed research combines psychophysical, neuroimaging, and computational modeling approaches to pursue three objectives, aimed at characterizing: (1) what properties of relations are perceived, (2) where relational information is represented in the brain, and (3) how relational structure is computed and represented. We focus on physical relations between objects (e.g., containment ["on"] and support ["in"]), as such relations are central to many other processes in the mind, including physical understanding (e.g., if the mat moves, will the cat too?). In the first objective, we will use rapid perceptual tasks to measure the influence of relational properties on similarity judgment behavior. In the second objective, we will identify which areas of the brain encode visual relational information, by identifying brain regions in which the participating objects (e.g., cat, mat) are encoded in an integrated, non-linear manner (i.e., where relational representations are not well-approximated by simple weighted sums of the representations of the participating objects). In the third objective, we will test the hypothesis that the brain implements a compositional representation of visual relations, by asking whether a model that explicitly encodes relational structure (e.g., mat as Supporter, cat as Supported) can predict neural patterns for novel relational scenes. The proposed research engages a new frontier in scene representation: how the human brain computes high-level information about the relational structure of the world. It also has direct implications for theories of spatial cognition, language, and intuitive physics.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
When you look out at the world, you'll notice different objects and their features, such as a brown dog, a soft cat, or a textured mat. But beyond the individual objects, you may also appreciate how they relate to one another: a dog chasing a cat, or a cat on a mat. Relations such as these are all around us; indeed, they're a fundamental way that we make sense of the scenes that we experience from one moment to the next. How does the mind represent such relations? Whereas how people recognize objects has been the focus of much work in vision science, how people apprehend visual relations has received much less scientific attention.


In this proposal, we explored how the mind represents visual relations and the visual scenes in which they are embedded. We tested the hypothesis that we automatically perceive many relations — much as we see more basic visual properties like colors or shapes without effort — and we sought to characterize this remarkable ability.


First, we investigated how the mind 'builds' representations of relations, such as of a book on a table or a plant on a shelf. Even though it may seem like we 'take in' the visual information from a scene all at once, we tested the possibility that the mind constructs relational representations sequentially. In other words, that it represents one object first, and then the other (in particular. by starting with more physically stable 'reference' objects, like tables and shelves, rather than 'figure' objects, like laptops and plants). Across several studies, we found evidence that this was indeed the case: people were faster to recognize (and had a preference to manually 'compose') scenes starting with reference rather than figure objects.


Second, we made key discoveries about how cognitive systems connect in the mind, using the relational property of 'symmetry' as a test case. Symmetry is ubiquitous in art, physics, and biology, and humans are exquisitely sensitive to visual symmetry. Yet symmetry goes far beyond the visuospatial world. Many words refer to symmetrical concepts (e.g., "equal", "marry"): if x equals y, it entails that y equals x. Is it just a coincidence that symmetry appears in both language and vision? We suspected not. To test this, we presented images of shapes that were symmetrical and non-symmetrical and asked people to choose from a set of words the one that best describes them. We found that people associated symmetrical images with words that have symmetrical meaning. Thus, we demonstrated that vision and language are connected at a deep level, involving abstract and structured representation of relational properties.


Third, we investigated a special kind of visual relation: that of caused state-changes. When the sun melts ice, a pin pops a balloon, or a flame ignites a log or cigarette, this is a change of state. Representing such changes involves representing a relation: how an object at one moment in time is linked to its past or future "self", despite its sometimes dramatically different properties. How does the mind represent state changes? In a series of studies, we found that human memory actively distorts or 'plays forward' such changes (e.g., melting ice): when people observe an object changing, they remember it as more changed (e.g., more melted) than it actually was. Thus, we discovered that the mind relates two states of an object to one another by playing forward the change in memory.


Finally, we investigated how the mind makes sense of our complex visual environment — not only how we perceive and remember visual relations, but how such processes interact when representing complex visual scenes, more generally. Memory is not like a camera: Rather than recording exactly what one sees, the mind may fill in details that were not actually there. A striking example of this memory distortion is boundary extension, whereby observers mistakenly recall a view that extends beyond what was actually seen. What causes this distortion? By exploiting a photographic technique called 'tilt-shift', we created a visual illusion of 'scale change': we made large-scale scenes appear as if they were 'miniature' scenes (like a diorama). In doing so, we discovered that the spatial scale at which the visual environment is viewed has deep consequences for how it is remembered.


Taken together, our work reveals how the mind constructs relational representations in visual scenes, how relational representations in vision 'connect up' with language, and how visual relations (and complex scenes in general) are represented and distorted in memory. Although this project is centered on how the human mind represents visual relations, there are direct implications of this work for understanding how relations are represented outside of vision, including in language. The findings also have implications for how memory represents and distorts complex visual scenes, including the relations embedded in those scenes.

This award was provided as part of NSF’s Social, Behavioral and Economic Sciences Postdoctoral Research Fellowships (SPRF) program. The goal of the SPRF program is to prepare promising, early career doctoral-level scientists for scientific careers in academia, industry or private sector, and government. SPRF awards involve two years of training under the sponsorship of established scientists and encourage Postdoctoral Fellows to perform independent research. NSF seeks to promote the participation of scientists from all segments of the scientific community, including those from underrepresented groups, in its research programs and activities; the postdoctoral period is considered to be an important level of professional development in attaining this goal. Each Postdoctoral Fellow must address important scientific questions that advance their respective disciplinary fields. Under the sponsorship of Drs. Eva Telzer and Keely Muscatell at the University of North Carolina—Chapel Hill, this postdoctoral fellowship award supports an early career scientist in advancing scientific knowledge about associations among racial discrimination, brain development, and self-regulation during adolescence, specifically among youth identifying with marginalized racial and ethnic groups. Additionally, this study investigates family values and school support as protective buffers against the effect of racial discrimination on brain development. The study supported by this award addresses the pressing need within the developmental literature to understand the long-term impact of discrimination on adolescent functioning. The timely and critical societal issue addressed in this study is of broad relevance to scientists, parents, schools, and policymakers. Findings have the potential to identify psychological processes affected by discrimination, cognitive processes that may be targets for interventions aimed at helping adolescents cope with discrimination, and potential mechanisms for social support within the home and the school. Further, this study promotes a greater understanding of the lived experiences of youth from marginalized racial and ethnic groups who are currently underrepresented in research on neurodevelopment. 

Adolescence is a critical period of development wherein the brain undergoes rapid reorganization and in which life experiences are formative to neurodevelopment. The life experiences of youth from minoritized racial and ethnic backgrounds are underrepresented in neurodevelopmental research, despite the fact that children and adolescents represent the most racially and ethnically diverse age group in the United States population. One salient experience among marginalized youth is racial and ethnic discrimination. Despite this critical issue, the effect of discrimination on neural development and implications for subsequent functioning are not well understood. The awarded study addresses these gaps using longitudinal network analysis and graph theoretic methods to identify associations among racial discrimination, neural connectivity, and self-regulatory functioning among youth of color. Further, the study examines familism and school support as protective buffers against the harmful effects of discrimination. To answer these critical questions, the study uses a subsample of youth from minoritized racial and ethnic groups (Asian, Black, and Latinx; n = 5,705) ages 9-10 years at the first assessment and 11-12 years at the last assessment from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study.

This project focused on understanding the short-term effects of racial discrimination experienced by 10-year-old adolescents from minoritized racial and ethnic backgrounds (i.e., Asian, Black, Latinx). The study aimed to explore the association between racial discrimination and two important outcomes: (a) how different parts of the brain communicate (brain network connectivity), and (b) the ability to control thoughts and actions (self-regulation), one year later. Additionally, the study examined the potential protective influence of familism (values related to family closeness and support) and school support. Results revealed that greater experiences of discrimination were associated with increased connectivity between attention networks in the brain and poorer self-regulation. Furthermore, for adolescents reporting low familism, the impact of discrimination on self-regulation was explained by greater connectivity between the brain's attention networks. Overall, findings suggest that discrimination can affect the functioning of the brain's attention networks during adolescence, which may negatively affect adolescents' abilities to engage self-control. However, high levels of familism may offer some protection against these negative effects. 

There are several strengths of this study. First, data were used from a large, nationally-representative dataset with multiple methods of assessment including self-report surveys, a lab-based experiment, and neuroimaging data. Second, a sophisticated analytic model (i.e., longitudinal moderated mediation) was used to address a pressing need within the developmental literature to understand the long-term impact of discrimination on adolescent functioning. This study is one of the first to identify an association between discrimination and brain functioning. Furthermore, this study complements current research by focusing specifically on the experiences of adolescents from minoritized racial and ethnic groups and by identifying environmental strengths that may protect youth from the negative effects of discrimination.

On a broader scale, the findings from this study highlight the importance of addressing discrimination as a societal issue rather than an isolated experience. Understanding the link between discrimination and adolescent brain functioning and self-regulation may fuel advocacy efforts and policy changes aimed at supporting and protecting minoritized youth who have experienced discrimination.

award.abstractText:
This project aims to understand the mechanics of growth and folding of the human brain at the early fetal stages of development. This work will advance the fundamental understanding of the relationship between brain folding, brain connectivity, and brain function. Brain folding provides important information about both normal and abnormal development of the human brain. Currently, the development of folds is based on simple simulation models that do not reflect the complicated structure of the human brain. This research will use advanced brain imaging and innovative computational simulations to elucidate how the human brain grows and folds during the early development of a normal fetal brain. The results of this work will characterize folding in normal brain development.  Future studies may reveal the origin of brain disorders that have structural discrepancies and connectivity disruptions such as autism and schizophrenia. The outcome of this research will promote the progress of health science and benefit national health. In addition to the scientific outcomes, this research will be integrated into a range of educational and outreach programs aimed at attracting underrepresented groups to engineering, improving undergraduate and graduate learning on biomechanics and mechanobiology. 

The overarching objective of this research is to discover the roles of differential tangential growth and neural wiring on the morphogenesis of the developing human brain, and their contributions to the variability and regularity of folding patterns. The research will contribute an in-depth understanding of the underlying mechanism that forms the secondary and tertiary folding patterns in the developing human brain on a comprehensive human brain scale. This research will use an innovative image-based multiscale modeling approach to the simulation of brain development, linking the mechanics at the tissue and organ level with the effect of axonal fiber bundles on the cellular level. The outcomes of this study are expected to fundamentally advance the field of brain folding mechanics and lay a foundation for investigating abnormal brain folding processes for brain disorders.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Understanding how the human brain transforms from a smooth fetal structure into the intricately folded organ that governs thought, sensation, and behavior remains one of the greatest scientific challenges of our time. This transformation is not just a matter of shape; it occurs alongside the development of the brain’s connectivity, the complex network of axonal fibers that link different regions (Figure 1). Our project aimed to uncover the physical and biological mechanisms driving both brain growth and folding, with a special focus on how the brain’s structural wiring develops in tandem with its evolving shape. By combining expertise from mechanical engineering, neuroimaging, computational modeling, and neuroscience, we have made significant advances in this critical field.

Our journey began by creating detailed growth models of the human brain directly from imaging data. We developed the most comprehensive mechanical model to date that captures how the brain grows and folds over time. Unlike previous studies that treated folding as a surface-level phenomenon, our approach integrates multiple scales from cellular components to whole tissue structures, revealing how mechanical forces sculpt the brain’s complex folds. A major breakthrough was our ability to predict not only the formation of the brain’s large folds but also the development of “sulcal pits,” the deepest points within the folds that remain remarkably consistent across individuals and serve as key landmarks in brain development (Figure 2). To support this, we built a computational pipeline that translates fetal MRI scans into personalized mechanical growth models, enabling subject-specific analyses and opening new pathways to investigate how variations in folding patterns relate to neurological disorders.

Building on these models, we connected the mechanics of brain growth and folding with the development of axonal fibers, the microscopic wiring essential for brain function. We formulated the first mechanical theory describing how these fibers grow and navigate within the folding brain, explaining why they tend to cluster on gyri, the ridges, rather than sulci, the valleys (Figure 3). This integrated perspective offers novel insight into the biological and mechanical interplay shaping brain structure, shifting the field from descriptive imaging towards predictive, physics-based understanding.

Beyond advancing fundamental science, our project has had meaningful impacts on education, workforce development, and public engagement. The research findings have been incorporated into graduate and undergraduate courses, enriching biomechanics curricula and equipping the next generation of engineers and neuroscientists with interdisciplinary skills. We also curated a permanent public exhibition at the Roberson Museum of Science and Art in Binghamton, New York, showcasing brain folding patterns and axonal fiber pathways across species (Figure 4). This exhibition has increased public awareness of brain science and inspired interest in STEM among diverse audiences, including K-12 students.

Importantly, our project has promoted diversity and inclusion in STEM by challenging stereotypes about mechanical engineering and encouraging women and underrepresented groups to pursue careers in engineering and neuroscience. Through workshops and presentations, we have reached hundreds of students, fostering an inclusive environment supportive of broad participation in science and technology.

Clinically, our improved understanding of brain folding mechanics and connectivity development provides a foundation for investigating developmental brain disorders such as autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, and polymicrogyria. By uncovering the physical mechanisms underlying normal and abnormal brain development, our work holds promise for informing earlier diagnosis and targeted interventions, ultimately benefiting public health.

To date, the project has produced more than fourteen peer-reviewed publications with additional manuscripts in development. Several conference presentations have disseminated our findings broadly. All generated data, computational pipelines, and codes have been made publicly available. Throughout the project, we trained graduate and undergraduate students in image processing, mechanical modeling, and computational simulations, preparing them for future careers at the intersection of engineering and neuroscience.

Overall, this project has transformed the understanding of brain development by integrating mechanical principles with cutting-edge imaging and computational methods. Its outcomes advance both biomechanics and neuroscience while fostering education, public engagement, and societal well-being.

award.abstractText:
Over the last couple of decades, deep learning approaches have achieved breakthrough performance in a broad range of learning problems from a variety of applications fields such as image recognition, speech recognition, natural language processing and others. Deep learning has also served as the main impetus for the advancement of recent artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. The main goal of this project is to develop new deep neural network (DNN) architectures, computational algorithms and foundational theory for deep learning in complex domains where the data are complex geometric objects.  The underlying geometry of the space will be utilized and exploited for developing the DNNs.  Such development will enable the application of deep learning models in medical imaging, computer vision, computer graphics, recommender systems and neuroscience to learning problems where the inputs are complex images, diffusion matrices, shapes or other geometric objects. In addition, results of the project will be integrated in a course on Geometry and Statistics for undergraduate and graduate students. The principal investigators will also be involved in the research training of students, possibly students from under-represented groups.
 
The main goals of the research program are to develop general deep neural network architectures on manifolds and take some major steps toward understanding their theoretical foundations. Specifically, this project will (1) develop extrinsic deep neural networks (eDNNs) on manifolds by generalizing the popular feedforward neural networks in the Euclidean space to manifolds utilizing equivariant embeddings; (2) develop intrinsic deep neural networks (iDNNs) on manifolds employing a Riemannian structure of the manifold; (3) develop general retraction-based convolutional neural networks (RCNNs) on manifolds; (4) characterize theoretical properties of eDNNs, iDNNs and RCNNs on manifolds by studying their approximation properties as well as the estimation error for a class of empirical risk minimizers over the DNN class on manifolds; and (5) develop user-friendly software packages that can be readily used by the practitioners. The research program explores the interface among geometry, statistics and machine learning, and aims to broaden the paradigm of deep learning by extending geometric deep learning to manifolds.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Throughout the funding period of this award, the PIs  (PIs Lin, Nguyen and Xu) have developed new deep learning architectures  on general manifolds and applied them to learning tasks such as regression and classification analysis on manifolds.  More specifically, new extrinsic and intrinsic deep learning frameworks have been proposed, with the former employs equivariant embedding  by constructing deep learning architectures on the image manifold after embedding while the latter employs  the Riemannian geometry of the  manifold in developing new deep learning tools. Theoretical properties of the estimators under these models have been thoroughly studied leading to foundational understanding of deep neural network models on manifolds.   The developed methods can be broadly applied to medical imaging analysis where the manifold-valued data are prevalent. 


The research development under the project can lead to broader society benefits by making available tools and algorithms that can be used for analyzing complex data such as medical imaging data which  are prevalent neuroimaging. Such as algorithms  for example can lead to better predictions and classifications for diagnosis purposes. 

 

In addition to research outputs that have led to a few publications and several currently under review, the PIs have trained four Ph.D students  and two postdocs  during the  funding period.

award.abstractText:
To understand how the brain functions and cure brain disorders, neuroscientists and clinicians need brain mapping devices.  This project will develop the next generation of stretchable and transparent electrode arrays with unprecedented scale and resolution for brain recording and stimulation. This program will not only generate broad impacts in neuroscience through proactive device translation efforts in and beyond this project, but also create unique opportunities for novel neuroprosthetics. Through generating neural interfaces that will allow human-like performance in neuroprosthetic limbs and retinal prostheses with chronic biocompatibility, this program will impact more than 3 million people in the U.S. who live with upper limb loss, paralysis due to tetraplegia, blindness due to retinitis pigmentosa, or epilepsy. The proposed multidisciplinary educational/outreach program will engage hundreds of students through research experiences for underrepresented K-12 students, active undergraduate research involvements, graduate leadership training in device translation, and augmented engineering curricula.

The research objective of this project is to investigate a set of foundational materials and device problems to for the first time establish a new unique device technology "multifunctional nanomesh microelectrodes" to shift the current paradigm of neural interface from rigid, opaque neuroelectrode arrays towards ultrasoft and transparent ones.  Stretchable and transparent neuroelectrode arrays are two emerging neural interfaces due to their chronic biocompatibility and multimodal compatibility, respectively. However, both systems are currently confounded by their scalability since fundamentally, no existing electrode materials can simultaneously provide the required system-level properties of electrochemical interfaces, electrical conductance, and chronic biocompatibility in addition to the mandatory mechanical stretchability or optical transparency. Based on strong preliminary results, the PI hypothesizes that multifunctional nanomesh microelectrodes can possess an unprecedented combination of all functionalities needed for this aforementioned paradigm shift including low impedance, large stretchability, high transparency, and chronic biocompatibility. This project will holistically test this hypothesis through innovative theoretical design, experimental realization, and system demonstration/validation, and proactively integrate closed-loop device translation and experiential education activities.  Vertically, the unprecedented combination of large throughput, chronic biocompatibility and multimodal compatibility of the resulting neural interface device will yield profound impacts to both our studying of complex networks in the central nervous system and interfacing with the brain. Laterally, the multifunctional-nanomesh device concept, theoretical framework, and fabrication knowledge can also be transformative in many other fields such as optoelectronics, energy storage, and nanogenerators if stretchability and/or transparency are desired.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Intellectual Merit: This project advanced the scientific foundations and technological capabilities of soft, multimodal bioelectronic materials and devices capable of chronic, high-fidelity integration with neural and physiological systems. The core innovation lay in developing a new class of flexible, stretchable neuroelectronic platforms that combined multimodal sensing-including electrical, mechanical, and electrochemical modalities-into a single, biocompatible material system. Over the life of the project, our team produced 10 peer-reviewed publications (including Advanced Materials, Nature Communications, and Biosensors and Bioelectronics), delivered 18 invited talks, and filed 3 patent disclosures. These outcomes significantly advance the state of the art in soft neuroelectronics, behavioral neuroscience tools, and multimodal physiological sensing. Key research highlights include: (1) Development of Nanomesh-Based Neural Interfaces: We engineered elastic, nanomesh electronics that provide cellular-resolution interfacing with the brain surface and studied their structure-property relationship. These devices exhibited submicron-level feature uniformity, mechanical properties that match cortical tissue, and robust signal quality for chronic recording. This work represents a step forward in conformal neural interface technology. (2) Electrochemical Uniformity in PEDOT:PSS Coating: We demonstrated an array-wide uniform potentiostatic deposition of PEDOT:PSS on multichannel microelectrodes, ensuring consistent impedance reduction across high-density electrode arrays. This method offers scalable and reliable performance for electrical recording and stimulation. (3) Mechanistic Study of Neural Probe Insertion: We investigated failure modes in soft probe insertion into brain-like hydrogels and identified critical thresholds for buckling, fracture, and tip deformation. This insight has direct implications for minimizing surgical damage. And (4) Crosstalk in Polymer Microelectrode Arrays: We performed a seminal analysis of the crosstalk between two adjacent polymer microelectrodes experimentally and through modeling. In addition to standardizing neural electrode array crosstalk characterization, this study not only reveals the dependence of the crosstalk in polymer microelectrode arrays on a variety of key device parameters but also provides general guidelines for the design of thin polymer microelectrode arrays for high-quality neural signal recording.

Broader Impacts: This project has important translational and societal implications. By developing soft and multimodal bioelectronic systems, we contribute to next-generation brain-computer interfaces, neurotherapeutic platforms, and continuous health monitoring technologies. These innovations are foundational to fundamental neuroscience, personalized medicine, and closed-loop neuroprosthetic interventions. Our education and training activities spanned high school through postdoctoral levels. This highly interdisciplinary project has particularly provided comprehensive training for students. Significantly, six Ph.D. students in the PI's group were supported by this project, and to date, three have graduated. They received interdisciplinary training in electrode array design, microfabrication, electrochemistry, materials and device characterization, and neural engineering. After graduation, one student joined a neurotechnology start-up in California, while two students became postdoctoral research fellows in the U.S., continuing in the neural device field. PI Fang also incorporated some fundamental knowledge from this project and recent breakthroughs in neuroelectronics in his teaching. In particular, the PI has transformed his previous materials and device training and recent neural engineering application practice into the development of a new graduate-level course at Dartmouth, ENGS 127 Bioelectronics, which introduces the fundamentals and applications of micro-and nano-technology-based bioelectronics. Finally, the nanomesh electrode arrays developed in this project are now enabling new investigations in collaborating labs, for instance, to discover neuronal firing patterns underlying anesthetic-induced slow waves. In summary, this project not only produced cutting-edge technological advances in brain-interfacing materials and devices but also created bioelectronic educational pipelines and translational pathways that will have long-term impacts on both scientific and societal levels.

award.abstractText:
Multivariate functional data, where continuous observations are sampled from multiple processes, are emerging in a wide range of scientific applications. A central problem in analyzing multivariate functional data is to understand the interdependency among the functions. This can be formulated as the problem of graphical modeling of multivariate functions. The majority of existing solutions, however, focus on random variables, and extension to random functions is far from trivial. This project is developing a class of novel statistical methods and associated theory for functional graphical modeling. This research is timely in that it responds to the growing demand for functional data analysis, and is expected to advance numerous biological and medical research areas, including the analyses of brain connectivity networks, gene regulatory networks, and protein-protein interaction networks. 

This project is studying three sets of problems: (1) nonparametric functional graphical modeling, which relaxes the Gaussian distribution or the linear structural assumptions, and avoids the curse of dimensionality and works for large graphs; (2) functional directed acyclic graphical modeling, which combines directed graph and functional graph, and offers a tractable solution for inferring directional dependency among multivariate functions; and (3) conditional and dynamic functional graphical modeling, which models graph that varies continuously with one or multiple external variables such as time. At the heart of its development is linear-operator-based statistical learning, which provides a highly flexible and efficient platform to handle massive and complex functional data. The accompanying estimation algorithms and asymptotic theory also make useful additions to the toolbox of multiple fields, including functional data analysis, network and graphical modeling, and statistical machine learning.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project created new statistical tools to help scientists analyze complex functional data that take the form of signals, curves, or images rather than single numbers. Such functional data are increasingly common in fields like neuroscience, biology, and public health. The central goal was to develop practical and theoretically sound methods for understanding how multiple functional signals interact and form networks.

(1) On the intellectual merit side, the project developed new methods for modeling relationships among multivariate functional data, including nonparametric models, models that capture directional influence, and models that describe how networks evolve over time or with external conditions. These advances fill major gaps in the existing statistical literature. The project also provided new theoretical foundations for operator-based statistical learning, supporting the analysis of large and complex datasets. Across the four-year period, the research generated 35 peer-reviewed publications in leading journals, demonstrating strong scientific productivity and impact.

(2) Regarding broader impacts, the project offers practical tools that can be used in many scientific areas, especially neuroimaging studies of brain connectivity in aging and neurological diseases. The research supported active collaborations with neuroscientists and contributed methods that can help analyze Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease imaging data. The project also played a significant role in education by mentoring graduate students in both statistics and neuroscience and incorporating new research findings into teaching.

(3) Overall, this award produced a set of flexible, scalable statistical methods for analyzing complex functional data; strengthened interdisciplinary collaborations; and contributed to training the next generation of data scientists. The outcomes advance both theoretical statistics and applied scientific research.

award.abstractText:
This work will generate new scientific knowledge about how concussion occurs in the brain. Concussion is caused by impact to the head that deforms the brain. Computational models of head injury are used to study how and where the brain deforms, and how the deformation leads to concussion. Many injury models exist to study deformation of the whole brain, or the deformation of an individual axon (nerve fiber).  However, these models have not been unified to study how whole brain deformation translates down to the axonal level. This award supports research to unify brain injury models at the large, medium, and small scales.  The unified models will then be used to study brain deformations at all scales caused by real-world head impact. This process will enable a comprehensive understanding of how a head impact causes injury. In the future, the results of this work may help correlate head impact with concussion symptoms and neuroimaging findings. The comprehensive understanding of how concussion occurs within the brain can be used to design better head protective gear, improve diagnosis of concussion, and support more precise treatment plans. Therefore, results from this award will benefit the U.S. society and eventually improve human health. Finally, this research will help broaden participation of underrepresented groups in research and positively impact engineering education.


Concussion occurs across the length scales of the brain. Current brain injury models focus on either the whole brain or an individual axon. However, little is known about how impact-induced brain deformation is transmitted through the length scales in specific regions of the brain. This research will fill the knowledge gap on the energy transmission process of external head impact at the macro, meso, and microscales. It will develop detailed injury models in key vulnerable brain regions. A microscale injury model will also be developed capable of adapting to local geometry. These organ-to-cell models will then be unified through a multiscale modeling framework to provide a comprehensive understanding of the biomechanical mechanism of concussion across the length scales.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project advanced understanding of how brain strains, a key metric to assess the likelihood of concussions — mild traumatic brain injuries — develop from head impacts down to cellular damage in an individual axon. Concussions are common in sports, military service, and accidents, yet predicting who will be injured and why remains challenging.

We created a multi-scale computational modeling framework that links brain injury processes across three levels:

  1. Tissue level (“meso-scale”) – Using advanced high-order finite element methods, we modeled detailed anatomical features such as the interface between gray and white matter, where tissue properties change abruptly and injury risk could be elavated.
  2. Cellular fiber level (“micro-scale”) – We built realistic models of axons, the long fibers that transmit electrical signals. These simulations revealed that female axons are mechanically more vulnerable to injury than male axons under the same conditions, suggesting biological factors in concussion susceptibility.
  3. Whole-brain level (“macro-scale”) – We developed a computational pipeline that converts real-world head impact data into whole-brain strain, then meso-scale strain at tissue interfaces, and finally axonal strain predictions.

Key findings:

  • Fine-scale anatomical detail changes predicted strain patterns compared to uniform brain models.
  • The gray–white matter interface introduces strain redistribution during impacts, making the region more vulnerable.
  • Female axons show higher vulnerability to mechanical injury in simulations.
  • The new pipeline links external impacts directly to multi-scale brain strain predictions.

Broader impacts:

  • The framework can inform helmet and protective headgear designs to reduce damaging strain concentrations.
  • Graduate and undergraduate students gained skills in biomechanics, neuroscience, and computational modeling.
  • Modeling methods and datasets were shared with the research community to advance brain injury prevention.
  • Outreach included presentations to local STEM students, promoting awareness of concussion science and brain health.

By unifying organ-, tissue-, and cell-scale models, and identifying sex-specific injury vulnerabilities, this work provides a foundation for more effective and personalized strategies for concussion detection and prevention.

award.abstractText:
From smart homes to smart cars and highways, and from smart health to precision agriculture, emerging technologies will soon demand ubiquitous connectivity for billions of wireless devices. The demand for more spectrum has finally started to outweigh resistance to spectrum reuse. There is currently strong impetus for introducing innovative spectrum sharing modalities that enable improved spectrum utilization and seamless cohabitation, without requiring tight coordination across legacy, scientific, government, military, and commercial users. Spectrum underlay is a promising paradigm towards this end. It provisions secondary transmissions that operate without disturbing the primary user. Practical means of accomplishing this without requiring tight coordination between the primary and the secondary system have remained elusive, however. This project develops practical spectrum underlay solutions which enable reliable secondary communication in scenarios where this would otherwise seem untenable: without primary-secondary coordination or channel state information, under potentially strong and time-varying interference from the primary system. The scope of potential applications includes Internet of Things (IoT), vehicular, and local area (e.g., WiFi) networks in congested spectrum areas.

Ensuring United States leadership in spectrum research, technologies, and commercial/scientific applications requires investments in spectrum sharing innovations and developing a well-educated and diverse spectrum workforce. This projects makes contributions towards both of these goals. The proposed research builds upon the principal investigator's prior work on statistical signal processing, machine learning, and matrix theory, as well as practical communications engineering -- an ideal combination to educate and engage diverse graduate and undergraduate students on the board and in the lab. The research will develop state-of-the-art theory and engineering solutions geared towards practical implementation. The scope of the work includes the following synergistic components, organized in five thrusts: T1) Incorporating finite alphabet and error control coding constraints into the basic algebraic framework. T2) Developing multi-access and random interleaving solutions to ``orthogonalize'' multiple secondary transmissions in multiuser settings. T3) Analyzing performance under fading scenarios, with adaptive modulation and coding. T4) Addressing key engineering issues, namely, secondary user synchronization and analog-to-digital conversion, which are challenging when the secondary signal is much weaker than the interfering primary signal. T5) Developing a software radio testbed and conducting experiments to validate the proposed solutions.
