award.abstractText:
Despite thousands of investigations on the neural basis of individual behaviors and even more studies on collective behaviors, a clear bridge between the organization of individual brains and their combinational impact on group behaviors, such as cooperation and conflict and ultimately collective action, is lacking. To address the grand challenge of inferring group cooperation from the functional neuroarchitecture of individual brains, this project will harness advances in data, experiment and computation. Specifically, it will integrate, for the first time, existing large-scale human functional neuroimaging data, prospectively collected individual and group behavioral data from a large cohort, with cutting-edge machine learning tools, hierarchical models and large-scale simulations. This is a collaborative effort between a team of neuroscientists, social scientists and data scientists, that aims to elucidate the neural basis of cooperation, a fundamental process in a functioning society and at the core of social environments. 

The project will first harness the combined wealth of existing neuroimaging and behavioral data from large-scale studies, including the Human Connectome-Lifespan (HCP-L) and the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) and will leverage recent breakthroughs in machine learning to characterize the diversity, individuality and commonality of neural circuits (the connectome) supporting cognitive function across the lifespan. It will then conduct large-scale (~10,000 individuals) online behavioral experiments to identify connections between individual behaviors, decisions and group behaviors during a Public Goods Game. The experiments will measure individual proclivity towards cooperation and the social welfare obtained by cooperation, leading to potentially transformative insights into the emergence of cooperation within groups via individual behaviors. The resulting first-of-its-kind dataset may become a very valuable resource to the research community. Large-scale simulations based on statistical models estimated from this and the assembled neuroimaging datasets will then assess the direct or indirect relationships between individual connectomes and cooperation in group settings, and will elucidate the role of group processes in amplifying or ameliorating individual differences towards collective outcomes. Findings from this project may have a transformative impact on the scientific community's currently incomplete understanding of how individual brains shape societal behavior via cognitive, social, and interactive mechanisms.

This project is part of the National Science Foundation's Harnessing the Data Revolution (HDR) Big Idea activity.

award.projectOutComesReport:
In this project, we investigated the association between cooperation and inhibitory control. Cooperation describes behaviors that involve paying costs to benefit others. Inhibitory control describes behaviors that involve using executive function to override automatic impulses. To investigate the connection between these two types of behaviors, we recruited a large number of Americans to complete an experiment in which they performed a variety of inhibitory control tasks as well as making choices about how to cooperate in both one-shot and repeated cooperative situations involving real monetary payoffs. We found evidence that people with greater inhibitory control were more inclined to cooperate across a range of cooperative settings. The only exception was situations in which one’s partner had chosen not to cooperate previously – in this case, where reciprocity would prescribe not cooperating oneself, inhibitory control was not robustly associated with cooperation. These findings help advance our understanding of cooperation, which is a cornerstone of human societies and social interactions. Our findings also contribute to the broader topic of inhibitory control and self-regulation, as we also found substantial variation across different measures of inhibitory control in their associations with cooperation (and with other factors). This observation emphasizes the complexity of inhibitory control as a phenomenon, and the importance of the specifics of which measures are used to understand inhibitory control.

award.abstractText:
The natural world is rich with patterns, and organisms learn these patterns through passive exposure. This presents a powerful and flexible means of learning about the world that does not involve explicit instruction that appears to play an important role in spoken language learning. However, not all patterns can be learned by passive exposure alone. This research project investigates how learning across patterns of experience proceeds when passive exposure is insufficient to drive learning and yet there is no explicit instruction. The prior work that this project builds on suggests that real-world statistical learning may capitalize on input regularities’ global temporal alignment with behaviorally-relevant actions and events to hasten learning. Learning across statistical regularities can be incidental, and not overtly driven by an intention to learn, while still taking place in the context of an active task that generates valuable predictions and rewarding outcomes. This perspective may be transformative in how we think about human learning of statistically-structured input in complex, naturalistic environments.  Findings from this research will inform the design of  learning interventions that capitalize on these learning principles to be useful for diverse communities of learners. 

The proposed research will advance a new research approach, empirical tests of mechanistic predictions, and complementary information from behavior, electrophysiology and functional magnetic resonance imaging to understand statistical learning under more natural circumstances involving interplay among active behavior, multimodal input, selective attention, and statistical input regularities. It pursues the twin hypotheses that (1) active engagement in a rich, environment can support statistical learning by virtue of loose temporal alignment of statistically-structured input with behaviorally-relevant actions, objects, and events and (2) that this incidental statistical learning drives the emergence of selective attention to behaviorally relevant regularities, creating a virtuous cycle that promotes later learning. The team will also conduct several outreach activities including collecting data from non-university samples via a “data-truck” and providing science of learning outreach to high school students.

award.abstractText:
This project aims to identify disease-specific changes in human brain connectivity in early stages by developing a novel Deep Learning framework applicable to data with arbitrary structure such as graphs. This is important because regional brain variations often do not manifest as cognitive changes until significant brain pathology has accumulated, and a better understanding of the brain may be possible by characterizing changes in connectivity defined by relationships between different brain regions. Recent techniques with Deep Learning have demonstrated successful results with human-level precision in various image analysis tasks such as image classification, object detection, and image segmentation, but they cannot be directly applied to analyze brain connectivity because of its arbitrary structure. The key is to derive effective representation of the data; however, it is still unclear how to derive sophisticated representations for complex data such as graphs and it often requires large-scale datasets. A novel Graph Deep Learning technique that can detect subtle changes in brain connectivity with small numbers of samples is therefore necessary. Success of this project will facilitate understanding of the relationship between brain connectivity and neurodegenerative disease, mechanisms for early diagnosis, and discovery of new treatments. 

Technically, the overarching goal of this project is to design a Convolution Neural Network (CNN) model for graph data and to determine the extent to which it yields new scientific findings in neuroscience. To meet the goal, this project will focus on: 1) Developing a novel transform for graphs (e.g., brain networks) for their novel multi-resolution representations that are theoretically described by convolution, 2) Developing an efficient deep learning architecture for graphs that operates within a small sample-size regime to improve performance of disease diagnosis and sensitivity of statistical inferences, and 3) Validating the developed models on a simulation study as well as real brain network datasets for Alzheimer’s Disease to characterize disease-specific patterns in the brain connectivity. The developed framework will benefit various areas of neuroimaging research with functional and structural brain connectivity that are locally carried at small scales, and spur development of further studies.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Objectives: The primary objective of this project was to advance graph machine learning methodologies, where a graph is an object that consists of nodes and edges. We proposed to develop novel multi-resolution graph representations that capture complex and arbitrary but distinctive patterns from a population of graphs. As a practical application, this project specifically focused on analyzing brain networks for Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) where the brain is parcellated into several anatomical regions of interest (ROI) and a graph is constructed by structural/functional interaction between the ROIs. By analyzing the connectomic features of brain networks, we expect to aid early diagnosis and simulate the progression of AD.

Project Outcomes:

1. Advanced Graph Learning Models: The project introduced novel machine learning methods specifically designed for graph data. The method utilizes the concept of “multi-resolution” to investigate graph data and finds the optimal resolution and corresponding parameters to successfully perform certain tasks, such as brain network classification for AD and generation of realistic graphs. Several papers were published at top-tier AI conferences and journals with this topic:

○      "Learning to Approximate Adaptive Kernel Convolution on Graphs" (AAAI 2024): Developed an adaptive kernel convolution method for modeling heterogeneous graph structures in brain networks.

○      "Multi-resolution Spectral Coherence for Graph Generation with Score-based Diffusion" (NeurIPS 2023): Proposed a method preserving multi-scale information for realistic brain connectivity graph generation.

○      "Dynamic Covariance Estimation via Predictive Wishart Process with an Application on Brain Connectivity Estimation" (CSDA 2023): Improved robustness in connectivity analysis using dynamic covariance modeling.

○      "Learning Multi-resolution Graph Edge Embedding for Discovering Brain Network Dysfunction in Neurological Disorders" (IPMI 2021): Developed the first multi-resolution graph edge learning representation with applications to analyze brain network data for AD and ADHD.

○      "Covariate Correcting Networks for Identifying Associations between Socioeconomic Factors and Brain Outcomes in Children" (MICCAI 2021): Disentangled external covariates from brain data for unbiased neuroimaging studies.

2. Longitudinal Alzheimer’s Disease Analysis: AD progression necessitates models handling temporal data. Significant advances were made in longitudinal brain connectome analysis to investigate the disease trajectory and how specific risk factors of AD affect the temporal variation in the brain.

○      "Mixing Temporal Graphs with MLP for Longitudinal Brain Connectome Analysis" (MICCAI 2023): Improved longitudinal brain data analysis by integrating temporal dynamics into graph representations.

○      "Disentangled Sequential Graph Autoencoder for Preclinical Alzheimer’s Disease Characterizations" (MICCAI 2021): Captured progression patterns in preclinical AD stages using disentangled representations.

3. Multi-modal Missing Measure Imputation: Addressed challenges of missing data with multi-modality.

○      "Modality-Agnostic Style Transfer for Holistic Feature Imputation" (ISBI 2024): Introduced a style-transfer approach for imputing missing neuroimaging data across different modalities.

○      “OCL: Ordinal Contrastive Learning for Imputating Features with Progressive Labels” (MICCAI 2024):  Utilized prior knowledge of ordinal disease spectrum to achieve effective data embedding and decoding missing measure generation.

Educational and Collaborative Contributions: The project fostered interdisciplinary collaboration among computer scientists, statisticians, neuroscientists, and clinicians. Graduate students gained experience in developing cutting-edge techniques and running experiments that lead to scientific discovery. The students contributed to high-impact research and publications in top-tier venues, and those who benefited from this project ended up with research and software developer positions in well-known places such as Genentech, Walmart/Sam’s Club Research, Mastercard, etc.

Intellectual Merit: This project significantly advanced the field of graph machine learning by addressing challenges in analyzing complex graph data with practical application in analyzing AD. By developing novel multi-resolution algorithms, it improved insights in investigating graph data in multi-resolution views to interpret brain networks with unprecedented accuracy and scalability. These methods offer the potential for widespread application in computational neuroscience and other fields requiring sophisticated graph analytics.

Broader Impacts: The societal impact of this research lies in its potential to transform the early diagnosis and understanding of Alzheimer’s Disease, a growing public health challenge. By providing tools to understand and monitor brain connectivity changes, the project contributes to developing personalized treatment strategies. Educationally, the project opened several  opportunities for graduate students to become experts on cutting-edge machine learning methodologies and their applications to neuroscience, fostering highly intellectual researchers equipped to tackle problems from interdisciplinary domains.

Scientific and Societal Impact: This project highlights the transformative potential of combining advanced machine learning techniques with neuroscientific inquiry, setting the stage for continued innovation in brain connectivity analysis. Scientifically, it provided tools to decode brain network structures, offering far more sophisticated insights into Alzheimer’s Disease progression in brain connectivity. Societally, these advancements contribute to early diagnosis and personalized treatment strategies, addressing a critical challenge in public health.

award.abstractText:
This project seeks to serve the national interest in excellent undergraduate STEM education by providing a model to enhance equity for students in general chemistry courses. Previous studies have shown that remediation and deficit-based approaches to supplemental general chemistry instruction do not provide significant long-term benefits to students.  This lack of impact is particularly noticeable for students in groups underrepresented in STEM. This project will develop and study a novel asset-based supplemental course that leverages the students’ many strengths to help them succeed in general chemistry. This one-credit supplemental chemistry course will run alongside the General Chemistry I course.  Students who are at risk of failing the general chemistry course will be invited to participate. The new supplemental course will seek to support student success by providing opportunities to practice key skills needed for success in general chemistry, such as mathematical and study skills.  It will simultaneously recognize and rely on strengths that students have developed in other areas of their lives, to channel these strengths toward their own and each other's academic success in chemistry. The intended project outcomes include reducing failure rates in General Chemistry I, characterizing the asset-based supplemental chemistry course, and developing resources to support replication of the course by other institutions. The research goal is to contribute to understanding how and why at-risk students at a diverse university can succeed in general chemistry, and the role of the institution in supporting this success.

This project will develop and study an asset-based supplemental chemistry course for students at risk of attrition from General Chemistry at the University of Massachusetts Boston, a public, urban, primarily commuter campus with an undergraduate population that is among the country’s most diverse. Design of the supplemental course will follow an asset model based on activity theory, with four design principles: (a) adopt the perspective of the student; (b) provide structure that lowers the activation barrier for students to increase their agency; (c) encourage collaborative and social engagement in culturally and personally relevant activity; and (d) support dialogue, chemical literacy, and resourcefulness. The impact of the course will be studied using a mixed methods approach based on the Anti-Deficit Achievement Framework for Research on Students of Color in STEM, and will address the following research questions: (1) Which elements of the supplemental course design are productive in supporting student success in general chemistry, and how so? (2) What are the lasting impacts of the intervention on student success in academic work for two semesters beyond general chemistry? (3) How does the University's system of supports function toward participants' negotiation of challenges and cultivation of meaningful relationships that support their academic success? and (4) How do the experiential realities of the supplemental chemistry students empower them to succeed as they intersect with the processes of support that surround them in the course, at the university, and in their lives? Student interviews and counter narratives will be the primary data sources to understand student success and experiences. These data will be supplemented by instructor diaries as well as interviews with faculty and staff involved in institutional support, including instructors, advising staff, and care counselors. The project’s success will be assessed through cycles of questioning and review by an external advisory board. Through two cycles of implementation improvements and one year of fidelity testing, the research will define the critical components of the course that relate to its successful implementation in the context of a highly diverse university. Products developed by the project will include modules that may be adapted by other higher education institutions, a facilitation guide for instructors, and resources for undergraduate learning assistants.  This project is supported by the NSF IUSE: EHR Program, which supports research and development projects to improve the effectiveness of STEM education for all students.  Through the Engaged Student Learning track, the program supports the creation, exploration, and implementation of promising practices and tools.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project developed and studied an asset-based supplemental chemistry course for students at risk of attrition from General Chemistry 1 (GC1). The design of the course followed an asset model based on activity theory, and the research design and methods aligned with the sociocultural underpinnings of activity theory. Students enrolled in GC1 were invited to enroll in the supplemental course at the beginning of the semester if they were determined to have a high likelihood (e.g., >50%) of a DFW outcome in GC1, based on three factors that were determined to be predictive based on prior years data: high school or transfer college GPA, course grade in the most recent math course taken, and whether retaking GC1.

The research focused on the impacts on student outcomes in GC1 due to participation in the supplemental course using a causal comparative design (quantitative study) of six semesters of data, and the structure and function of the intervention (qualitative study) based on counternarrative interviews of supplemental course participants from five semesters supplemented by observations of the classes and instructor diaries. The quantitative study examined three comparison groups: students who participated in the intervention, students who were invited/eligible but did not participate, and students who were not eligible. The study revealed that the combination of participating in the asset-based supplemental course and using a non-traditional, context-based, student-centered curriculum in GC1 resulted in GC1 grade outcomes for students in the supplemental course that were not statistically different from students who were not invited to the supplemental course. Examination of outcomes in GC2 revealed that how many total credits students were enrolled in during the semester they were in GC1 provided differential inoculation against DFW outcomes in GC2. The qualitative study revealed that six critical components of the supplemental course bolstered the success of students in general chemistry: (1) instructors who were supportive, nurturing, welcoming, and available; (2) multimodal activities; (3) having near-peers as instructors and mentors; (4) inclusion of study strategies alongside content learning; (5) collaborative activities; and (6) small class size.

The quantitative study was published as open access in the Journal of the American Chemical Society Au, and is the fourth chemistry education research article ever to be published in JACS. The supporting information attached to the JACS paper includes an example semester of instructional materials and instructor resources. The qualitative study has been completed and will be published as well. In addition to publications, findings from the study were disseminated in multiple ways, including conference papers and posters, as well as research seminars presented to chemistry departments at many universities. Throughout the project, 11 chemistry graduate students taught sections of the supplemental course, and 22 undergraduate students were learning assistants in the supplemental course sections. From fall 2020 through spring 2024, a total of 336 students enrolled in the asset-based supplemental chemistry course.

award.abstractText:
Sleep represents one third of everyone’s life and affects the quality and the health of everyone’s life. Traditionally, long-term characteristics of sleep patterns (sleep phenotypes) are largely unknown due to the lack of convenient monitoring devices and automatic algorithms.  Recently, massive health sensing data such as activity data, electroencephalogram, respiratory monitoring data and electrocardiography are being collected in clinics and at home, which brings unprecedented opportunities for understanding sleep phenotypes outside clinics. However, there are tremendous challenges to translate these noisy and unreliable multimodal sensing data into accurate phenotypes such as sleep stages and apnea events. Beyond sleep, many neurological conditions such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s all expect objective tracking of long-term disease progression, which is currently impossible. This project will provide the computational capability to conduct phenotype tracking at home with the focus on sleep phenotypes. Machine learning methods and software will be developed to conduct accurate phenotyping of sleep with minimal effort on sensor instrumentation, data collection and analysis. 


This project aims at developing DeepSense, a deep learning toolbox to model massive data streams including in-clinic monitoring data such as polysomnography and novel radio frequency signals from a wireless sensing device. The research team will develop accurate deep learning methods to automate sleep monitoring using polysomnography data. They will invent adversarial deep learning methods for modeling radio frequency  signals and leverage large historical polysomnography data to help improve models for radio frequency signals. They will develop interpretable models that leverage and expand medical knowledge on sleep phenotypes. Finally, all the proposed models will be validated through a prospective study with a goal of automating manual sleep studies and assessing the feasibility of sleep studies via radio frequency signal data. The research team plans to release the open-source software and large datasets from this project that can benefit computer science, engineering and medical community.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The Deep Sense project, titled "SCH:INT: Collaborative Research: Deep Sense: Interpretable Deep Learning for Zero-effort Phenotype Sensing and Its Application to Sleep Medicine," aimed to revolutionize the way we understand and treat sleep-related health issues by developing innovative, contactless, and interpretable deep learning models. The project ran from October 2020 to September 2024 and was a collaborative effort involving the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, MIT, and Harvard Medical School. It focused on the intersection of artificial intelligence, sleep medicine, and wireless sensing technologies.

One of the primary achievements of the project was the development of deep learning algorithms to automate the analysis of sleep data collected through standard polysomnography (PSG) and radio frequency (RF) signals. These methods successfully created accurate automation models that reduced the workload for clinicians by providing reliable sleep staging and apnea detection. The RF-based sleep monitoring approach introduced a novel, contactless way to conduct sleep studies, which could greatly benefit home-based sleep diagnostics. This has the potential to make sleep health assessments more accessible, especially for populations unable to easily attend clinical sleep centers.

The project's models achieved high accuracy in sleep staging (80.5%) using RF signals, comparable to the agreement between different human experts. Furthermore, the models demonstrated equitable performance across different demographics, including variations in race, sex, and age. They also successfully detected sleep apnea (achieving an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve of 0.89) and provided accurate measures of the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (Intraclass Correlation Coefficient of 0.90). The robustness of the models across a range of health conditions—including respiratory, cardiovascular, immune, and neurological diseases—highlights the broad applicability of this technology.

The project also made significant strides in training the next generation of researchers. It provided interdisciplinary training for PhD students and postdoctoral researchers across the participating institutions, fostering expertise in AI-driven healthcare solutions, non-invasive monitoring technologies, and clinical research. Students and researchers gained hands-on experience in machine learning for healthcare applications, resulting in a number of high-impact publications and presentations.

The research findings were widely disseminated, with eight peer-reviewed articles published in prestigious journals such as Sleep, Neurology Clinical Practice, JMIR AI, and Scientific Reports and top AI conferences such as NeurIPS. The project also emphasized open access, making the findings available to both academic and clinical communities to ensure the broadest possible impact.

Overall, the Deep Sense project has demonstrated significant advancements in sleep medicine and artificial intelligence, providing new tools for non-contact health monitoring and contributing valuable insights into the relationship between sleep and various health conditions. These findings are expected to foster further research and development in non-invasive health monitoring and personalized medicine, ultimately improving healthcare accessibility and quality.

This Project Outcomes Report for the General Public is displayed verbatim as submitted by the Principal Investigator (PI) for this award. Any opinions, findings, and conclusions or recommendations expressed in this Report are those of the PI and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Science Foundation; NSF has not approved or endorsed its content.

award.abstractText:
Smart services are deeply embedded in modern cities aiming to enhance various aspects of citizens' lives, including safety, wellness, and quality of life. Examples include intelligent traffic control and air quality control. Given these services, monitoring a city's safety and performance collectively is crucial, yet also challenging due to many potential conflicts among the number increasing of services deployed. Researchers have accumulated abundant knowledge on how to design these services independently. However, underlying expected or unexpected couplings among services due to complex interactions of social and physical activities are under-explored, which leads to potential service conflicts. Developing approaches of reducing conflicts is essential for ensuring social inclusion and equity of city services because when conflicts occur, their impacts are likely to be concentrated in some sub-communities (e.g., specific geographic locations, specific user groups like patients with respiratory illness, etc.) meaning that some citizens will experience lower quality services than others due to the diversity. Put differently, service conflicts contribute to a digital divide in service provision.

The key intellectual merit of the proposed project is the development of a socially aware conflict management theory and its deployment for smart cities, consisting of 5 sequential components as follows. (1) a novel, template-based requirements specification component/tool that integrates social and technical requirements to formally define a conflict; (2) a social diversity aware detection approach that utilizes machine learning and conflict correlations to detect conflicts in practice; (3) a multi-objective yet equity-centric resolution method that accounts for socially acceptable trade-offs, behavioral models, and control theory to resolve existing conflicts; (4) a participant-based conflict prevention solution that employs Game Theory and Reinforcement Learning in a scalable, decentralize fashion to prevent future conflicts; (5) a social intervention approach based on education outreach and professional training to disseminate the proposed technology to empower the community. The real-world implementation of this theory by working with the city partners in Newark NJ will show its effectiveness and broader impacts on a diverse set of stakeholders of conflict management from city operators, to service providers, to average citizens.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Key outcomes of the project include the development of a socially aware conflict management framework for digital public services; the deployment of operational dashboards for the City of Newark; the creation of new machine learning, optimization, and control methods for smart city conflict sensing and mitigation; and the strengthening of interdisciplinary collaboration between technical and social science researchers.

The project also generated broader impacts through training and workforce development. Across the four years, the project supported more than ten graduate students and at least six undergraduate students at Rutgers, the University of Virginia, Stony Brook University, and the University of Connecticut, as well as a postdoctoral researcher. Students and researchers received training in machine learning, control, public management, smart city analytics, transportation systems, community-engaged research, and responsible digital public-service design.

Training and Professional Development

The project provided substantial training and professional development opportunities for graduate students, undergraduate students, and a postdoctoral researcher across Rutgers, the University of Virginia, Stony Brook University, and the University of Connecticut. More than ten graduate students and at least six undergraduate students participated in the project. They received interdisciplinary training in machine learning, graph learning, spatio-temporal data mining, transportation systems, control theory, reinforcement learning, cyber-physical systems, public management, privacy and fairness analysis, and community-engaged research.

Students also gained practical experience working with city agencies, integrating heterogeneous urban datasets, designing operational dashboards, preparing research publications, and translating technical results into decision-support tools for public-sector users. The project contributed to new and updated smart city courses and independent studies, giving students additional educational pathways to connect research with real-world public-service applications.

Community Dissemination

The results have been disseminated to multiple communities of interest, including academic researchers, public agencies, city staff, and community stakeholders. The research team published more than 40 peer-reviewed papers in major computer science, engineering, transportation, cyber-physical systems, and public administration venues, including ACM KDD, WWW, CIKM, IMWUT, SIGSPATIAL, NeurIPS, CSCW, ICRA, IROS, ACM Transactions on Cyber-Physical Systems, IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems, IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing, IEEE Internet of Things Journal, IEEE International Conference on Data Engineering, and Public Administration Review.

The team also disseminated results directly to the City of Newark through regular meetings with multiple departments, a community advisory structure, operational dashboards, multimodal resident training materials, and in-person training sessions for city staff. The dashboards developed through the project have been incorporated into Newark’s decision-support workflow and highlighted in city reports. The project website, https://smartcities.rutgers.edu, also serves as an online dissemination point for project information.

award.title: SCC-IRG Track 1: Socially Informed Services Conflict Governance through Specification, Detection, Resolution and Prevention

award.abstractText:
Focusing on ecological research in the dynamic Everglades Ecosystem, this Instrument provides a platform to aggregate and compare many environmental data sets. It also evaluates the effect of algorithms on ecological model outputs. The instrument leverages experiences and regional access to pilot studies on the Florida Everglades. The expected outcomes are likely to constitute a significant advance in state-of-the-art, novel discoveries in the fields of computing and ecology. By developing a better understanding of spatial and temporal synergies in ecosystem dynamics, scientists will be able to predict complex ecosystem responses and guide risk assessment, planning, and solution development. The enabled research will produce evidence-based science, useful in land-management decisions. The Instrument is a pilot, expandable to other regions and to the national or global scale. All software and FIU-produced data will be open-sourced.

This Instrument supports research that requires the integration of large multimodal heterogeneous datasets to address the challenges with current data-driven ecosystems research and instruments, including scaling of different data; generic global models and algorithms; calibration; and exponentially-growing acquisition of remotely sensed data. Specific enabled research activities involve multi-dimensional fuzzy logic on spatiotemporal data; multimodal image analysis; and machine learning. The system comprises a data repository, a Multimodal Ecosystem Data Aggregator, and analytical and visualization tools. Existing large repositories of global datasets do not readily allow the incorporation of vast amounts of multidimensional, historical locally-acquired datasets. The platform provides comprehensive local data integration and its correlation to global data.  While the Instrument will house a well-curated collection of environmental data, its unique service will transcend mere curation, with built-in tools for data mining, fuzzy-logic reasoning, image analysis, and visualization -- developed and interfaced to empower both student and faculty researchers.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.abstractText:
This project will develop a novel innovative smart surgical instrument as a multimodal sensing system to advance surgical health care. Modern surgical paradigms, including minimally invasive laparoscopic surgery and robotic assisted surgery, have deprived surgeons of important tactile information that this project aims to partially restore and expand into new dimensions. This project builds a tiny multimodal system that includes optical, electrical, thermal, mechanical and ultrasound sensors that is affixed to a basic surgical device such as a grasper or scalpel (either hand-held or used by an advanced surgical robot). This will turn the device into a diagnostic instrument able to measure blood oxygenation (SpO2), physical damage, and potentially other tissue states like cancer. Advances in machine intelligence are required to process this raw, multidimensional, data into information that is clinically useful to the surgeon. This novel system will promote safer and more effective manipulation of tissues in complex surgical situations protecting delicate tissues easily damaged unintentionally or tissues that are hard to visually identify. The project will support graduate and undergraduate students, including from underrepresented groups, in their STEM studies, and support participation by the PIs and students in outreach events designed to promote and broaden participation in STEM educational programs. 

This project, proposed by a multidisciplinary team, aims to advance health discovery through combining advanced machine learning with a novel multimodal sensing system aimed at improved surgical outcomes. This project will obtain the first ever simultaneous in-vivo measurements of pulse oximetry (blood oxygen saturation, SO2), temperature, electrical impedance (1-100kHz), pressure, and acoustic properties at multiple sites in multiple functioning organs. It will develop, test, and demonstrate a novel, highly integrated, multimodal sensing surgical grasper suitable for endoscopic use. The instrument will generate a continuous stream of a new type of sensed data specific to surgical work with tissues. This project will generate the first such database of in-vitro and in-vivo data along with ground truth from surgical videos, imaging studies, expert evaluations, and post-operative pathological analysis of tissues. The new data set will be shared openly online via an achieved open repository. The new classification and clustering machine learning systems will correlate measured tissue properties with organ anatomy and physiology, especially at interfaces between tissues, aiding in surgical planning and execution, and potentially supporting new modes of clinical care.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project, proposed by a multidisciplinary team at the University of Washington, Seattle, aimed to advance surgical techniques through combining advanced machine learning / AI with a new surgical instrument in which tiny advanced sensors make real-time measurements of the tissues being touched. The low cost and tiny size of today's sensors enable us to envision smart surgical instruments, detecting in real time the physiological and biomechanical properties of the tissues they manipulate. The benefit will be to support safer and more effective manipulation of tissues in complex surgical situations due to delicate tissues easily damaged unintentionally or tissues that are hard to visually identify. Modern surgical methods including minimally invasive laparoscopic surgery and robotic assisted surgery have deprived surgeons of important touch/palpation information which we hope to partially restore and expand into new dimensions.

To prevent surgeons from being overloaded or struggling to interpret this new flood of information during an operation, we developed novel machine learning systems to apply supervised and unsupervised learning to the data.

One example instrument we developed is a surgical grasper with a miniature ultrasound transducer on its grasping surface.

This device consists of a modified laparoscopic surgical grasper with ultrasound transducers added to the grasping tip. In use, while grasping simulated tissues (grocery store chicken), we see two waves, first the “ringdown” in which the ultrasound transducer continues to vibrate in response to the pulse of driving energy, and second, a fainter echo in which the pulse of vibration travels through the tissue and bounces off the other grasper tip.

When ultrasound travels through a thin tissue (such as for example intestinal walls), the echo can overlap with the ringdown (lower trace above). Existing ultrasound methods cannot separate the echo from the ringdown in this situation. In some ultrasound applications, a thick spacer is even included to separate the echo. Our paper Sosnovskaya, Yana, Eli Shlizerman, Blake Hannaford, and Mika N. Sinanan. "Comparison of Deep Learning and Signal Processing Methods for Removing a Ringing Artifact from Ultrasound Signals." In 2023 IEEE Sensors Applications Symposium (SAS), pp. 1-6. IEEE, 2023. showed for the first time that AI methods were superior in separating echo from ringdown compared to traditional methods.

Another example was a later result in which the grasper was fitted with four miniaturized sensors measuring force, displacement, temperature, as well as the ultrasound transducer were used in combination to detect small thin metal discs placed inside grocery store chicken samples. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was trained to read the four sensing modalities and determine whether or not the disc was present in the tissue.

Other experiments demonstrated the ability to identify organs being grasped during live pig surgery. Organs included liver, stomach, leg muscle and small intestine tissues. The grasper and a similar CNN-GRU model (figure above) achieved 94% classification accuracy for these tissues.

Broader Impacts: We demonstrated feasibility of using miniaturized sensors on the tips of surgical instruments to classify an characterize the tissues being worked on. We expect this to have significant impacts on future medical device and instrument design. One indication of this is that we successfully applied for the NSF’s PFI-TT grant which explicitly funds applied/translational work enabled by “legacy” NSF grants (specifically this grant). Thus a competitive review process validated our hopes for this impact. Another impact we are proud of is the Ph.D. degree earned by graduate student Yana Sosnovskaya while funded by this program. She is now in an exciting industry position leveraging her advances skills in electronics, instrumentation, and AI.

award.abstractText:
The recent successes in image and video analysis have been largely in the domain of supervised learning. Supervised learning methods  assume the availability of extensive amounts of manually annotated/labeled training data, which limits the applicability of existing methods to complex and unseen environments. This has motivated growing interest in developing semi-supervised, and even unsupervised, methods for image and video analysis, i.e., methods that have limited or even no manually annotated data. These methods focus on how to learn visual analysis models with limited labeled data; however, the problem of what to label is far less addressed. If one can identify the optimal subset to label, it is likely that the learning process will be more efficient than randomly choosing representatives that are labeled by a human. This project will focus on mathematically rigorous approaches on how to choose these samples to label.

The project will investigate information theoretic approaches, coupled with an understanding of the inherent structure in visual data, that would help identify samples that require annotation. A well-known idea in information theory is typical sets. The concept of a typical set is based on the intuitive notion that some portions of a dataset carry more information than others. The project will investigate the applicability of this notion of typicality from information theory to select a minimal set of most informative samples, which will be manually labeled, such that visual analysis models (e.g., classifiers) designed on this subset can maximize performance (of the task of interest) on the entire dataset. The inherent structure in visual data will be combined within this information theoretic framework to obtain the optimal set of representatives to label. The approach will be analyzed in the context of various learning paradigms, including active learning, transfer learning, and weakly supervised learning. The project will involve theoretical analysis of the representative selection process, algorithm design, and experimental evaluation on applications in image segmentation, activity recognition, and target re-identification.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The recent successes in machine learning have been enabled largely by the availability of extensive amounts of labeled training data, which limits the applicability of existing methods to complex and unseen environments. For example, models for autonomous driving are trained for detecting other vehicles and pedestrians in certain environments, but struggle in new environments where the conditions may be different. This has motivated growing interest in developing machine learning based methods that require only a fraction of the labeled data. This raises the question of what is the most informative data to label in order to train these models. In this project, we focused on this problem in the context of image and video analysis methods, and developed a suite of methods that can worked with limited labeled data, even as the environmental conditions change.

 

Following are some of the specific outcomes of this project.

 

  1. 1.     Selecting the most informative samples for training a machine learning model. We have developed methods to evaluate the performance of pre-trained models, and based on this, used human feedback to label a small subset which can be used to update the models. For this purpose, we have developed novel methods for quantifying the uncertainty of model performance.  

  

  1. 2.     Weighted ensemble of models. There are numerous models that are available nowadays for machine learning tasks. A challenge is to select a subset of these models during an application. We have developed methods on how to decide the subset of models during test phase. This is a critical step in many modern large language and multimodal models which use an ensemble of simpler ones.  

 

  1. 3.     Learning structure in the data. Selecting the most informative datapoints in images and videos requires understanding of the structure in the data, which is common in almost all such data, e.g., chairs and tables often occur together. We have developed methods to estimate this structure using scene graphs. Making this even more interesting is that we have shown that there may not be a unique result for this problem, and we have shown how to estimate a set of scene graphs for a scene, thus accounting for uncertainty. 

 

  1. 4.     Privacy preservation without access to training data. Privacy and security concerns abound in machine learning applications, and often require deletion of concepts learned by the models. However, the original data that was used to train the models may not always to available. Thus, we have shown how to forget concepts in such scenarios where the original training data is no longer available.

 

Overall, the results from this project will lead to huge benefits in all applications where analysis of video is critical, including security, robotics, medical image analysis, and environmental monitoring, to name but a few.

award.abstractText:
Over the past decade the data science revolution has transformed the way scientists, engineers, and businesses work. A key enabler is the rise of interactive data visualization tools, which allow users to filter, analyze, and understand large data sets. Beyond static charts and graphs, interactive data visualization allows users to view data in different ways and from different perspectives, to build deeper understanding of trends, and to test hypotheses. However, Blind and Visually Impaired People have not been able to fully participate in this data revolution. Common tools for data analysis and data exploration are based on interactive spatial graphics, displayed on 2D screens. These spatial diagrams, charts, and other representations are not easily conveyed through speech or text – the typical ways in which Blind and Visually impaired people consume information through computers. This lack of access to common tools has presented a barrier for Blind and Visually Impaired People to enter STEM fields. History teaches us that, with the right tools, Blind and Visually Impaired People can contribute fully to highly technical fields. For example, many blind people are engaged as programmers and network administrators across a range of industries.  It is evident that, if Blind and Visually Impaired People are provided with accessible tools that are functionally equivalent to those used by others and are able to interact with and generate their own data, they will take their place in the world of work, alongside their sighted peers. To address these issues, this project will work to: (1) increase understanding of data literacy amongst Blind and Visually Impaired People; (2) develop new tools and techniques, using touch and audio, to help prepare Blind and Visually Impaired People’s to understand and explore data. This is expected to begin to increase access to STEM concepts and materials in the BVI community, where access has previously been limited.  Spatial information is ubiquitous in STEM; finding effective ways to make it accessible to everyone is imperative. Increasing access to Interactive Data Visualization tools will help prepare the Blind and Visually Impaired to participate as data scientists, software engineers, and informed citizens.
 
This research will work to make fundamental contributions in the fields of information visualization, assistive technology, and haptic perception, advancing our understanding of techniques for effective encoding and exploration of spatial information in alternate forms to graphical representation. It will also expand on guidelines for multi-modal haptic interaction with spatial information and create new open source software to enable these interactions. Finally, it will contribute to the field of informal STEM learning, providing understanding about data literacy and personal data exploration as a pathway to engage the Blind and Visually Impaired community in data science and STEM activities. The research will use a mixed methods approach, using co-design, qualitative and longitudinal field studies, and quantitative lab studies. Through 4 synergistic research themes, this project will expand knowledge of broadening access to interactive data visualization for Blind and Visually Impaired People by investigating: (1) current practices, gaps and needs in data literacy for Blind and Visually Impaired People; (2) how task goals affect exploration strategies for tactile perception of data for BVI people; (3) data exploration and manipulation strategies through co-design using an interactive tactile display; and (4) the efficacy of interactive tactile data exploration to expand data literacy for BVI people.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Interactive graphs and charts are powerful tools for making sense of data—helping us track personal health, understand public trends like the spread of a pandemic, and support learning in schools. However, because these tools rely heavily on visuals, they often leave out people who are blind or have low vision (BLV).

 

This grant focused on identifying the barriers BLV individuals face when accessing and interpreting data and designing novel audio-tactile tools that build on their strengths and exploration strategies. We began with a multi-part study that included an expert audit of online data visualizations, a nationwide survey of user experiences, and in-depth observational sessions to reveal specific challenges and tactics used by BLV users when interacting with data.

 

Our findings uncovered a major gap in timely, accessible data for BLV individuals and highlighted key needs—including building user confidence, improving data literacy, and supporting interactive engagement. These insights shaped recommendations for designers and researchers and guided the development of several innovative systems:

 

Slide-Tone and Tilt-Tone are systems that translate data into tactile cues that mimic the way we feel and interpret the shape of objects in the real world. These simple systems effectively convey data features and support data tasks on par with tactile best practices, but can also be easily reprogrammed to communicate new datasets.

 

Audio Data Narratives use algorithms informed by design workshops to automatically integrate textual descriptions of data with sonification (non-speech audio cues). By interleaving the two, users gained significantly more insights than when hearing them sequentially.

 

Tangible Stats is a hands-on learning platform where students can build data sets using physical tokens while hearing and feeling how key statistics change in real-time. Teachers can tailor the feedback, and learners can explore diverse data concepts and datasets. A co-design with two blind high school students, a statistics teacher, and a teacher for the visually impaired uncovered ways such a system can promote conceptual and contextual understanding of statistics, and also contributed a broader set of accessibility-first design principles for supporting data and statistical learning.

 

The UofM team also engaged in a longitudinal study with teachers of the visually impaired to examine the use of multimodal representations of information in classroom settings. They worked with two teachers and their students to provide just-in-time tactile materials with speech overlays for geography lessons, and to provide maps for a middle school student learning their way around their new highschool building. Their findings revealed a greater degree of self-paced learning when students were able to access tactile image features co-located with layers of spoken information embedded in maps and charts.

 

Taken together, this research uncovers a range of non-visual methods—rooted in BLV users’ access needs and strategies—that enable them to access, explore, understand, and build competency in data.

 

Additionally, this work supported translational workshops for sharing our findings and best practices directly with stakeholders, including Blind students, Accessibility practitioners, and educators.

 

Finally this project led to  the publication of several journal papers and conference proceedings.  This work supported 3 PhD students, and led to the completion of 2 PhD theses, with another forthcoming.

award.abstractText:
Self-tracking of physical activities can support people of all ages in understanding their lifestyle behaviors and making healthy choices, reducing chronic disease risks. For older adults, movement behaviors are especially critical. They help people maintain functional abilities and live independently. Smart watches and other activity tracking technologies have become available, making self-tracking easier than before, but older adults have adopted them less. One barrier is that current physical activity trackers do not effectively identify and track older adults’ activities. This project aims to understand (1) what kind of data are needed from older adults to make activity tracking work for them; and (2) how to engage older adults to collect the needed data. This project will develop a new approach to personalizing older adults’ activity tracking. It will open up new research avenues on personalized and multimodal self-tracking that affect healthcare, quality of life, and privacy. This project is expected to make broader impacts for older adults in enhancing their motivation to engage in physical activities, as well as societal impacts in nurturing a culture of diversity and inclusion that benefits the lives of older adults and people with and without disabilities or health conditions.

This project uses “teachable interfaces” to facilitate personalized, self-tracking for older adults’ physical activities, while considering their changes in mobility and diverse physical characteristics. The teachable interfaces are intended to help people provide personalized activity labels, which will be used to recognize their unique movements. They will also enable self-tracking of meaningful and modifiable movement and non-movement activities, supporting older adults to displace inactivity with physical activity, which can provide significant health benefits. The research team will investigate: (1) older adults’ movement and non-movement activities that they wish to change; (2) new personalized, multimodal activity trackers that provide opportunities for self-reflection through teachable interfaces; and (3) commonalities and differences in efficacies for subgroups of older adults (e.g., people with mild dementia) and what adjustments are needed to accommodate them. Combining expertise from human-computer interaction, interactive machine learning, accessibility, aging, and kinesiology, the project will employ a mixed-methods research approach: co-design with older adults, technology design and development, and evaluations both in the lab and in people’s natural environments.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Wearable activity trackers have grown increasingly popular as tools for promoting healthy, active lifestyles. Yet most commercial systems are designed around data from younger adults and tend to emphasize vigorous, structured exercise, leaving important questions about how well these technologies serve the diverse needs and movement patterns of older adults. This project set out to design and build personalized activity tracking systems that better reflect older adults' lifestyles, physical capabilities, and values, with the long-term goal of supporting older adults to more actively engage in physical activity on their own terms.

A central innovation of this work was the concept of "teachable interfaces," a mechanism that enables older adults to capture data about their own activities and use those examples to train a machine learning algorithm tailored to their personal patterns. Research has shown that activity recognition models trained on younger adult populations do not transfer well to older adults, motivating the need for individualized approaches. To address this, the team developed MyMove, a smartwatch app that allowed older adults to label their activities using spoken descriptions in real time. These verbal reports were aligned with data from a research-grade accelerometer to build and evaluate personalized activity recognition models.

A 7-day deployment study of MyMove found that smartwatches were a feasible and well-accepted tool for verbal activity annotation. Older adults wore the devices for an average of 11.6 hours per day and provided a rich mix of prompted and self-initiated activity reports, capturing 1,224 verbal reports in total. Older adults rarely described their activities in terms of structured exercise. Instead, they reported a wide range of low-to-moderate intensity activities and expressed variability in how intensely they experienced even routine tasks. Subsequent work examined the challenges of collecting reliable ground truth data from older adults in real-world settings, finding that while triangulating multiple data sources improved data quality, it also introduced costs in terms of data shrinkage and data contributors’ and data stewards’ burden.

Interview studies revealed that older adults hold a rich and sometimes competing set of values that shape which activities feel meaningful to track. We found that older adults did not always equate activities that are personally meaningful with activities they wished to track, and some preferred not to track activities where the goal was full immersion due to the cognitive demands of annotation. A key implication is that activity tracking research and intervention design should attend more carefully to low-intensity activities that fill much of an older adult's day, rather than focusing exclusively on moderate-to-vigorous exercise.

Later phases of the project extended this work through co-design, a participatory approach in which older adults collaborated with researchers to shape the design of the tracking system itself. Through co-design sessions, the team identified older adults' preferences for multimodal data input to support more accurate and less burdensome activity annotation, and uncovered how older adults think about labeling quality in terms of accuracy, precision, and granularity. A companion line of work explored behavior displacement (replacing sedentary time with other activity), identifying key personal and social factors that shape older adults' decisions to move and highlighting the need for personalized, adaptive interventions that respect individual preferences and agency.

The project also expanded its reach to include older adults living with dementia or mild cognitive impairment. Interviews with 29 participants revealed a wide range of emotions and attitudes toward tracking—from acceptance and positive anticipation to resistance and aversion—shaped by individual routines, relationships, and broader social and institutional contexts. This work emphasized that tracking technology designed for this population must be sensitive to ambiguity, personal history, and the emotional dimensions of living with memory concerns.

Across the life of this award, findings were disseminated through peer-reviewed publications at leading venues including the ACM CHI, ACM ASSETS, ACM UbiComp, and IMWUT journals. The project supported the training of many students, who presented their work at international venues. The work also informed national policy: one team member contributed to the President's Council on Sports, Fitness & Nutrition's 2023 Midcourse Report on physical activity in older adults, which highlighted gaps that this project's findings directly addressed.

In sum, this project shed light on the unique needs and values of older adults as self-trackers and helped lay the groundwork for a new generation of personalized, inclusive activity tracking technologies, with broad implications for health monitoring tools and behavioral interventions aimed at promoting wellbeing across the full diversity of the older adult population.

award.abstractText:
U.S. college students are facing critical challenges for their career development and job mobility, which is vital for their long-term career success, especially during global pandemic times. Indeed, the questions that often puzzle students include what career choices to choose next, how to update skills for future new jobs, and which learning opportunities to take. These challenges have been increasingly observed among different groups of students in different majors and socioeconomic statuses at many universities. This project collects and analyzes academic curriculum and student career data, discovers useful patterns about college curriculum and students’ career development, studies students’ career choices, and develops sophisticated solutions to improve their career mobility. This study makes significant contributions to the fields of data mining, machine learning, and education and career data analytics. The results of this project can bring new ways for understanding and improving college graduates’ career success, provide useful insights and tools for students to make their decisions on career development, and augment the service capability of college career and academic advising offices. This project integrates the research with education through new course module development, involving graduate and undergraduate students in research, and research showcases for local K-12 students. 

This project focuses on the following three specific aims (SA): mining and informing useful semantics and patterns about college curriculum and graduates’ career development; studying the career choices of college graduates; and developing sophisticated solutions to improve career mobility of college graduates. To achieve the first SA, this project develops a novel context-aware deep learning method for mining semantics from heterogenous textual data and discovers insightful horizontal and vertical patterns. To solve the second SA, this project mines multiple-scale career path patterns and develops a new hierarchical neural network method to model and predict graduates’ career choices. To achieve the third SA, this project develops novel reinforcement learning methods to recommend learning items for both graduated students and enrolled ones.  The results of this project will be disseminated in the form of peer-reviewed publications, publicly available data set, tutorials, seminars, and workshops.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project set out to help students and workers navigate increasingly complex education and career choices using data and artificial intelligence. The central idea was to treat schools, companies, jobs, and people as an interconnected "talent network," and to design computational tools that learn from these networks to understand which career paths work well, which skills matter most, and how universities and organizations can better support long‑term success.

The project first focused on talent networks that connect college graduates, universities, startups, and investors. By building large network maps from public data and applying modern graph‑based AI methods, the team showed that the makeup and connections of a startup's founders and early employees can help predict whether that startup will thrive. The project also developed models that analyze talent networks inside organizations using anonymized, aggregated information about how employees communicate and collaborate. These models identify key connectors, departmental communities, and unusual interaction patterns that may signal risks such as siloed teams or overburdened staff. To support this work, the team created general algorithms for detecting unusual sequences of events and for making multi‑step inferences over large knowledge graphs, strengthening the technical foundation for analyzing complex career and organizational data.

As digital platforms increasingly mediate both learning and work, the project studied how AI can better understand items and user preferences in online environments. The team developed a knowledge‑driven approach that represents products in e‑commerce by combining text descriptions with structured background information (such as categories and attributes), improving matching, search, and classification. Building on this, the project designed methods that summarize information from product images and text, then train large language models to track a user's evolving interests and predict what they are likely to choose next, leading to more accurate and interpretable recommendations. A related line of work developed a risk‑aware recommendation framework for treatment decisions in critical care, which combines time‑series medical records with clinicians' notes and explicitly models uncertainty so that suggested treatments come with statistical guarantees on reliability. The same principles of multimodal, uncertainty‑aware recommendation are directly relevant to future systems that might advise students about courses, training options, or jobs.

The project also focused on higher education and large‑scale societal outcomes. Using resume information from professional networks, the team built a graph-based model that follows graduates as they move from universities into different industries and companies over time. The model more accurately predicts employment outcomes and quantifies how different institutions influence career trajectories, offering a way to assess educational quality based on real-world career results rather than inputs alone. In parallel, related techniques were adapted to design industrial operating policies that balance productivity with carbon emissions. By learning from the best historical examples and imitating them while pushing operations toward stricter sustainability targets, this work points to data-driven tools that can help industries move toward carbon-neutral processes.

The project advanced the state of the art in graph representation learning, organizational network analysis, sequence modeling, recommendation systems, and risk‑aware decision‑making. The research produced multiple peer-reviewed publications in leading venues in data mining and machine learning, including ICML, SIGKDD, AAAI, and IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering. Four Ph.D. students completed their degrees while working on problems stemming from this award, including two who have taken assistant professor positions at major universities

The project offers new, data-driven ways to support students in planning their education and careers, universities in understanding how their programs translate into employment outcomes, and organizations in managing and growing talent more effectively. Extensions to sustainability and healthcare show how methods for analyzing complex networks of people, institutions, and decisions can benefit society well beyond the labor market. Overall, this project illustrates how modern AI techniques can turn complex data about education, work, and organizations into actionable insights that support individuals, institutions, and the broader economy.

award.abstractText:
Sleep represents one third of everyone’s life and affects the quality and the health of everyone’s life. Traditionally, long-term characteristics of sleep patterns (sleep phenotypes) are largely unknown due to the lack of convenient monitoring devices and automatic algorithms.  Recently, massive health sensing data such as activity data, electroencephalogram, respiratory monitoring data and electrocardiography are being collected in clinics and at home, which brings unprecedented opportunities for understanding sleep phenotypes outside clinics. However, there are tremendous challenges to translate these noisy and unreliable multimodal sensing data into accurate phenotypes such as sleep stages and apnea events. Beyond sleep, many neurological conditions such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s all expect objective tracking of long-term disease progression, which is currently impossible. This project will provide the computational capability to conduct phenotype tracking at home with the focus on sleep phenotypes. Machine learning methods and software will be developed to conduct accurate phenotyping of sleep with minimal effort on sensor instrumentation, data collection and analysis. 


This project aims at developing DeepSense, a deep learning toolbox to model massive data streams including in-clinic monitoring data such as polysomnography and novel radio frequency signals from a wireless sensing device. The research team will develop accurate deep learning methods to automate sleep monitoring using polysomnography data. They will invent adversarial deep learning methods for modeling radio frequency  signals and leverage large historical polysomnography data to help improve models for radio frequency signals. They will develop interpretable models that leverage and expand medical knowledge on sleep phenotypes. Finally, all the proposed models will be validated through a prospective study with a goal of automating manual sleep studies and assessing the feasibility of sleep studies via radio frequency signal data. The research team plans to release the open-source software and large datasets from this project that can benefit computer science, engineering and medical community.

award.abstractText:
Despite the importance of navigational skill, people’s ability to find their way around and the approaches they take vary widely. Yet we do not know why this variation exists or how different strategies are used during everyday navigation. In robotics, self-driving cars, and other autonomous systems, it has become increasingly clear that a one-size-fits-all approach is not viable for all environments and user needs. Similarly, producing autonomous systems with different navigational strengths could improve the capacity of autonomous systems as a whole, such as teams of exploring or search-and-rescue robots. This project brings together researchers from neuroscience, cognitive psychology, computer science, and robotics to study variability in navigation abilities and strategies in complex environments. The researchers combine behavioral, neuroscience, and computational approaches. Pinpointing the neural and behavioral markers that underlie individual differences will lead to customized solutions to navigational challenges and optimize the performance of autonomous systems for differing environmental conditions. The outcomes of this research will have the following specific benefits to society and scientific discovery: 1) advancing theoretical understanding of the processes involved in spatial navigation, 2) understanding the advantages of variation in both humans and robots, impacting how people approach both fields, 3) implications for improvements in self-driving cars, GPS wayfinding devices, and transportation signage, and 4) broader dissemination of virtual reality (VR) technology.

The overarching cross-disciplinary aims of this study are to 1) test whether human spatial navigation is a singular competence or whether multiple abilities contribute, 2) establish the neural markers of human navigational abilities through multi-modal imaging, and 3) implement and test different navigational abilities in robots in real-world situations. This study will be the largest to date (n = 270) to study human navigation abilities, using both structural equation modeling and multivariate analysis of imaging data to deeply address this question. Furthermore, the project will broaden the scope of abilities to relate navigation skills to working memory, learning, personality, and other factors. Implementing navigational strategies and abilities in robots provides a controlled test of their tradeoffs. By manipulating the planning and mapping strategies of robots, the researchers can isolate particular abilities and their contributions to navigation, testing both navigational theory and practical advantages for autonomous systems. The interdisciplinary approach of this project harnesses the strengths of cognitive science, robotics, and neuroscience to test the fundamental nature of human individual variability.
