award.abstractText:
Graphs are ubiquitous data structures in numerous domains, such as social science (social networks), natural science (physical systems, and protein-protein interaction networks) and knowledge graphs. As new generalizations of traditional deep neural networks to graph structured data, Graph Neural Networks (or GNNs) have demonstrated the power in graph representation learning and have permeated numerous areas of science and technology. However, GNNs also inherited the drawback of traditional deep neural networks, i.e., lacking interpretability. Moreover, the complexity of graph data introduces the scalability as a new limitation for GNNs because graph structured data are not independent. These drawbacks have raised tremendous concerns to adopt GNNs in many critical applications pertaining to fairness, privacy, and safety. Thus, this project aims to tackle the major drawbacks of GNNs and greatly enlarge their usability in critical applications. To achieve the research goal, this project systematically investigates advanced principles for scalable GNNs and new mechanisms to interpret GNNs. The proposed research extends the state-of-the-art GNNs to a new frontier, investigates original problems that entreat innovative solutions and paves the way for a new research endeavor effectively tame graph mining. As many real-world domains problems requires scalable and interpretable graph mining techniques, the project has potential to benefit many real-world applications from various disciplines such as Computer Science, Social Science, Healthcare and Bioinformatics. 



This project proposes novel principles and mechanisms for scalable and interpretable graph neural networks to facilitate the adoption of GNNs on critical domains, investigates associated fundamental research issues and develops effective algorithms. The project offers the first comprehensive investigation on these directions, and the designed novel methodologies and tasks will deepen our understanding on the inner working mechanisms of GNNs and contribute to real-world applications. The success of this project will be (1) New scalable and interpretable GNNs with state-of-the-art graph representation learning and predictive performance; (2) Theoretical analysis such as convergence and complexity; and (3) Open-source implementations of all key algorithms and frameworks. Disparate means are planned to disseminate the project and its findings, such as web enabled data and software repositories, books, journal and conference publications, special purpose workshops or tutorials, and industrial collaborations. The project can be effectively integrated to undergraduate and graduate courses as well as in student research projects.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project aims to develop novel principles and mechanisms for scalable and interpretable graph neural networks to facilitate the adoption of GNNs on critical domains, investigates associated fundamental research issues and develops effective algorithms. Significant results include (1) we proposed the first linear convergent algorithm with compression, LEAD to speed up the training process for GNNs; (2) we have studied strategies for graph condensation which aims to condense the large, original graph into a small, synthetic and highly-informative graph, such that GNNs trained on the small graph and large graph have comparable performance and (3) We provided understandings for when GNNs can work from both the empirical and theoretical perspectives. We have applied these algorithms to real-world applications from multiple domains such as social media, education, biology and political science. The project offers the first comprehensive investigation on these directions, and the designed novel methodologies and tasks can deepen our understanding on the inner working mechanisms of GNNs and contribute to real-world applications. The project has resulted in more than 20 publications from top conferences and journals among. There are 7 students involved in this project including 3 female students and 1 African American student.  There are two Ph.D. students graduated: one is now a tenure-track assistant professor at NJIT and the other will join NC State as a tenure-track assistant professor at Fall 2022. Parts of the findings and research results have been incorporated into both graduate and undergraduate level courses. More than 10 invited talks are given to a variety of universities and industrial labs. Four tutorials have been given associated with top conferences including KDD21, IJCAI21,  SDM21 and AAAI21. Three workshops have been organized from KDD, IJCAI, and AAAI. In addition,  the project results in the first comprehensive book in deep learning on graphs. A free preprint has attracted downloads from more than 150 countries and regions.  I led a team to apply GNNs for single-cell analysis and my team is the Top 1 winner in the task of modality prediction from OpenProblems-NeurIPS2021 Single-Cell Multimodal Data Integration.

award.abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of a rapid and automated scene understanding technology to intelligently evaluate existing conditions of vulnerability and assess potential disaster risks more proactively and effectively.  This technology may help make informed decisions regarding steps to reduce the impacts of disasters. Developing and implementing the technology to reduce disaster risk requires identifying and assessing the sources of potential risk effectively, but a lack of a rapid and automated tools makes practitioners rely on manual inspection. The proposed innovation is to make the current disaster risk assessment process more intelligent and efficient by reducing time-consuming and labor-intensive manual inspection. If the project is completed successfully, the proposed innovation will enhance scientific and technological understanding of rapid and automated visual sensing and analytics for disaster risk prediction and assessment.

This I-Corps project is based on the development of the integrated analysis of low-level image features together with high-level semantic models, which enables robust scene understanding and risk prediction in complex environments. By leveraging large-scale data from multimodal visual sensors (e.g., drones, security cameras, etc.), the technology automatically encodes the context of potential disaster risk into machine vision algorithms to identify the elements at risk on video recordings and assess the degree of vulnerability and the elements at risk in complex environments. The system generates site-specific managerial information in an automated manner, which may enhance risk-informed decision-making for disaster mitigation and preparedness, thereby reducing both the level of risk and the impacts of disasters effectively. The proposed innovation may also provide the foundation for further vision-based reasoning for disaster management.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The outcomes of this project involve the business model to transition the current proof-of-concept into a commercial product/service and find a potential market fit towards which the team will direct the commercialization efforts to pursue further opportunities like a startup.The major focus is to engage with many individuals and companies, explore the potential commercial value of the technology, and prototype a business model to transition the proof-of-concept into a commercial product/service. One of the key value propositions is that the technology prototyped allows a rapid and easy disaster risk analysis that enables practitioners to predict and assess potential disaster risks more proactively and effectively. The initial plan toward commercialization was to create a start-up company and then collaborate with channel partners. In this plan, the consulting engagements would provide immediate revenue for the start-up to grow. However, based on the feedback from potential customers, it is expected that directly selling the product to the end user would be challenging, particularly at the early stages of the business. Developing strategic alliances with channel partners who have built reputations and credentials in the market could be beneficial, especially for early commercialization. The findings from this project could benefit society as it will inform decision making on proactive risk mitigation and help prioritize resilience investments in preparation for potential natural disasters. In addition, this project provided excellent educational and training opportunities in the context of entrepreneurship and technology commercialization, especially for the graduate students involved in the project. This project was in a unique position to impact related practices through the dissemination to companies in the Construction Industry Advisory Council at Texas A&M University.

Plastics that can conduct both electrons and ions are important for numerous applications such as bioelectronic sensors that convert biological nerve impulses into signals readable by digital electronics, energy storage devices that can deliver high currents for short times, and next-generation computers that mimic the function of the brain. One of the factors limiting technological developments in these fields is limited understanding of how ions inject into and transport within these semiconducting plastics. This project addresses this question by analyzing polymers (plastics) at the nanometer scale using advanced microscopy techniques. These methods can determine where polymers are swelling from ion injection and can correlate that response with the chemical signature of the ion using infrared light, also at the nanoscale. The microscopic information is then compared to transistor measurements to gain a fundamental understanding of how the polymer processing and structure influences ion motion. The scientific knowledge from this project enables better design and processing/manufacturing of polymers for the applications noted above. The project additionally builds upon the track record of the principal investigator in education by enabling development of new outreach materials such as polymer electrochemistry kits that are suitable for integration into existing outreach programs and networks. The project also provides direct support for undergraduate research through continuation of the successful partnership with the Rainier Scholars organization to provide pathways to assist under-represented groups and first-generation college students succeed in the sciences. 


The scientific goal of this project is to gain a fundamental understanding of the structure/function relationships controlling ion injection in pi-conjugated polymers operating as mixed ionic/electronic conductors while using blended organic electrochemical transistors as an experimental testbed. These polymers and blends typically exhibit features on the scale of tens of nanometers, and therefore this project uses advanced scanning probe microscopy tools to investigate the ion transport process at the nanoscale. Conjugated polymers have emerged as promising electronic and photonic materials for transducing signals at the interface between the biological and digital environments, and the proposed project will explore fundamental structure/function properties of these materials relevant to these applications in a way that is distinct from other efforts through a combination of unique local and bulk methods. Specifically, the project will: 1) use a new method, photoinduced force microscopy (PiFM), to make nanoscale maps probing how local chemical structure and morphology combine to affect local ion injection; 2) apply electrochemical strain microscopy (ESM) to measure local swelling due to ion uptake in homopolymers, block copolymers, and blends; and, 3) do so while exploring new blend and composite architectures as a means to overcome the bottlenecks of existing materials performance. Notably, this project uses nanoscale infrared microscopy to probe blends of conducting polymers and ionic conductors to test the hypothesis that decoupling the high electronic mobility component and high ionic mobility component can enable improved electrochemical transistors. The principal investigator has shown in previous work that ion injection and electronic mobility are often anti-correlated in mixed conductors, which serves as a device bottleneck. These experiments yield a distinct set of measurements that enable multimodal analysis of the structure-function relationships underpinning ion injection. The project provides important insight into how mobility and volumetric capacitance in mixed ionic-electronic conductors are related, and whether it is possible to rationally improve conducting polymers and polymer blends design by focusing on how ions move into the polymer from the ground up.

Plastics that can conduct both electrons and ions are important for numerous applications including bioelectronic sensors that convert biological nerve impulses into signals that are readable by digital electronics, energy storage devices that can deliver high currents for short times, and next-generation computers that mimic the function of the brain. These materials offer much technological promise; however, one of the factors limiting technological developments in these fields is our limited understanding of how ions inject into and transport within these semiconducting plastic materials.

In this project, supported by a grant from the Division of Materials Research, we have investigated the fundamental properties that control ion transport in soft polymeric semiconducting materials. We studied these materials using a combination of microscopy and measurement methods like optical microscopy, atomic force microscopy, and device data. Using these techniques, we studied several different materials, revealing new insights the properties that control the ion injection process, as well as the ion expulsion process. First, we combined optical measurements with atomic force microscopy (AFM) techniques to probe the effects of using polymer nanowire films on the kinetics of ion injection. Polymers normally form an amorphous film but can be engineered to form long wire-like strands. We showed that ions more easily penetrate the nanowire matrix compared to an amorphous film, causing a significant improvement in the speed of turn on due to faster ion injection, and we used combined AFM with infrared laser excitation to directly show that ions aggregate on the surface in the non-nanowire film. Next, we worked with a range of different polymers to understand the effect of changing the chemistry of the sidechain on the speed of switching. By changing the position of an oxygen atom on the sidechain of a semiconducting polymer called polythiophene, we could observe significant changes in ion injection speed and transistor performance. Next, we applied these techniques to a polymer that does not have any sidechains yet is an efficient ion transport material, a fact that has confused researchers for many years. We showed that this sidechain-free polymer, called BBL, can swell in salt solution as soon as a voltage is applied to the water, allowing for ions to penetrate between crystallites due to this swelling effect. This observation provided key insight into how to design polymers without sidechains that still work with ions. Lastly, we recently completed work studying the asymmetric kinetics of ion injection into conducting polymers. Researchers have commonly observed this phenomenon, where ions are very slow to enter a material but quick to leave the material (“doping” and “dedoping,” respectively). We used optical microscopy on devices to show the ion injection profiles in realtime, and we used these data to develop a model that explains why ions inject into the film relatively slowly.

Our reports provide a set of work that help explain the different properties that control ion injection, from exploring the polymer structure and sidechain chemistry to fundamental studies of the ion injection/expulsion process. These experiments combined AFM measurements and optical studies, and the work generated by this grant has laid the groundwork for future studies into understanding how to exploit kinetics for devices that mimic memory cells.

In addition, this project supported workforce development through the interdisciplinary training of several graduate and undergraduate students, and supported the core Ph.D. work of 2 students who graduated with their doctorates (one is now working in the U.S. semiconductor industry, and one now working for a U.S. national laboratory),  one student who graduated with a masters degree, and multiple summer undergraduates students who were recruited through partnerships with local organizations that focus on provide opportunities to hard-working, low-income students, many of whom are the first in their families to attend college.

award.abstractText:
Transfer learning provides crucial techniques for utilizing data from related studies that are conducted under different contexts or on diverse populations. It is an important topic with a wide range of applications in integrative genomics, neuroimaging, computer vision and signal processing. This research work will provide new tools to scientific researchers who routinely collect and analyze high dimensional and complex data across different sources and platforms. This project aims to develop new analytical tools to improve conventional methods by delivering more informative and interpretable scientific findings. The developed transfer learning algorithms, which can reliably extract and combine knowledge from diverse data types and across different studies, will help address important issues from genomics applications. User-friendly software packages will be developed and made publicly available. Scientific researchers can use the tools to translate dispersed and heterogeneous data sources into new knowledge and medical benefits. This will help improve the understanding of the role of various genetic factors in complex diseases, and accelerate the development of new medicines and treatments in a cost-effective way. 

Transfer learning for large-scale inference aims to extract and transfer the knowledge learned from related source domains to assist the simultaneous inference of thousands or even millions of parameters in the target domain. We aim to develop a general framework to gain understanding of the benefits and caveats of transfer learning in a wide range of large-scale inference problems including sparse estimation, false discovery rate analysis, sparse linear discriminant analysis and high-dimensional regression. Our research addresses two key issues in transfer learning: (a) What should be transferred? (b) How to transfer and prevent negative learning? We aim to pursue three major research goals. The first is to develop a class of computationally efficient and robust transfer learning algorithms for high-dimensional sparse inference. The general strategy is to first learning the local sparsity structure of the high-dimensional object through auxiliary data and then apply the structural knowledge to the target domain by adaptively placing differential weights or setting varied thresholds on corresponding coordinates. The second is to formalize a decision-theoretic framework for high-dimensional transfer learning that is applicable across the sparse and non-sparse regimes. Along this direction, we aim to develop a class of kernelized nonparametric empirical Bayes methods for data-sharing shrinkage estimation and multiple testing. The third is to address the urgent needs and new challenges arising from important genomics applications using the newly developed methods.

Motivated by a range of important applications, this project aims to develop new methodologies and theory for integrative large-scale data analysis and statistical inference, where the goal is to effectively incorporate relevant structural and external information in the analysis and inference of data collected from thousands and even millions of study units/variables. There are four major research goals to be pursued. One is to develop an integrative framework for inference of two sparse objects that can handle a wide range of dependence structures such as those arise in multiple testing for high-dimensional linear regression, large covariance/correlation matrices, and Gaussian graphical models. A second is to develop novel theories and methodologies for a class of structured simultaneous inference problems, including optimal sequential multiple testing with online false discovery rate control, estimating a high-dimensional mean vector with heteroscedastic errors and identifying hierarchically structured patterns. The third is to develop a general frame- work for set-wise simultaneous inference and solve related problems such as replicability analysis, simultaneous conjunction tests and multi-stage adaptive testing. The fourth is to address the urgent needs and new challenges arising from important genomics applications, including detection of genes-environment interactions, differential gene network analysis and SNP set analysis, using the newly developed methods. 

Intellectual Merit. Integrative large-scale data analysis and statistical inference is an important topic with a wide range of applications in genomics, neuroimaging, astrophysics, climate studies, and signal processing. The new integrative framework that will be developed in this project provides a powerful approach for extracting and pooling information from various parts of massive data sets with complex structures. The new inference procedures and analytical tools will improve the power of conventional methods and deliver more informative and interpretable scientific results. The proposed research will make important contributions to multiple testing, simultaneous estimation and statistical decision theories. The methodologies developed in this project will address important issues from genomics applications. 

Broader Impacts. The research will provide new methodologies and technical tools to researchers in various scientific fields who routinely collect and analyze high dimensional data. The PIs’ close collaboration with researchers at Harvard School of Public Health and the Perelman School of Medicine at Penn will lead to major applications in genomics, including detection of genes-environment interactions, differential gene network analysis and SNP set analysis. The collaborative research will help translate dispersed and heterogeneous data sources into new knowledge and medical benefits. The procedures and algorithms developed in this project will be implemented as user-friendly and accessible software packages in R and/or Matlab and made available on the web along with the associated research reports. This project will also make important contributions to the development of Ph.D. students and postdoctoral fellows. This is a promising field for young researchers who are interested in interdisciplinary research.

High-dimensional arrays commonly arise from modern scientific and technological research and have been a central topic in modern statistics and data science. Some areas such as genetics, microbiome studies, brain imaging, hyperspectral imaging, etc., yield a large amount of high-dimensional array data; while in some other areas, data can be recast into high-dimensional array form to facilitate analysis. In these situations, the target parameter is often high-dimensional/high-order, but the important information may lie in dimension-reduced subspaces induced by various structural conditions. How to efficiently exploit these subspaces poses significant statistical and computational challenges. This project aims to address these challenges from a perspective of subspace learning. By taking into account dimension-reduced and low-order subspaces, the PI aims to address a series of statistical and machine learning questions by developing new methodologies and theories with statistical and computational advantages. 

This project will progress along three major directions: (i) fast estimation and inference for high-dimensional arrays via important subspace sketching; (ii) high-order clustering with theoretical guarantees; (iii) ultrahigh-order tensor singular value decomposition via a tensor-train parameterization. The research will be applicable to a variety of topics involving high-dimensional matrix and tensor data, such as genetics and genomes, reinforcement learning, neuroimaging analysis, material science, recommender design, etc. The PI will also develop user-friendly software packages for the new algorithms and make them available for public use. The PI is committed to training students, especially those from groups underrepresented in STEM, through involvement in the research project.

award.abstractText:
Learning to make decisions is important in almost all aspects of our lives. How humans learn is a topic of intense study in many diverse fields including psychology, linguistics, and the neurosciences. Learning to categorize is particularly crucial for humans and other animals in our interactions with our environments - whether it is a friend or a foe, edible or non-edible, the word /bat/ or /hat/ etc. As we learn to categorize information, our brain and behavior fundamentally change. These longitudinal trajectories evolve differently in different individuals and across brain systems. While recording and analyzing human behavior and neural function have become sophisticated, statistical methods for characterizing local similarities and differences in the underlying neural and behavioral process dynamics across individuals and groups are still emerging. This project aims to address this critical gap through the development of novel statistical frameworks for complex behavioral data on learning in adults. This collaborative project will provide trainees with experiences in a broad range of interdisciplinary topics.

A common theme underlying the statistical research undertaken in this project is the assessment of the local dynamic behavior of the learning processes - how similar or different these processes are, including especially how similarly or differently they might be influenced by the associated predictors, across learning stages and brain networks. Through innovative adaptation and amalgamation of classical ideas and recent advances in diverse areas in statistics, including sparsity inducing priors, tensor factorization techniques, functional data analysis methods, locally informative sampling strategies, etc., novel generic statistical frameworks and associated computational machinery for local inference in longitudinal settings will first be developed. This frameworks will then be adapted to specific models for neural learning processes. The principal investigators will use carefully designed learning experiments in one domain of research - how adults learn novel speech categories and theories to validate the results obtained by the new statistical models. While human speech learning is an interesting and well-studied problem on its own, insights gained from this application are generalizable to other domains of studies that involve human learning.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Auditory processing and learning play critical roles in our lives. While human behavioral and neuroimaging studies have become increasingly sophisticated, there remains a lack of robust statistical methods to characterize systematic local similarities and differences in the underlying process dynamics across individuals and groups. This project aimed to address some of these gaps by developing novel statistical techniques to assess perceptual and neural processes involved in auditory processing and learning, providing new insights into these processes, and how they vary and evolve.

 

The first aims of this project focused on new methods for understanding the perceptual mechanisms underlying auditory category learning from behavioral data.

 

Drift-diffusion models, which simulate evidence accumulation in the brain via latent diffusion processes, are widely used computational tools for inferring categorization processes from behavioral proxies such as response times and accuracies. However, much of the previously existing literature focused on binary alternatives and simple study designs, which rarely capture the real-world complexity of category learning, where individuals seldom distinguish only between two exemplars. Moreover, the relationships between exemplars evolve throughout the learning process. Previously existing statistical methods were insufficient to address these complexities. To overcome these limitations, we developed novel longitudinal drift-diffusion mixed models for multi-category learning, providing a robust framework for studying more complex categorization processes. Our analysis provided novel insights into how novel auditory categories are learned over time and how they vary between good and bad learners.

 

Even though fitting drift-diffusion models requires data on both response categories and response times, response accuracy is often the primary metric used by behavioral scientists to describe human learning, overlooking response times. Moreover, in many practical scenarios, such as online experiments during the COVID-19 pandemic, accurately recording response times may not be feasible. The question whether drift-diffusion parameters can be recovered from accuracy data alone is therefore an important one but had never been addressed before. In this project, we explored this question. We noted that a new class of inverse-probit drift-diffusion models for response categories alone can be easily obtained by integrating out the response times, now considered latent, from our joint model for response categories and response times before. This marginal model, however, introduces significant statistical challenges, including identifiability issues that prevent the recovery of all parameters from the original joint model. By carefully addressing these issues, we developed a robust framework that can capture the general trends underlying learning based on data on response categories alone.

 

The final aims of this project focused on new methods for inferring undirected and directed brain networks involved in auditory processing, both in general and in response to stimuli, from neuroimaging data.

 

One of the main tools we use is called a graphical model, which helps map out two-way relationships between several variables. Previous methods to analyze this kind of data were slow and complicated, particularly when handling large amounts of information. In one of our works in this project, we created a general new method, which we called the "precision factor model”, that works faster and more efficiently, even when analyzing thousands of variables at once. We took this idea further by creating a method for if the data aren’t normally distributed which is often the case with neuroimaging data. Using this method, we found strong connections between specific areas of the brain involved in auditory processing.

 

Another challenge in brain research is figuring out how brain activity flows over time between different regions. To do this, we used a technique called Granger causality analysis, which helps reveal the direction of brain activity flow (i.e., which region influences another). Previously existing approaches for this kind of analysis worked only for small data sets and group-level inference, whereas our new methods can handle much larger data sets, capturing the important details, and enabling more accurate and efficient analyses of directed brain networks, both at the group and individual levels.

 

To date, the project has produced eight peer-reviewed publications, and several more manuscripts in progress. All the statistical methodologies developed have been made publicly available through open-source code. Significant efforts were also dedicated to developing user-friendly R packages, with one already available on the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) and several others currently in preparation. The project also provided training opportunities for multiple graduate students, undergraduates, and postdoctoral researchers. Those working on the statistical side were exposed to collaboration-driven methodological research and trained in a wide range of statistical areas, including conditionally autoregressive models, drift-diffusion models, partition models, hidden Markov models, hidden Markov random field models, longitudinal mixed models, mixture models, spline models, tensor decomposition models, and vector autoregressive models. Similarly, students and postdocs in auditory neuroscience gained experience in applying these advanced statistical models to their research.

award.abstractText:
Sound is rich with information about the surrounding environment. If you stand on a city sidewalk with your eyes closed and listen, you will hear the sounds of events happening around you: birds chirping, squirrels scurrying, people talking, doors opening, an ambulance speeding, a truck idling. In addition, you will also likely be able to perceive the location of each sound source, where it’s going, and how fast it’s moving. This project will build innovative technologies to allow computers to extract this rich information out of sound. By not only identifying which sound sources are present but also estimating the spatial location and movement of each sound source, sound sensing technology will be able to better describe our environments with microphone-enabled everyday devices, e.g. smartphones, headphones, smart speakers, hearing-aids, home camera, and mixed-reality headsets. For hearing impaired individuals, the developed technologies have the potential to alert them to dangerous situations in urban or domestic environments. For city agencies, acoustic sensors will be able to more accurately quantify traffic, construction, and other activities in urban environments. For ecologists, this technology can help them more accurately monitor and study wildlife. In addition, this information complements what computer vision can sense, as sound can include information about events that are not easily visible, such as sources that are small (e.g., insects), far away (e.g., a distant jackhammer), or simply hidden behind another object (e.g., an incoming ambulance around a building's corner). This project also includes outreach activities involving over 100 public school students and teachers, as well as the training and mentoring of postdoctoral, graduate and undergraduate students.
 
This project will develop computational models for spatial sound scene description: that is, estimating the class, spatial location, direction and speed of movement of living beings and objects in real environments by the sounds they make. The investigators aim for their solutions to be robust across a wide range of sound scenes and sensing conditions: noisy, sparse, natural, urban, indoors, outdoors, with varying compositions of sources, with unknown sources, with moving sources, with moving sensors, etc. While current approaches show promise, they are still far from robust in real-world conditions and thus unable to support any of the above scenarios. These shortcomings stem from important data issues such as a lack of spatially annotated real-world audio data, and an over-reliance on poor quality, unrealistic synthesized data; as well as methodological issues such as excessive dependence on supervised learning and a failure to capture the structure of the solution space. This project plans an approach mixing innovative data collection strategies with cutting-edge machine learning solutions. First, it advances a novel framework for the probabilistic synthesis of soundscape datasets using physical and generative models. The goal is to substantially increase the amount, realism and diversity of strongly-labeled spatial audio data. Second, it collects and annotates new datasets of real sound scenes via a combination of high-quality field recordings, crowdsourcing, novel VR/AR multimodal annotation strategies and large-scale annotation by citizen scientists. Third, it puts forward novel deep self-supervised representation learning strategies trained on vast quantities of unlabeled audio data. Fourth, these representation modules are paired with hierarchical predictive models, where the top/bottom levels of the hierarchy correspond to coarser/finer levels of scene description. Finally, the project includes collaborations with three industrial partners to explore applications enabled by the proposed solutions. The project will result in novel methods and open source software libraries for spatial sound scene generation, annotation, representation learning, and sound event detection/localization/tracking; and new open datasets of spatial audio recordings, spatial sound scene annotations, synthesized isolated sounds, and synthesized spatial soundscapes.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The Spatial Sound Scene Description (S3D) project focused on developing computational approaches for describing living beings and objects in real environments by the sounds they make. In particular the project’s efforts centered around (1) developing solutions for the synthesis of spatial soundscapes at scale; (2) collecting and annotating datasets of real spatial sounds scenes; (3) proposing novel representation learning solutions for spatial sound; and (4) advancing scene description solutions that identify and localize sound events in 3D.

 

Notably, the project produced the first, open framework for the large-scale generation of spatial soundscapes, Spatial Scaper; advanced the state of the art in audio representation learning with novel multimodal and audio-only approaches; and created a first of its kind self-supervised acoustic imaging approach, Latent Acoustic Mapping (LAM), combining classical spatial signal processing methods with the scalability and robustness of modern machine learning solutions. In addition it advanced our understanding of biases and robustness in audio representation learning, proposed new evaluation paradigms for sound event detection and localization, augmented audiovisual machine learning research by increasing our understanding of the challenges and limitations of vision-centric models, and advanced research in machine learning for acoustic modeling and room parameter estimation. These contributions hold the potential to speed up machine learning research into spatial audio, from modeling and simulation, to representation, classification, localization and reasoning, and create opportunities for technology transfer, with the project already exploring applications of these techniques in urban and industrial monitoring, media production and extended reality.  

 

Importantly, the project made important contributions to the development of human resources in science, engineering and technology. We provided mentoring and training opportunities for 13 post-doctoral researchers and doctoral students specializing in STEM areas including acoustics, machine learning, signal processing, and sound technologies. It is worth mentioning that nearly half of these scholars self-identify as women or non-binary, and a third as BIPOC. Eight of them started full time jobs in industry and academia within the duration of the project. In addition the project provided training opportunities for over a dozen master's, undergraduate and high school students, and collaborated to provide STEM training for 70+ middle school students from the NYC public school system.

award.abstractText:
Big data are increasingly encountered across society and all of the sciences and pose novel challenges for statistical analysis, due to their complexity and size. Challenging data analysis tasks that motivate this research originate in brain imaging, genomics, the social sciences and many other areas of current interest. To make sense of such data and extract relevant information requires principled statistical methodology that is suitable for the analysis of large samples of complex data. Examples include networks or age-at-death distributions for which common algebraic operations such as sums or differences are not defined. In many instances such data objects may also be repeatedly observed over time, and the quantification of their time dynamics is then of great interest. For example, one might be interested to determine whether sudden changes occur and where these are located in time.  Statistical methodology will be developed that addresses these data analytic needs, along with theory and efficient computational implementations. This new methodology is expected to lead to substantial new insights. For example, it will be possible to quantify phenomena such as changes in temperature, mortality or income distributions over calendar years, or changes in brain connectivity networks as a function of age, which will aid in distinguishing normal and pathological brain aging. The new methodology will also make it possible to detect differences between groups of complex data, for example between the mortality distribution of countries, including the identification of clusters. The project also provides research training opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students. 

The focus of this research is the development of statistical methods and theory for random objects, i.e., metric space valued random variables, including object-valued functional and longitudinal data. Due to the lack of Euclidean structure, existing methods from high-dimensional and functional data analysis are generally not applicable for metric-space valued random objects. This motivates the development of novel approaches that address the challenge of a lack of Euclidean structure.  Major lines of inquiry will be regression and change-point models for random objects on one hand and methods for trajectories of random objects including complex functional data on the other. New regression and change-point models to be studied include distributions as predictors; regression models for point processes; inference and single index modeling for Frechet regression; and change-point analysis for sequences of object data under various scenarios. For object-valued functional data, an emphasis will be the development of time warping models for random objects and of models for longitudinal random objects in various spaces, including the case where the data are only sparsely and irregularly observed in time. Tools and theory for principled statistical analysis of random objects to be developed will rely on empirical process theory for M estimators in metric spaces, U statistics and related approaches. These developments will lead to the creation of a toolbox suitable for data analysis of object data and associated freely available software.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
New statistical methodology was developed in the areas of functional data analysis and object data analysis.  These are rapidly expanding areas within the field of nonparametric statistics, which serve the need to analyze new types of data that are increasingly common. In functional data analysis one deals with data that are recordings of one or several functions per subject or experimental unit, while object data are complex data such as distributional data, where each data element in a sample is an entire distribution. Common other types of object data are samples of data located on spheres such as wind directions, and also data consisting of networks or trees, among many other types of complex data.

Specifically, in this project the following results were achieved:  Based on functional data analysis methodology,  new models for the dynamics of Covid-19 and other infectious diseases were developed  that allow for more precise estimation of the time delay between exposure and infection; new tests were obtained for the mean function in functional data analysis, e.g., whether two or more than two sets of functional data have the same mean function. Other research outcomes included  methods to determine the order of development of the components of human growth, for example whether leg length increases before arm length when either boys or girls enter puberty; new  methods to rank baseball players and to determine how volatile their ranks are over one season. Two applications of functional data analysis were in neuroimaging for MRI based quantification of longitudinal brain development for a situation with very sparse measurements and in social sciences where the historical trajectories of political ideology and their changes over their tenure were studied for U.S. Supreme Court justices.

For the area of object data, a challenging  extension of functional principal component methodology to  the analysis of smooth random trajectories on  Riemannian manifolds  was developed for the  case of sparsely observed data and furthermore a simple approach based on distances from the mean function was discovered and analyzed,  with emphasis on networks.  Several extensions were made to a relatively new  method of Fréchet regression where one has Euclidean predictors and object responses, an increasingly common regression setting. These extensions included subprojects on a total variation penalized version of Fréchet regression,  on the selection of covariates and on single index Fréchet regression motived by the need for dimension reduction in the predictor space. Basic properties of distributions of random objects were explored with distance profiles, which also were used as  the basis for a new two-sample test and for change-point detection in sequences of random objects.  Applications include the assessment of  brain connectivity, including quantifying changes in brain networks associated with early life brain development and brain aging in late life; New York taxi traffic data;  the secular evolution of mortality; quantifying the relative performance of baseball players; assessing human growth across various parts of the body; the relation of air pollution and wind in Sacramento; the evolving distributions of maximal and minimal temperatures over calendar years; and various other outcomes.

The new methodology was coded in software. The resulting R packages are publicly available. Several graduate students were trained to participate in both statistical methodology and in collaborative applied research. Several students graduated with PhDs on topics in functional data analysis and object data.  The results of the research conducted in this project informed the curriculum of graduate classes. The newly developed methods were successfully applied in a number of interdisciplinary projects,  leading to new scientific insights. The results were disseminated in publications and in invited talks at national and international conferences and at universities.

award.abstractText:
This Faculty Early Career Development (CAREER) grant investigates machine learning-based sensing and control methods to improve the efficiency and quality of scalable and high-precision subtractive and additive micromanufacturing processes.  Machine learning-based methods take advantage of massive amounts of data collected from sensors and actuators to discover patterns and draw inference using mathematical algorithms and statistical models.  This represents a new avenue for innovation in process monitoring and control for emerging micromanufacturing technologies (e.g., roll-to-roll printing of flexible electronics) where prior knowledge is limited but sensor data is rich. By leveraging advanced machine learning methods that are guided by physical manufacturing knowledge, this research increases understanding of sensing-based control, thus enabling significant enhancement in the process performance, stability and adaptiveness required for high-precision and high-rate manufacturing.  Ultimately this work benefits society by enabling next-generation manufacturing that is more precise, more reliable and that produces more complex products with less material waste, lower defect rates, and higher efficiency. The knowledge obtained from this research is used to support the education and training of future manufacturing scientists and engineers recruited from a diverse and dynamic group that includes underrepresented minorities and women in this field.

The goal of this project is to advance the fundamental understanding of data-driven machine learning-based precision control for micromanufacturing processes. The novel unified framework and methods developed in this research transform state-of-the-art process control from a model-based standard to a data-driven model-free paradigm, ultimately pushing new levels of accuracy and precision of complex micromanufacturing systems. The major innovation involves a novel sensing-perception-learning-control framework that leads to meeting the following research objectives: 1) create a low-dimensional and low-noise latent state representation from abundant multimodal sensor data for process state estimation through probabilistic deep learning methods, and provide fundamental knowledge required to realize high-quality monitoring; 2) establish a novel Perception-based Iterative Learning Control (PILC) method with controllers to achieve unprecedented accuracy in precision process control, and 3) experimentally demonstrate and validate the unified framework and a set of sensor-based deep inference and learning-based control algorithms on two specific advanced micromanufacturing processes, ion-mill etching (subtractive) and roll-to-roll gravure printing (additive).  The fundamental understandings directly advance the real-time control capability of high-precision manufacturing processes with tighter tolerance, and guide potential routes for achieving manufacturing capabilities augmented by sensing technologies and advanced data analytics.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.abstractText:
The prevalence of high-speed data management and communication systems have produced countless large volumes of high-veracity, real-time data collections across many domains. For example, natural disasters initiate a myriad of human communications, data exchange, and situational assessments. It is crucial to quickly collect and analyze all of the relevant data, as life or death decisions may rest on the outcome. Hurricane Irma in 2017 caused the largest civil evacuation in Florida’s history and emphasizes two critical problems in emergency management: 1) pre-storm evacuation coordination; and 2) post-storm support for shelter-in-place locations. Disaster information integration and fusion technologies have the potential to deliver enhanced situational awareness tools across all sectors, enabling a more efficient, effective, and automated emergency management and recovery process. However, there is no discernible approach to identify and exploit the underlying patterns of each dataset while also minimizing possible drawbacks. This project aims to utilize multimodal data, such as text messages, images, videos, traffic information, and geo-referencing information, from various sources including social media, news, government announcements, and radio broadcasts. This work will investigate the analysis and fusion of this information to provide useful insights for aiding the decision-making process for both residents and government agencies. The goal is to develop new tools and technologies that can support emergency managers to better evaluate the effectiveness of disaster management policies such as evacuation. 

The proposed research provides potential solutions to solve crucial information analysis challenges related to disaster information management while leveraging the team's previous work. In addition, the team's research approach offers rapid key information identification, efficient multimodal data integration that facilitates emergency management, and enhances dynamic community disaster information sharing. Moreover, solutions developed could later be extended to other domains in the information management field. This project fosters collaboration among two institutions, Florida International University (FIU) and University of Tokyo, as well as institutions across the public and private sectors, to develop advanced techniques for effective emergency response and disaster management. The broader impact of this work will lead to scientific advances in the preparation, response, recovery, and mitigation of major disasters. As the largest graduate Hispanic Serving Institution in the continental United States, FIU will also benefit from the impact of this project that expands the participation of underrepresented groups in STEM fields. The research findings of this project will be broadly disseminated via publications, presentations, and an organized workshop.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This award fostered the international collaboration between US and Japan teams from the Florida International University and The University of Tokyo and prepared the teams to get ready for developing data-driven tools to aid emergency managers for emergency response and disaster management. Disasters initiate a myriad of human communications, data exchange, and situational assessments. It is crucial to quickly collect and analyze all the relevant data as life or death decisions may rest on the outcome, which can facilitate emergence responses and disaster management. Therefore, in this project, the research team has conducted research to answer the following three questions: (1) How we can collect the data essential for disaster management and response; (2) What forms of data integration, fusion, and visualization will aid emergency responders, and how these tools can be used to improve disaster response; and (3) How population mobility data can be utilized to help formulate disaster evacuation planning.

The research team gathered a collection of multimodal data, including social media, mobility, and other disaster-related information, to effectively improve situation monitoring, estimation, and prediction for disaster management. A number of community-identified applications were developed to facilitate disaster management and support decision making for the managers. Specifically, we found it important to identify the communities in crisis after disaster events. The research framework for the in-crisis community identification problem has been designed by integrating expertises from both US and Japan teams. Meanwhile, data-driven analytics techniques to process disaster-related multimedia data for disaster scene detection, building damage estimation, human mobility nowcasting during disasters, etc., have been investigated and developed.

In response to the emerging challenges due to COVID-19 pandemic, we have also investigated potentials of pandemic management based on the proposed framework of this project. To better understand the art of the existing data-driven approaches in COVID-19 and pandemic management, the team conducted a comprehensive survey on data-driven methods for COVID-19 management and existing public data sources for COVID-19. On top of that, the infection prediction model under various mobility restriction policies, as well as techniques to estimate economic impacts of pandemics, have been tackled. Currently, in total, 11 journal and conference articles have been published or accepted for publication in the top venues in the related domains, such as artificial intelligence, data mining, and disaster management.

During the research and development, the team closely worked with the community stakeholders and partners to understand the problems in practice and validate the usefulness of the proposed research ideas. The research team has delivered the integrated analysis based on the developed research outcomes to support public authorities, including the Miami-Dade Emergency Operations Center, Cabinet Office of Japan, Tokyo Metropolis Government, and Nagasaki Prefecture Government.

Furthermore, two workshops were held to gather community stakeholders, county representatives, and institute and academy members and to obtain feedback and suggestions from the community. In the first workshop, titled ?Hurricanes and COVID-19: Impact and Lessons Learned,? we engaged with multiple upper ranks of emergency managers from Miami-Dade Emergency Operations Center and learned the pain points that can arise when dealing with hurricanes along with COVID-19. In the second workshop, titled ?Hurricanes and COVID-19: Lessons Learned and Directions for the Future,? we brought together multidisciplinary researchers with expertise in disaster management to provide an open dialog to exchange ideas and generate new research topics regarding responding to the hurricanes while considering the impact of COVID-19. Some valuable research directions, such as utilizing multimodal information on the internet of things (IoT) and smart cities to enable the formation of efficient disaster management systems, were discussed. We refined and solidified our research plan based on the discussions and obtained feedback from both workshops.

The broader impacts of this project have been three-fold. First, the proposed techniques have provided the opportunities to build a first-of-its-kind framework to better understand the disaster situation to assist the disaster preparation and recovery for the community while our preliminary studies have illustrated the effectiveness of multimodal data integration in solving many use-inspired problems in disaster management; Second, the developed multimodal data analyses could enable effective and continuous monitoring and understanding of the people under the impact of disasters and the communities in crisis. The proposed techniques in this project can prevent unexpected losses by avoiding inappropriate policies and supporting decision-making during disasters in United States, Japan, and all other counties and regions over the world; Third, this project provides a new computational approach to analyze and synthesize the data of human behaviors, geographical information, economic and societal status, etc. Such methods can be broadly applied to many other fields and domains, such as geographical information system, social science research, epidemiology modeling, and public health applications.

To advance the use of novel technologies to increase student learning outcomes, educational technology must be coupled with a deep understanding of how students learn and retain information. Thus, technology and the learning environment must work together to enable pedagogical approaches that promote student-centered learning. To set a research agenda for the technology-enhanced learning environment of the future, this collaborative project will conduct a series of events that explore the Future of Innovative Learning Environments.  These events will include a series of interactive, online discussions followed by an in-person workshop. Workshop participants will include twenty-nine expert participants from academia, industry, and nonprofits.

This project aims to inform the future of learning environments in STEM higher education.  The project will consider the near-term and longer-term impacts, opportunities, challenges, and future research initiatives related to the development and implementation of innovative learning environments. This project will include three components: 1) Interactive, online discussions (microlabs) prior to the workshop will introduce participants to different innovative learning environments and solicit feedback from a range of stakeholders;  2) Participants at a two-day in-person workshop will engage in creative activities that help them envision how innovative learning environments might transform STEM higher education; and 3) the PIs and invited participants will synthesize the discussions and produce a report that can guide future.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The eXploring the Future of Innovative Learning Environments (X-FILEs) project team organized a variety of student- and faculty-focused events to learn how they can better use technology in STEM higher education. The first and largest event was a workshop held in 2018 for 30 faculty and education researchers to envision how technology-enhanced learning environments could transform STEM higher education within the next seven years (2019-2026). Stakeholders such as university administrators, technology developers, and students were also represented in the workshop. Workshop participants discussed and explored four main technology categories as they relate to STEM teaching and learning: personalized and adaptive learning, multimodal learning, cross reality (XR), and artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML). In order to frame the examination of where and how these technologies may impact students? learning experience, participants addressed opportunities for gains, challenges/barriers, implementation strategies, and future research questions related to each. In each case, they examined the impact on the various aspects of teaching and learning: Presentation and Instruction, Interactions and Communications, and Evaluation and Assessment Techniques.

Participants synthesized the ideas, questions, challenges, and solutions proposed during the workshop into a scholarly book, Innovative Learning Environments in STEM Higher Education, published by Springer in 2021. Examples of education research discussed at the workshop appear in a special issue of special issue of the journal Interactive Learning Environments titled ?Cross Reality (XR) and Immersive Learning Environments (ILE) in Education,? published in 2020 and co-edited by several workshop organizers.

The next phase of this project was to understand the perspective of students regarding their use of technology in STEM classes. The project team hosted a one-day Student Jam event in February 2020 and another in April 2021. Working in teams, college students majoring in STEM disciplines created solutions to improve or enhance college-level STEM education using various technologies. The second Student Jam, occurring towards the end of social distancing and masking requirements, focused more on post-pandemic STEM education. Keeping with connective themes of the original 2018 X-FILEs Workshop, the same four technology categories and aspects of teaching and learning were incorporated into the Jam. Each team?s ideation process was captured and transcribed. A summary of the first Student Jam is included in the X-FILEs workshop book mentioned earlier.

The COVID-19 pandemic occurred soon after the first Student Jam. The ensuing social distancing and masking requirements caused college faculty to quickly change the way they teach traditionally hands-on STEM activities (e.g., lab experiments) to online instructional settings. How faculty and students use mundane technologies like video conferencing apps and their access to technologies like wifi became critical to students? education. In fall 2021, the research team decided to pivot to explore this issue, rather than focus on more cutting-edge technologies such as artificial intelligence and cross reality.

 The research team held online discussions in fall 2021 with faculty who, in spring 202, had little to no prior experience with remote/online teaching or using extensive educational technology in their classrooms. Participants shared the challenges that they faced while others presented unexpected advantages of using technologies related to online education. They also conveyed how their experiences shape their attitudes towards future use of technology in STEM education. These findings about teaching and learning during the pandemic are consistent with themes that are emerging in the education research literature. The project team continues to study this.

In spring 2022, the research team conducted a series of focus groups with college STEM majors who had experienced STEM courses before the COVID-19 pandemic, during the pandemic?s disruption, and after students returned to face-to-face classes. The research team is analyzing the focus groups? transcripts now.

award.abstractText:
This project concerns consistency in scientific inferences. Multiple observations of the same phenomenon rarely produce identical results. Statistical noise may be the first complication that comes to mind, but there are plenty of other possible discrepancies as well: different antenna arrangements; different camera angles; different modalities, e.g., images and text; and more. Inferring the true underlying phenomenon requires sophisticated mathematics. This project focuses on matrix methods. Hiding within the simple numerical entries of a matrix are intricate patterns called eigenvectors that are connected to the harmonics of musical instruments. Even though different kinds of measurements may produce different numerical values, they may share the same eigenvectors when observing the same objects. One of the goals of the project is to pull consistency out of inconsistent data. In theory, measurements on the same object from different instruments should agree in certain ways, but because of statistical noise and other sources of error and uncertainty, each instrument provides an inexact view of the world, and the two instruments will not agree perfectly with each other. The goal is to bring the measurements into alignment using mathematics and therefore likely into better agreement with the true state of the universe. The project will be completed at a Primarily Undergraduate Institution, and introducing undergraduate students to research in STEM fields is a primary objective.

The mathematical focus of the project is simultaneous diagonalization of commuting Hermitian matrices. In theory, commuting Hermitian matrices share a common eigenvector matrix. However, numerically-computed eigenvectors may differ wildly in the presence of ill conditioning. A numerical method for simultaneous diagonalization seeks, either explicitly or implicitly, small perturbations of the input matrices that commute exactly. The project objectives include contributions to theory, method, and application. First, a reconsideration of "near commutativity" is planned, in which eigenvalues are fixed in place and attention shifts from the space of Hermitian matrices to the unitary group of eigenvector matrices. Second, the project will pursue new numerical methods for simultaneous diagonalization, motivated in part by relatively recent spectral divide-and-conquer methods. Third, the new approaches will be applied to applications such as independent component analysis and unsupervised machine learning with multimodal data.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors arise throughout science and engineering, for example, in the resonant frequencies and vibrational modes of a physical structure. This project considered situations in which two or more systems share eigenvectors. This can happen, for instance, when the systems arise from different views of the same underlying phenomenon. Often, the combination of observations provides a deeper and clearer view than any one of the observations alone. At the same time, this opportunity presents a challenge: for the results to make any sense, a mathematical or computational method must recover consistency from potentially noisy observations.

The project work focused on new mathematical and computational methods for the simultaneous eigenvector problem. The outcomes include new algorithms capable of handling much larger problems than have been feasible in the recent past. The algorithms are also quite flexible, leveraging existing methods for the single matrix problem: as advances continue to be made on the single-input problem, the new algorithm will automatically benefit.

The impacts of our algorithm may be felt in areas such as data science and physics. An example application to data science is multimodal classification, in which different kinds of views of the same object, e.g., images and verbal descriptions, are combined to organize unstructured data sets. Within physics, there are sensitive systems and special symmetries that benefit from our algorithm's ability to balance multiple inputs.

The work was supported by the program "Facilitating Research at Primarily Undergraduate Institutions," and four of the participating researchers were undergraduate students. They participated in an intense summer-long research experience, during which they collaboratively investigated original research questions and shared their findings in writing and through oral presentations. Participants have also presented their work at conferences and have prepared a technical article.

award.abstractText:
Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a skin disease caused by a parasitic infection, which affects up to one million people each year. There are many shortcomings to current drug treatments for this disease, including hearing loss and kidney damage. The goal of this joint North Carolina State University (NCSU) and Ohio State University (OSU) project is to understand the unique functionality of a microscale biosystem containing microneedle array that (a) emits light from an optical component and subsequently (b) provides local release of a drug with antiparasitic activity. This project seeks to better understand a new type of microscale device technology that both (a) uses focused light to treat the parasitic infection and (b) uses a small pump to deliver an antiparasitic drug directly to the site of infection. Functionality of the novel device that provides both light therapy and drug therapy will be compared with devices that provide either light therapy or drug therapy alone. Goal of the project is to evaluate the feasibility of the multimodal technology to enhance treatment efficiency by comparing with different types of therapies. Graduate students will be trained in fiber optics and microfabrication of functional biosystems technologies   and will be mentored in effective methods for teaching large groups. The PI will disseminate results from the project through quarterly Science Saturday lectures and hands-on activities at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences. The technical benefit of this project lies in forming the basis for multimodal technology that will have significant impact on new types of precise treatments for cancer and other diseases.

The intellectual merit associated with this project involves developing a better understanding of multimodal technologies, which include two or more types of pharmacologic therapy and/or device-based therapy; this technology is considered an emerging area of engineering research. Objective 1 will involve fabrication of a microscale biosystem containing optical fibers, a pump, and a microneedle array. Objective 2 will involve testing and validation of the microscale biosystem. Objective 1 and 2 will be performed at NCSU. Objective 3 will involve evaluation of the efficacy of the microscale biosystem in which optical functionality and drug delivery functionality are provided together; comparisons of this multimodal approach to drug therapy alone and light therapy alone will be performed at OSU. The feasibility study supported by this project will enable submission of a full proposal on comprehensively understanding the design of the microscale biosystem. It is anticipated that this microscale biosystem can provide a more effective treatment of cutaneous leishmaniasis than conventional drug therapy, which is associated with repeated dosing, long treatment times, and toxicity.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This EAGER project, which was performed by North Carolina State University (NCSU) and The Ohio State University (OSU), examined the development of a light-integrated multimodal microscale biosystem for transdermal delivery of amphotericin B to treat cutaneous leishmaniasis. It should be noted that microneedles offer several benefits for antileishmanial and antiparasitic therapy, including low manufacturing cost, ease of use, absence of pain, and minimization of trauma at the treatment site. 

In one study, microneedles were loaded for the delivery of amphotericin B, the gold standard therapy for cutaneous leishmaniasis and fungal infections. One of the main drawbacks of conventional polymeric microneedles is their limited capability for effectively loading a sufficient amount of a drug. Furthermore, the loading process itself may potentially cause damage or affect the potency of certain drugs. In the paper Machekposhti SA, Kadian S, Vanderwal L, Stafslien S, Narayan RJ. Novel hollow biodegradable microneedle for amphotericin B delivery. MedComm. 2023 Aug;4(4):e321, a previously unexplored form of biodegradable hollow microneedle was successfully described. Creating biodegradable hollow microneedles involved the use of a biodegradable material known as Gantrez® AN 119 BF, which was processed into the desired shape. In order to load the hollow microneedles with a powdered version of the drug amphotericin B, a process was utilized that involved both vacuuming and shaking simultaneously. Through this particular approach, a significantly large quantity of medication was able to be successfully loaded into the microneedles. In order to measure the mechanical properties of the microneedles, nanoindentation and mechanical testing were employed. The technique known as laser confocal microscopy was utilized in order to precisely measure the exact dimensions of the microneedles. The results from antifungal testing revealed that the microneedles containing amphotericin B were effective in inhibiting the growth of Candida albicans.

In another study that is under review by the Informa (Taylor & Francis) journal Drug Delivery, the NCSU and OSU researchers showed that microneedle-based injection of Fungizone/Amphotericin B is an effective treatment for American cutaneous leishmaniasis in a murine model We considered the use of hollow microneedles to directly deliver Amphotericin B to localized cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) lesions. Our hypothesis suggests that this method would effectively inhibit parasite growth without causing any systemic toxicity. A three-by-three array of 1 mm tall stainless steel hollow microneedles was utilized to successfully administer Fungizone/Amphotericin B into the skin. In order to accurately assess the effectiveness of our treatment, we conducted experiments using Leishmania mexicana-infected BALB/c mice as a model. After administering 10 and 20 consecutive days of microneedle treatments, our results demonstrated a significant decrease in parasitic burden in both trials, with the 20-day trial showing particularly promising results in limiting lesion growth compared to the control groups who received a placebo. A notable finding from the 10-day trial was the absence of any increase in blood serum creatinine or blood urea nitrogen levels, suggesting that there was no kidney toxicity. The results of this study have shown potential for use of hollow microneedles for the treatment of cutaneous leishmaniasis. The utilization of these products has the potential to significantly decrease the burden of cutaneous leishmaniasis among those affected by cutraneous leishmaniasis.

We also examined another multimodal microneedle device, which contained sensors. In Kadian S, Kumari P, Sahoo SS, Shukla S, Narayan RJ. Machine learning enabled microneedle-based colorimetric pH sensing patch for wound health monitoring and meat spoilage detection. Microchemical Journal. 2024 Mar 19:110350, our team successfully created a user-friendly and affordable machine learning-powered microneedle-based colorimetric pH sensing patch, which has the potential to transform wound health monitoring. The 3D-printed microneedle array enabled autonomous fluid extraction and pH sensing via surface tension. In order to determine the precise pH level based on the observed color on the pH-test strip, a machine learning model was meticulously developed using a collection of various color images acquired from numerous experiments with known pH solutions. In order to support to the needs of older individuals and those with color blindness, a user-friendly and accessible web application that utilizes the developed machine learning model was implemented. In order to demonstrate the effectiveness of the developed patch, a proof-of-concept study was conducted. Based on the analytical results, the newly created machine learning enabled microneedle-based colorimetric pH sensing patch shows potential for wound health monitoring.

Presentations were delivered at the Society for Biomaterials Annual Meeting, the MS&T Annual Meeting, the MDPI Sensors Webinar Series, as well as invited seminars at CEA-Leti (France), RMIT University (Australia), and Florida State University.

Graduate students at NCSU and OSU received training in microfabrication, biosystem integration, and analytical methods.

The research team provided demonstrations on microneedle fabrication, biosensing, and bioprinting to educators and North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences visitors. These events promoted public engagement with science & engineering topics; moreover, the events sought to inspire interest among the museum visitors in STEM careers.
