award.abstractText:
The human brain has been studied extensively for centuries, but the role of biomechanics remains mostly unknown. Recent advances in medical imaging, experimentation, and computational modeling, however, have led to a growing body of evidence linking biomechanics of the human brain with major processes in brain development, disease, and damage. Brain biomechanics establishes a relationship between the brain’s structure, function, and motion using the methods of applied mechanics. This Leading Engineering for America's Prosperity, Health, and Infrastructure (LEAP-HI) project combines novel medical imaging methods, image analysis, computational modeling, and mechanical testing to determine the fundamental mechanical properties of living brain tissues and the differences in properties between healthy and diseased tissues, and may enable the early diagnosis and prevention of neurological disorders, such as stroke, traumatic brain injury, and dementia. As such, the project has the potential to reduce the financial burden on society and increase the quality of life for millions of people. Outreach activities in brain mechanics will be provided for underrepresented groups in science and engineering, as well as training opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students, and postdoctoral researchers.

The research will provide a novel platform for investigating the mechanobiology of the human brain in health and disease. The research team will develop a novel approach to merge advanced neuroimaging tools and multi-physics brain modeling into a semi-automated pipeline for the in vivo investigation of brain mechanics. Ultrahigh field magnetic resonance imaging technology merged with automated imaging-modeling integration will be utilized to enable the subject-specific investigation of brain mechanics across disparate spatio-temporal scales. Specifically, ultrahigh resolution mechanical, structural, and connectomic neuroimaging tools will be developed and integrated with automatic brain segmentation and mesh generation for finite element and isogeometric analysis to create multi-scale brain mechanics computer models. These tools will then be utilized to provide an in-depth characterization of the mechanobiochemical response of traumatic brain injury, in decompressive craniectomies for stroke patients, and the coupling between prion-like protein progression and cerebral atrophy in dementia. By developing a pipeline for the creation of personalized, data-driven brain models, the research team will demonstrate the transformative power of combined imaging, modeling, and machine learning techniques towards better understanding, improved treatment, and ultimately preventive medicine for neurological disorders.

award.abstractText:
Virtual Reality (VR) promises to provide a compelling, effective, and convenient means for training and reskilling the workforce. The objective of this project is to devise a computational design framework for guiding the synthesis of personalized virtual training environments for human performance. Designers and general users can intuitively apply this framework for synthesizing a variety of immersive and engaging VR training scenarios in a fully automatic, fast, scalable, and low-cost manner. As a showcase of the proposed framework, the project will demonstrate how to synthesize personalized virtual training environments for workforce training, such as safety inspection training for employees, workplace supervisors, and safety inspectors. This research project offers a novel interdisciplinary perspective for generating personalized VR training content by bringing together expertise and insights from human-computer interaction, virtual reality, computer graphics, machine learning, and optimization, as well as domain expertise in instructional design, safety, emergency management, and engineering. Designers and general users can use this framework to synthesize personalized VR training content for a variety of scenarios such as rehabilitation, safety training, disaster response training, as well as workforce training for different domains such as manufacturing, construction, logistics, transportation, retail management, and public safety.

To achieve the project’s objectives, the researchers will address the following research question: (1) How to track human performance under virtual scenarios? A VR station will be set up which is capable of tracking multimodal body data such as gaze, body pose, hand movement, and the locomotion of a trainee in performing tasks in a virtual workplace. Based on such tracked data, machine learning models are trained to analyze and characterize the trainee’s skill levels. (2) How to synthesize virtual environments for personalized training? Optimization approaches will be formulated for synthesizing realistic and highly immersive virtual environments for adaptively training the trainee considering his/her skill levels, preferences, and personal training goals. (3) How to evaluate VR training effects? The investigator will evaluate the effectiveness of the synthesized VR training experiences by comparing with alternative training approaches quantitatively in terms of performance gain and knowledge retention; and qualitatively by obtaining domain experts’ and participants’ feedback about the effectiveness, enjoyment, and engagement of the training experience. To facilitate easy deployment and widespread adoption of personalized VR training, the investigator will publicly disseminate the software tools and toolkits devised through project websites, workshops, and research papers. In addition, the investigator will disseminate the research by (1) setting up an open-access VR station at the George Mason University’s Makerspace where faculty, students, and staff from various disciplines can conveniently experience personalized VR training; (2) organizing interdisciplinary VR training workshops and demo days to disseminate the VR training research findings, to showcase the VR training demos to the public, and to stimulate the research and adoption of VR training in different disciplines; (3) broadening the participation of first-generation underrepresented undergraduate students in computing and VR training research via a series of focused mentoring activities organized in collaboration with the Louis Stokes Alliance for Minority Participation program at the university.

award.abstractText:
Since the first COVID-19 case was diagnosed and reported at the end of December 2019, there have been more than 1.6 million COVID-19 cases reported, causing more than 100,000 death worldwide as of April 10, 2020. The outbreak of COVID-19 has significantly affected individuals and our society as a whole, and many national and international events have been canceled over COVID-19 fears, including NBA, NCAA events, Mobile World Congress. For the sake of either individual, institutes, or governments, a risk prediction and update system are urgently needed. However, to design and implement such a system, there are several system challenges. First, how to derive the infection risk level from different granularities, i.e., individual-, event-, and institution-levels? Second, how to dynamically update the risk level based on the latest outbreak news? Third, how to preserve user sensitive data while sharing adequate data for risk level calculation? To attack these challenges in this RAPID project, researchers at Wayne State University and Henry Ford Health Systems design and implement CORPUS, an edge intelligence-assisted, multi-granularity COVID-19 Risk Prediction, and Update System, which includes a mobile app running on personal phones, as well as a large-scale distributed protocol behind the app collecting and updating the information. First, CORPUS will build a multi-granularity risk analysis model, from fine-grained personal risk to small clustered meeting risk, to coarse-grained large clustered event risk, and institutional/organization risk. Second, CORPUS employs a data propagation protocol to build and update the risk analysis model. The data that can contribute to CORPUS include spatial data (such as GPS signal), temporal data (such as calendar event), as well as the input from the user (such as meeting with a specific person). Third, CORPUS leverages privacy-preserving algorithms such as node-level feature pooling and anonymous parameter of the model instead of raw user data, to ensure the confidentiality of personal information when multi-granularity models request personal risk information. 

With the rapid expansion of COVID-19, there is an urgent need for the individual to know their infection risk when traveling to a place in the foreseeable future. CORPUS can meet their needs by leveraging personalized information and edge intelligence. For a group or an organization, CORPUS will provide risk-related information to help them to judge the feasibility of holding a meeting or an event during an outbreak, especially for large-scale international events (such as the Olympics and World Cup). They can also proactively take action based on the risk information provided by CORPUS to reduce the spread of COVID-19. CORPUS will help governments perceive the risk of infection in their jurisdictions, and thus guide infection prevention and control for effective governance.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project developed a cloud-edge-device framework to support the risk level analysis and prediction for the region, event, and person during the pandemic. In general, we have completed six tasks: (1) collecting and analyzing the pandemic data collected from trustworthy data providers; (2) implementing a cloud-edge-device layered framework to provide prediction service; (3) launching a mobile application for end-users to receive personalized risk level analysis and prediction; (4) developing the risk prediction models that can protect user’s privacy; and (5) building the SafeCampus platform for campus-wide pandemic forecasting; and (6) developing the SafeClassroom App for Android and iOS.

(1) Data source: The data collected are composed of two types. The first type of data was retrieved from trustworthy sources regarding the number of infections, deaths, and ICU. Another type of data is obtained from News websites about the early infection spread given region information. The dataset covers a long period of time from the start of the pandemic in March 2020 to Nov 2021.

(2) The cloud-edge-device layered framework: Then, we developed a cloud-edge-device layered framework for risk level prediction. It is composed of (a) a mobile app installed on the user's smartphone, monitoring surrounding infection situations, and calculating the user's risk level based on his/her moving trajectory; (b) an edge node interacts with the mobile app, monitoring either a certain region area or a newly held event; (c) a cloud node interacts with the edge nodes to provide information and retrieve pandemic-related data globally.

(3) Mobile app: Next, we launched an Android app that backend by the layered architecture and provides risk level prediction. The main functions of this app include (1) tracing personal risk level, (2) retrieving local early exposure news, (3) searching region risk level. With the goal of preserving user privacy, all the data are stored and processed locally unless obtained uploading permission from users. The app collects GPS signals based on the user's moving speed, tracking and predicting the risk level based on the moving trajectory, close contact, and regional risk.

(4) Machine learning models: For the COVID-19 predictions, we developed a novel Spatial-Temporal Synchronous Graph Transformer network (STSGT) which uses the historical COVID data to forecast the future infected and death cases for all the US states. We leveraged the AutoML tool to automatically selects the most proper model given the infection-related data. The layered system maintains a model pool for different regions and updates timely based on the newly collected data. We forecast the future COVID cases for short-term, i.e., next-day forecasting, and long-term, i.e., forecasting over the next 12 days.

(5) SafeCampus platform for campus-wide pandemic forecasting: We then implemented a COVID-19 pandemic forecasting platform for academic institutions after resuming academic activities. The design of this multimodality work is steered by video, audio, and tweets.  We first train diverse models to extract meaningful information from video, audio, and tweets, respectively. Then, we feed the multimodal analysis results with daily confirmed cases data and social distancing metrics into the trained model to predict the daily increase rate of confirmed cases for the main buildings of a university campus. The paper was featured by IEEE Internet Computing Magazine in the Jan/Feb issue of 2022. 

(6) SafeClassroom App for Android and iOS: We also have developed an Android App for the instructors of Wayne State University, named SafeClassroom, which can (1) perform real-time face mask detection (optional), (2) check the QR code of the campus daily screener, and (3) mail the attendee list to the instructor.  The App and has been used by the CSC 8990 Graduate Seminar for Fall 2021 and Winter 2022. Furthermore, we have instructed a group of undergraduate students to develop an iOS version of the SafeClassroom App, which is their capstone project for the undergraduate course CSC 4996 Senior Project and Computer Ethics. The students were very excited to apply what they learned in the classroom to address real-world problems.

award.abstractText:
Transfer learning provides crucial techniques for utilizing data from related studies that are conducted under different contexts or on diverse populations. It is an important topic with a wide range of applications in integrative genomics, neuroimaging, computer vision and signal processing. This research work will provide new tools to scientific researchers who routinely collect and analyze high dimensional and complex data across different sources and platforms. This project aims to develop new analytical tools to improve conventional methods by delivering more informative and interpretable scientific findings. The developed transfer learning algorithms, which can reliably extract and combine knowledge from diverse data types and across different studies, will help address important issues from genomics applications. User-friendly software packages will be developed and made publicly available. Scientific researchers can use the tools to translate dispersed and heterogeneous data sources into new knowledge and medical benefits. This will help improve the understanding of the role of various genetic factors in complex diseases, and accelerate the development of new medicines and treatments in a cost-effective way. 

Transfer learning for large-scale inference aims to extract and transfer the knowledge learned from related source domains to assist the simultaneous inference of thousands or even millions of parameters in the target domain. We aim to develop a general framework to gain understanding of the benefits and caveats of transfer learning in a wide range of large-scale inference problems including sparse estimation, false discovery rate analysis, sparse linear discriminant analysis and high-dimensional regression. Our research addresses two key issues in transfer learning: (a) What should be transferred? (b) How to transfer and prevent negative learning? We aim to pursue three major research goals. The first is to develop a class of computationally efficient and robust transfer learning algorithms for high-dimensional sparse inference. The general strategy is to first learning the local sparsity structure of the high-dimensional object through auxiliary data and then apply the structural knowledge to the target domain by adaptively placing differential weights or setting varied thresholds on corresponding coordinates. The second is to formalize a decision-theoretic framework for high-dimensional transfer learning that is applicable across the sparse and non-sparse regimes. Along this direction, we aim to develop a class of kernelized nonparametric empirical Bayes methods for data-sharing shrinkage estimation and multiple testing. The third is to address the urgent needs and new challenges arising from important genomics applications using the newly developed methods.

Tony Cai has been supported by DMS-2015259 "Collaborative Research: Transfer Learning for Large-Scale Inference: General Framework and Data-Driven Algorithms" ($250,000) from 07/01/2020 to 06/30/2023. Over these 3 years, the PI has been working on a range of problems concerning the theoretical and methodological aspects of transfer learning and distributed learning as well as statistical inference with differential privacy guarantees.  He led a research group of Ph.D. students, postdocs, and collaborators on developing theories and methodologies for statistical machine learning and applications in genomics and engineering. 

Major Outcomes and Activities:
1. Published 36 journal papers during the period, including more than 20 papers in leading statistics journals such as the Annals of Statistics, Journal of the American Statistical Association, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society (Series B), and Biometrika. The newly proposed procedures were implemented in R and/or Matlab. All the papers and software were made freely available on his website.
2. Motivated by a diverse array of contemporary statistical applications, a central focus of Tony Cai's research over the past three years has been the development of statistical methodologies and optimality theories for transfer learning as well as statistical inference under non-statistical constraints, including privacy, communication, and computational considerations. These areas are recognized as pivotal in the ever-evolving landscape of data science, extending beyond the traditional boundaries of statistics. Together with his students and postdocs, he has published/finished a series of papers aiming to gain fundamental understanding on transfer learning and the tradeoffs between statistical performance and privacy, communication, or computational constraints. Furthermore, this research has encompassed a diverse range of applications, with notable contributions in the field of biomedical studies. 3. Presented 11 plenary/distinguished lectures, 8 invited talks, and 7 colloquium talks at scientific conferences and universities, including the Laplace Lecture of the Bernoulli Society  at the 10th World Congress in Probability and Statistics in 2021, the Frontiers of Science Award Lecture at the International Congress of Basic Science in 2023, and the Gottfried E. Noether Award Lecture of the American Statistical Association in 2023. These conferences brought together statisticians, probabilists, and medical researchers to advance the theory, methodology and applications of statistical machine learning and high-dimensional statistics. They also provided opportunities for scholars from diverse disciplines to interact and strengthen each other's knowledge and expertise in analyzing data with complex structure to yield maximal new knowledge toward the establishment of rigorous statistical and biological foundations for the better understanding of health and disease. 

Intellectual Merit: 
Under the support of this NSF grant, Tony Cai developed new statistical methods for a range of statistical problems, including large-scale multiple testing, nonparametric regression and classification, high-dimensional linear regression, and high-dimensional generalized linear models, in various settings. These results advanced the theoretical understanding and methodological development for statistical machine learning and analysis of Big Data. Tony Cai's work also advanced fundamental understanding on the tradeoffs between statistical performance and privacy, communication, or computational constraints. In addition, he addressed a range of applications in medical research. 

Broader Impacts:  
The results developed by Tony Cai have significant impact in the broad scientific community. They provide theory, methodology, applications, as well as technical tools to researchers in other scientific fields who collect and analyze high-dimensional data sets. These fields include astronomy, biology, engineering, bioinformatics, as well as various clinical research areas in general. In the last three years, Tony Cai trained (and is training) 3 postdocs and 10 Ph.D. students, including 1 female postdoc and 2 female students. To disseminate the newly obtained results, he taught advanced topics courses on asymptotic theory and high dimensional statistical inference to Ph.D. students and postdocs at Penn. He also gave public lectures on big data at other institutions. All the papers and implementations of the procedures in R/Matlab were available online.

award.abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of a biofeedback training tool to increase student academic performance. As pressures to improve academic performance continue to increase, students are increasingly coming to school emotionally unprepared to learn. This is frequently compounded by the lack of a healthy social and emotional environment within the school to support, motivate, and emotionally engage students. As research has illuminated the important connections between emotions, learning, and performance, it has become apparent that effective school-based interventions are needed to foster and integrate students’ emotional, social, and academic development to provide them with tools and skills needed to increase self-awareness and emotional self-management; promote effective communication; practice healthy, responsible behaviors; and build functional, collaborative relationships. 

This I-Corps project is based on the development of a peripheral autonomic biofeedback training device as an effective process by which patients self-monitor heart rate, skin conductivity, peripheral skin temperature, and respiration rate while attempting to alter their internal responses. Breathing exercises and mindfulness techniques paired with biofeedback display has proven a powerful tool when teaching self-regulation of stress and anxiety. Not surprisingly, a number of studies have closely examined college student populations and their response to biofeedback training. The technology provides an emotion-aware, mental health and wellness platform that uses multimodal peripheral biofeedback, wireless sensor technology, and a goal-oriented software agent that will automatically refine the user experience based on the users’ real-time feedback from emotion-analyzing and gesture-tracking modules. Augmented by software agents, the interactive virtual objects will possess rich personality and emotional states flexible enough to respond to user’s interactions with intelligence and affective awareness. The results of this project will enable further development and translation of gamified, multimodal biofeedback training.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project, Digital Therapeutics using autonomic regulation training for students challenged with debilitating stress, anxiety and depression, began with students taking PI Scott Ransom's Neural Engineering Tech Studio course in 2018.  The student team, called "Panic Away", developed a phone app and devised wearable electronics that would monitor a student's anxiety level and intervene with preprogrammed therapy before the onset of a panic attack.

Panic attacks are debilitating for students, causing missed classes, awkward social exchanges, and additional stress and anxiety about being in public.  Sufferers report an increasing desire to avoid people so that an attack does not happen in a social setting.

Therapies for such attacks are limited, and usually are not at the point-of-care.  The team's idea was to leverage the ubiquitous cell phone as a vehicle for therapy.

PanicAway’s initial prototype relies on a user with access to an iPhone and an Apple Watch that is acting as a heart-rate monitor. When a user’s heart rate exceeds a certain threshold, PanicAway goes to work, first prompting the user and then offering a number of coping features via the phone app.

Their work caught the interest of Geekwire, which published a story about the students and the course (see link below).

 UW students rely on input from professor’s son to create prototype for app that eases panic attacks - GeekWire

After completing the class, the team paired with LifeSpan Digital Health, which provided additional resources and leadership for the project.   

The iCorps grant allowed the team to explore several avenues and develop a minimally viable product (MVP).  During the course of the iCorps program the team was mentored by program faculty and provided funds for travel to do customer discovery.  Over the course of the program the team interivewed over 120 individuals including patients, therapists, counselors, and parents to build an understanding of product-market fit. 

One of the outcomes from this work was the importance of addressing under-served markets.  Minority and low income students indicated a large need for access to these types of therapies.  Access to other therapies is limited in these communities.  Providing this therapy to these groups became a priority for the team.

The customer discovery provided through this grant also helped the team narrow their student focus.  Originally the team was targeting students across academic years, but after conducting customer discovery interviews they realized the two greatest needs were with high school seniors and college freshman.  Students in these transitional years had the greatest incidence of anxiety and panic attacks.  The team decided to focus their efforts on counselors and support groups in these institutions.

The grant provided access to school counseling centers, which are currently partnering with the team to pilot their device and app to students in need, free of charge.  These first-use cases will validate several aspects of the therapy and aid the team in developing future iterations.

Due to the global pandemic, the grant monies earmarked for travel for customer discovery interviews and conference attendance could not be used.  That money was returned to NSF.  Although NSF was able to provide a no-cost extension, and travel restrictions have been lifted as of the time of this writing, the extension was unable to keep the grant active until travel was once again allowed.

While it is unfortunate that the team could only make use of a portion of the grant funds, they made the most with what they had.  They leveraged Zoom and other virtual meeting platforms to engage in customer discovery, and drove to local universities and high schools to meet with counselors and students when such visits were allowed.

Overall the customer discovery results and mentoring provided by the iCorps team were invaluable in helping the team develop their MVP and target appropriate markets, providing the initial product-market fit necessary to progress the therapy further.

award.abstractText:
To access computers, blind people have to use screen readers and/or Braille displays, which make the content of the computer screen accessible, but require much time and patience because users have to search the screen sequentially for relevant content and controls. The goal of this Project is to develop Feel-IT, a portable hardware-device that will enable blind people to interact with computers much faster by using an audio-tactile (hearing and feeling) interface. Blind people will be able to use portable tactile Feel-IT gloves to “feel” the content of the computer screen while moving their hands on the surface of a regular desk. Combining the tactile and auditory sources of feedback will enable Feel-IT users to process information on the computer screen significantly faster. It will also reduce the information overload because they will no longer have to listen to all content that is on the screen. Tactile feedback will make computers more accessible for blind people, thus enabling them to participate fully in our digital society. The transformative idea of Feel-IT is that it will be a single device that will make all screens (including non-touch screens) of any size accessible with audio-tactile feedback. Feel-IT will be evaluated with blind computer users in real-life scenarios. Feel-IT will enable the study of the strategies that blind people employ for audio-tactile interaction with computer, improve our understanding of the optimal audio-tactile interface design, and provide a design blueprint for future assistive technology devices. This Project will also provide accessibility research training to undergraduate and graduate students, especially those with vision impairments.

The goal of this project is to develop ‘Feel-It,” a new human-computer interface that will improve the ability of blind and low-vision people to interact with computers. The interface will compensate the users’ inability to see the screen content by enabling them to both hear the content and feel its tactile representation with both hands.  The portable hardware-device will connect to any computer (touchscreen or not) or smart phone device via Bluetooth, and allow users to interact with their devices by putting their hands in/on a pair of haptic “gloves” and moving them on any flat surface, e.g., a desk or a table.  The Research Plan is organized under three objectives.  OBJECTIVE 1 is to design and develop the Feel-IT gloves to support high-resolution tactile feedback and portability. Features of the glove include: TULAs (Tiny Ultrasonic Linear Actuators) that are placed on the distal phalanxes of fingers and act similarly to Braille Cells but enable increased resolution and require less voltage/bulk and wires; infrared LED lights on each finger that will enable a camera to track finger position and orientation; a stabilizer that enables more comfortable placement of the hand on the glove and greater control over movements; and buttons to click links or zoom in and out of any segment.  OBJECTIVE 2 is to design audio-tactile interfaces that enable general exploration of the computer screen and enable standard office apps. The design will build on a current Interface Manager and Finger Tracker that supports one glove and only enables tactile interaction with web pages.  User Interface (UI) Automation and/or standard vision segmentation algorithms will be used to obtain information about the computer screen content and convert it to tactile representation. The interface manager, which will be limited to MS Windows, will represent. in tactile form, open windows, app icons, menu elements, and the content of app windows. The system will enable the user to “zoom” into any window, feel its components, listen to the content, and then zoom out.  OBJECTIVE 3 is to conduct human subject research in laboratory and in-situ settings. Eighty low vision and blind subjects will be recruited to conduct user studies on a typical screen with multiple icons, windows, menus, etc., and with typical office applications, e.g., word processors, spreadsheets, etc.  Performance measurse include time to perform task, effort to perform task, and failures.  Satisfaction measures will be determined by an After Scenario Questionnaire, a System Usability Scale (1-10) and a System Preference Questionnaire.  Expected research outcomes include: (1) Design and software implementation of novel haptic interfaces for computer access; (2) Understanding tactile behaviors and strategies employed by blind and low-vision people; and (3) Insight into how dynamic haptic feedback can help improve computer interaction.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Modern computer interfaces are designed primarily for sighted users and rely heavily on visual layouts. People who are blind or have low vision typically interact with computers using screen readers that convert text into speech. While effective, audio-only access can be slow and cognitively demanding because information must be processed sequentially.

This project explored a new approach to accessibility: combining touch and sound to create an “audio-tactile” method of computer interaction. The central idea was to enable users to feel the layout of a computer screen using small, controllable tactile elements, while continuing to use audio feedback for detailed content.

Over the course of the award, the research team developed and refined the design of a novel device called Feel-IT. The proposed device is a mouse-like glove that would allow users to move their hand across a desk surface while small actuators under the fingertips raise and lower pins to represent screen elements such as windows, sections, and interactive controls.

The project made significant advances in both hardware design and software architecture.

On the hardware side, the project explored the design of compact tactile modules intended to render screen information through fingertip stimulation. Multiple generations of designs were developed using ultrasonic linear actuators, with extensive mechanical modeling, circuit design, and embedded control development.

Project produced detailed engineering designs and analyses identifying key technical barriers, including actuator performance under load, mechanical packaging constraints, wiring complexity, and component availability. These results provide guidance for future development of portable tactile interfaces.

On the software side, the project developed methods for transforming complex computer interfaces into structured representations that could be rendered through touch. This included research on creating uniform overlays that simplify diverse user interfaces and techniques to improve how blind users navigate complex online discussions. These contributions advance understanding of how non-visual users process digital information and how multimodal interfaces can reduce cognitive load.

The intellectual merit of this work lies in advancing Human–Computer Interaction and Accessibility research by establishing design principles and system architectures for audio-tactile computing. The project contributes new knowledge in actuator control, embedded system integration, and interface transformation for non-visual access.

The broader impacts center on improving digital accessibility. By exploring how tactile feedback can complement audio interfaces, this research lays the groundwork for future technologies that may help blind and low-vision users navigate digital environments more efficiently and independently. The project also supported graduate student training in accessibility research, embedded systems, and inclusive interface design.

Although Feel-IT remains a research design and engineering blueprint, this award established foundational knowledge and technical specifications that can guide future development of tactile-augmented computing technologies.

award.abstractText:
The ability to effectively work as a team is essential to meet the demands of the modern world and workforce. However, the COVID-19 crisis has drastically changed how teams collaborate, including periods of extended remote work, mixed remote and in-person teams, blurred home and work boundaries, elevated stress and anxiety, and extreme uncertainty about the future. The swift onset of the crisis required individuals, teams, and organizations to abruptly adapt to rapidly changing circumstances with little to no preparation. The proposed research will investigate disruptions to teamwork and how teams adapt during the COVID-19 crisis and in the ensuing recovery period. The project will investigate 30 real-world teams over a three-month period while in the midst of the crisis and for an additional one-month follow-up as events unfold. The goal is to understand how teams respond to changing contexts, how teams support each other, how conflict is managed, and how teams develop, adapt, and sustain the rhythms of teamwork during COVID-19 and in the ensuing recovery period. This foundational research will be essential to help organizations establish team structures and collaborative processes that enable them to more successfully address disruptions in the current and in future crises. The project will provide unique opportunities for interdisciplinary training of students in computer science and psychology, will broaden participation by recruiting diverse students, and will share a rich and unique dataset with the broad scientific community.
 
The specific aims are to: (1) understand states, processes, and behaviors (e.g., team cohesion, communication patterns, collective stress) of teams during the COVID-19 crisis with a focus on factors associated with team performance; (2) investigate how individuals and teams experience and adapt to major COVID-related life events, such as school closings, enforcing of social distancing, budget cuts, illnesses, and so on; and (3) identify patterns in team states and behaviors over time, detect disruptions to these patterns, and study how new patterns emerge during the crisis and in the ensuing period of recovery. The project will use wearable sensors to track heart rate, sleep, physical activity, and relative location (home or away), communication tools (e.g., team calendars, email metadata), ecological momentary assessments (EMAs), validated survey instruments, and semi-structured interviews to investigate team states, team processes, team behaviors, and team performances in context and over time. The findings will contribute basic knowledge on teaming under the unique context of COVID-19, what factors are associated with team performance, and whether changes teams adopt are temporary or permanent.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The ability to effectively work as a team is an essential skill to meet the demands of the modern world and its workforce. However, the COVID-19 crisis drastically changed the nature of work and how teams collaborate. At the onset of this project (starting Fall 2020), previously co-located teams were engaged in extended remote work with home and work boundaries becoming blurred (if not eliminated); the stay-at-home orders and the economic shutdown caused considerable financial strain for people and organizations; almost everyone (at least knew someone who) was experiencing elevated stress and anxiety brought on by personal, work-related, and societal factors; and there was widespread uncertainty about what would come next. The swift onset of the pandemic required individuals, teams, and organizations to abruptly adapt to rapidly changing circumstances with little to no preparation. 

Accordingly, this project investigated disruptions to teamwork and associated adaptation strategies during the COVID-19 crisis and in the ensuing transition to a ?new normal? of work and teamwork. We used longitudinal precision tracking (using behavioral/physiological sensing) to enable a deep understanding of how teams responded to changing context, how teams supported each other, how conflict was managed, and how teams developed, adapted, and sustained the rhythms of teamwork during COVID-19. 

The main outcomes of this two year project include:

  • Longitudinal, multimodal data. Collection of longitudinal, multimodal data from real-world teams by utilizing consumer-grade wearable sensors that track heart rate, sleep duration, physical activity, and relative location (home or away), communication tools (e.g., team calendars), ecological momentary assessments (EMAs), validated survey instruments, and semi-structured interviews to understand team states, processes, (e.g., team affect, team conflict, communication), and performance in context and over time.
  • Latent diversity: Identifying the concept of latent diversity. In the wake of the abrupt transition to working from home, participants became aware of latent diversities that had remained inconspicuous and predominantly inconsequential while teams had been working in the office. These included diversity in the homelife responsibilities of team members as well as their diverse work rhythms and sleep/wake cycles.
  • Sleep alignment. Documenting a curvilinear relationship between team members? misalignment in sleep behaviors (bedtime, waketime, sleep duration) and their perceptions of teamwork in that too much or too little alignment (as sensed via the wearable device) was found to be negatively associated with teamwork.
  • Work location. Finding that work location (private home office, shared home office, workplace) was not associated with team members? perceptions of teamwork. However, the association of work location with team conflict was moderated both by job autonomy and the degree of task interdependence in the team.
  • Emotion contagion. Discovering that supervisors? positive affect influenced their team members? positive affect and that team members? negative affect influenced their supervisors negative affect. In other words, positive affect flows downwards (from supervisors to members) whereas negative affect flows upwards (from members to supervisors)

 

Broader impacts of the research include dissemination of the findings in seven publications, one community talk on the future of teamwork, a keynote, partly supporting two PhD students and two part-time postdoctoral researchers. In terms of societal impact, this foundational research, which could only be meaningfully conducted in the context of an authentic crisis, will be essential to prepare future teams to collaborate effectively in similar circumstances. Specifically, this research helped shed light on the structures and rhythms of teams to understand how teams adapted to the crisis. This can have impacts in helping organizations establish team structures and collaborative processes that enable them to more successfully address disruptions caused by this and future crises and thrive in the new normal of work from home.

award.abstractText:
Due to the outbreak of the 2019 novel Coronavirus and the shock to the healthcare systems, it is critical to conduct fundamental research and scientific studies on the development of smart and scalable technologies that can be produced rapidly and in large scales for (a) continual in-home and in-hospital objective tracking of multiple symptoms using wearable sensors, (b) detecting early
health anomalies from the measured multiple symptoms, and (c) predicting potential adverse events from the measured historical data. This project will address the aforementioned aims to transform the current subjective infrequent telemonitoring for COVID19 patients to continuous objective monitoring and help to reduce the burden on the health care system and the corresponding social and economic impacts. The successful development and deployment of the wearable device will further open doors to conducting fundamental research on the temporal evolution of COVID19 symptoms and behavior.

The project will develop a wireless smart Internet of Things (IoT) necklace, containing multimodality sensors that can accurately and objectively track multiple vital symptoms of respiratory malfunction and infection, covering a large spectrum of COVID19 symptoms. It will be capable of recording and telereporting, the sound and vibration dynamics due to breathing and coughing together with the body temperature, heart rate, and fatigue-related mobility. In addition, peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) will be measured and fused with the collected data by the IoT necklace. The project will also develop novel machine learning models to detect early health anomalies in the multidimensional biosignal space and predict the upcoming adverse events over a future temporal horizon based on the past time-series captured by the device. By partnering with industry, this technology can be used not only for COVID-19 but also for patients with other causes of pneumonia and other respiratory conditions, including lung cancer. The project will generate a unique transdisciplinary educational environment by conducting workshops and undergraduate projects with a focus on promoting STEM-related activities within underrepresented groups.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Intellectual Merit:

1) Hardware and Knowledge Translation: The project resulted in the design and implementation of a multimodal wearable wireless smart IoT device (composed of a smart head-piece and a smart neck-piece) that is capable of continuously tracking and wirelessly reporting vital signs of patients, including SPo2, body temperature, heart rate, breathing and cough, and fatigue-related mobility and physical ability. Specific attention was paid to the wearability and robustness of recordings. A provisional US patent and a PCT Application were filed, and the work was licensed to Tactile Robotics Inc., Canada. Collaboration with the industry is ongoing toward commercialization. The concept is published as follows.  

  • S. Mehrdad, Y. Wang, and S. F. Atashzar, "Perspective: Wearable Internet of Medical Things for Remote Tracking of Symptoms, Prediction of Health Anomalies, Implementation of Preventative Measures, and Control of Virus Spread During the Era of COVID-19," Frontiers in Robotics and  AI, vol. 8, p. 610653, Apr. 2021, DOI: 10.3389/frobt.2021.610653. [Online]. Available: http://dx.doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2021.610653

 

2) Computational Prognosis Model: We also developed an artificial intelligence prognosis model to evaluate if a patient with COVID infection is going to experience health deterioration in the following 3 to 24 hours using the sequential monitoring of routine triadic patient biomarkers , including time-series of (a) oxygen saturation level, (b) heart rate, and (c) temperature. The model was also provided with basic patient information, including gender, age, obesity status, vaccination status, vaccination date, hypertension status, and diabetes status. The proposed model was trained using data from 37006 patients who tested positive for COVID-19.  The proposed model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.808-0.880 for  3 to 24-hour deterioration prediction. An occlusion experiment revealed the significance of monitoring the sequential recording and variations in the dynamical history of the biomarkers. The model was motivated by wearable systems that longitudinally measure vital signs and can be used to avoid unrecognized patient deterioration.

  • S. Mehrdad, F. E. Shamout, Y. Wang, and S. Farokh Atashzar, "Deterioration Prediction using Time-Series of Three Vital Signs and Current Clinical Features Amongst COVID-19 Patients," arXiv [cs.LG], Oct. 12, 2022 [Online]. Available: http://arxiv.org/abs/2210.05881

3) Publication: Paper: In addition to the citations above, we have published several papers covering various aspects of the project. Please check the publication list associated with the project here: https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2031594&HistoricalAwards=false

 

Broader Impact:

Our smart wearable for tracking common vital signs and our AI model for forecasting the deterioration of COVID-19 patients provide valuable yet convenient tools for the diagnosis and treatment of COVID-19 patients. The results of this project can be used not only for COVID-19 but also for the development of intelligent health assessment technologies for patients with other causes of pneumonia and other respiratory conditions, including lung cancer.

Our project also has several educational components, including scientific workshops related to the focus of this project, special issues to promote research in the field, vertically integrated projects for undergraduate research, and events to promote diversity. 

(a)  Workshop:  "Impact of COVID-19 on Medical Robotics and Wearables Research" at The 2021 International Conference on Robotics and Automation. The workshop was composed of a collection of leading talks, round-table discussions, and posters. This workshop aimed to bring together leaders and young researchers, and stakeholders from academia and industry to generate a unique environment focusing on the future of modern healthcare and the contribution of AI, smart wearable, and medical technologies. 

  • The link to the event: https://sites.google.com/ualberta.ca/2021-icra-workshop/home
  • The link to the 6-hour recording: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d-r4Mjb_tO0&t=195s

(b)  Vertically Integrated Projects (VIP): The project includes a vertically integrated project for undergraduate students. The team won the best Research Excellence Exhibit Award at NYU Tandon School of Engineering. This team of undergraduate students was able to publish the results of their research in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letter (impact Factor: 4.3), and the paper is invited for presentation at IROS2022 (10.1109/LRA.2022.3191238). Link: https://wp.nyu.edu/meriit/undergraduate-vertically-integrated-projects-smart-wearable-bio-tracker-for-telehealth/

(c)   New K-12 Program: We have initiated a two-year MERIIT-K12-STEM program mainly for students from under-represented minority groups. The goal is to make them familiar with the foundations of telehealth, wearable technologies, and telerobotics early in their careers. Link: https://wp.nyu.edu/meriit/meriit-k12-stem-program/

 (d)  Special Issue: We have edited a successful special issue on "Robotics, Autonomous Systems and AI for Nonurgent/Nonemergent Healthcare Delivery During and After the COVID-19 Pandemic". We accepted  35 articles for publication from 183 authors in total, which so far resulted in 30K full article downloads. Link to the special issue: https://www.frontiersin.org/research-topics/14462/robotics-autonomous-systems-and-ai-for-nonurgentnonemergent-healthcare-delivery-during-and-after-the#impact

(e)    Promoting Diversity in Academia: We have organized several workshops to promote diversity in academic careers, with an emphasis on diversity in signal processing. In this regard, we collaborated with the IEEE Signal Processing Society and organized IEE SPS PROGRESS at ICIP2022, ICASSP 2022, ICIP 2021, and ICASSP 2021. PROGRESS aims to motivate and prepare women and underrepresented minority groups to pursue academic careers in signal processing. Link to the event: https://ieeeprogress.org/.

award.abstractText:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is bringing significant benefits to human society with outstanding potential to address essential human concerns in the future. Deep neural networks have shown significant improvements in many AI applications. However, the benefit comes at the high cost of computational resources and engineer resources. For mobile devices with a tight power budget, such high demands for computation become prohibitive. On the other side, there is a shortage of experts who can design neural networks, which are notoriously hard to tune. This project systematically investigates efficient neural network architectures and their hardware accelerators to make them run fast at low power. It also aims to accelerate the design cycle by AI-based design automation (AI-designed AI). Such design methodology can support machine learning research and education,, while significantly improving the productivity of machine learning models. People no longer have to hand-tune the model, but it is automated, enabling non-experts to build efficient machine learning models. It will democratize AI to a more diverse community. 

The project aims to auto-generate both efficient neural networks and their hardware implementations that can generalize to high-dimensional representations, through automatic machine learning (AutoML) techniques. It will design a hardware accelerator to provide more computation per unit cost. The algorithm hardware co-design approach unveils a larger design space that conventional wisdom has been limited to. It is expected to shorten the design cycle of neural architecture search by two orders of magnitude over existing work. With AutoML, powerful hardware, and the co-designed efficient algorithms, it is possible to solve more challenging AI tasks on high-dimensional data that are previously difficult or impossible, hindered by the computation resource, such as videos and 3D point clouds. These techniques give rise to a deeper understanding of the high dimensional representations and produce state-of-the-art neural network architectures that can efficiently run on mobile devices as well as protect user privacy.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Artificial intelligence has achieved remarkable progress, but powerful models often require large amounts of computation, memory, energy, and specialized hardware. This project addressed a central challenge: making advanced artificial intelligence faster, smaller, more energy-efficient, and more widely deployable, from tiny sensors and mobile devices to large-scale cloud systems.

Over the life of the award, the project developed new algorithms, software systems, and hardware-aware design methods for efficient machine learning. Early work focused on bringing deep learning to highly resource-constrained devices. The project developed MCUNet, which enabled ImageNet-scale inference on microcontrollers with very limited memory, achieving 70.7 percent ImageNet accuracy with only 2 megabytes of flash and 512 kilobytes of SRAM. Follow-on work, including MCUNetV2 and tiny on-device training methods, further reduced memory requirements and made it possible to run or adapt neural networks on edge devices that previously could not support such workloads.

The project also advanced automated machine learning and hardware-aware design. Once-for-All networks allowed one trained model to be specialized for many hardware platforms, reducing search cost and carbon footprint by orders of magnitude. Neural Accelerator Architecture Search jointly optimized neural network structure, accelerator architecture, and compiler mapping, demonstrating the value of co-design across algorithms, software, and hardware. These methods helped establish a practical path toward greener and more sustainable artificial intelligence.

As artificial intelligence shifted toward foundation models and generative artificial intelligence, the project expanded to efficient large language models, image generation, video generation, multimodal systems, and robotics. The project developed SmoothQuant and Activation-aware Weight Quantization to reduce the cost of large language model inference; StreamingLLM and related sparse attention methods to support long and streaming contexts; and efficient serving systems such as LServe and QServe to improve throughput and reduce deployment cost. These systems showed substantial gains, including up to 13.5 times faster attention computation, up to 3.5 times higher serving throughput, and approximately 3 times lower serving cost.

The project also produced major advances in efficient generative artificial intelligence. It developed techniques for faster image editing, efficient diffusion models, compressed latent representations, autoregressive image generation, and long-video generation. Later results enabled faster image and video generation, real-time video understanding, and more efficient training for reasoning models. These findings demonstrate that high-quality artificial intelligence can be achieved not only by scaling models larger, but also by carefully redesigning algorithms and systems to use computation more effectively.

The broader impacts of the project include open-source software, education, workforce development, and technology transfer. The team released many public software systems that have been used by researchers, students, and industry practitioners. The project’s open-source tools have attracted tens of thousands of GitHub stars and influenced companies including NVIDIA, Intel, Amazon, Google, Meta, AMD, and IBM. Several methods have been adopted in production or integrated into major artificial intelligence software stacks.

The project also had significant educational impact. EfficientML.ai, a graduate course on efficient machine learning systems, teaches model compression, pruning, quantization, neural architecture search, and efficient generative artificial intelligence through hands-on laboratories. Students learn to deploy large language models on laptops and other resource-constrained devices. Course materials have been adopted by multiple universities and viewed widely online, broadening access to practical training in efficient artificial intelligence.

Overall, this award helped advance the intellectual foundations and practical tools for efficient artificial intelligence. By reducing computation, memory, energy, and cost barriers, the project made artificial intelligence more practical, sustainable, and accessible for research, education, industry, and society.

award.abstractText:
How much information can be transmitted through the skin? Conventional wisdom would say not as much as vision or hearing. The researchers argue, however, that there is a need to better understand how to "talk" to the skin in its own language. The team has recently devised a sleeve with 24 vibrators that delivers speech sounds in the form of distinct vibration patterns. Testing results from more than 100 normal-hearing individuals (in addition to one participant with a severe hearing loss) show that the vibration-based representation of speech sounds can be easily learned and combined to "sound out" English words in isolation. The best learners have demonstrated an ability to learn one English word per minute, up to a vocabulary size of 500 English words. This is an exciting breakthrough that can lead to a communication device for people with severe hearing impairments and for those whose hearing is temporarily compromised due to noisy environments such as firefighters. The main objective of this project is to systematically explore ways that the communication rate through the sleeve can be increased. Our goal is to reach at least 60-80 words per minute, a communication rate that has been demonstrated by the Tadoma method of speech communication, in which persons who are both deaf and blind place a hand over the face and neck of the talker to understand speech. Such a communication rate will make the sleeve a practical solution for the community of people who need an alternate means for speech communication, such as the ones with both hearing and vision impairments. If successful, the project will facilitate a better quality of life (in terms of social interactions as well as employability) for this disadvantaged community.

This project addresses the fundamental question of the information capacity of the sense of touch within the context of increasing communication rates through a haptic display of speech. The project leverages the team's research and development experience on: (i) natural speech communication methods used by the deaf and deaf-blind; (ii) wearable haptic technologies; (iii) an information-theoretical approach to assessing human performance; and (iv) psychophysical properties of the tactual sense. The project builds upon the researchers' recent success at demonstrating their ability to develop tactile codes for the 39 phonemes of English that were highly recognizable in isolation and in words formed from sequences of phonemes. The research is focused on increasing the rate at which information can be transmitted through touch by trained participants that include observers with normal hearing as well as those with sensorineural hearing impairments who represent a major category of potential end users of the device. The overall goal is to achieve transmission rates of tactile speech stimuli that are comparable to those achieved by deaf-blind users of the Tadoma method, and to employ effective methods of training users of the display for reception of connected speech signals with a high degree of accuracy. Experiments will be carried out in which users of the tactile system are trained and tested on their ability to recognize phonemes, words, short phrases, and finally conversational sentences. Durational properties of the stimuli will be explored in these experiments with the aim of establishing the lower limits on phoneme duration and the intervals between phonemes and words. Estimates of effective communication rates will take into account both the transmission rate and accuracy of reception, with the goal of demonstrating effective communication rates on the order of 50-100 words per minute. A lower-bound estimate for haptic communication rate in terms of bits per second can then be derived from the transmission rate achieved at the end of this project.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project studied the capabilities of the sense of touch for the communication of speech and language. Tactile speech communication can be beneficial for persons with severe auditory and/or visual impairments, in situations that require silent communication, and for any situation where the normal sensory channels of hearing and sight are impaired or overloaded.  The goal of this work was to develop a tactile display of speech that allows users to receive connected speech at communication rates of 50 to 100 words per minute, comparable to slow rates of speech communication through hearing.  The research conducted on this project has led to the achievement of this goal.  We summarize below the results that led to an increase in effective communication rates from our previous maximum rate of 30-35 words per minute to the estimated rate of 53 words per minute achieved in this project.

First, our strategy in the development of a tactile speech communication system was the use of a phoneme-based display such that tactile codes were created to represent each of the 24 consonants and 15 vowels of English. These tactile phonemes were delivered through a 24-channel array of vibrators (the Tactile Phonemic Sleeve?TAPS) that stimulated the dorsal and ventral surfaces of the left forearm (see Figure 1 for schematic of TAPS).  We modified an original set of codes for increased transmission rate and intelligibility. For consonants this included assigning the shortest duration (140 ms) to the most frequent consonants , coding them at one of six areas on the TAPS display, and decreasing the duration of the longest consonants from 400 to 300 ms.  For vowels, the  haptic codes of two vowels that were often misidentified were changed to create more robust and discriminable sensations. Vowel durations were 300 ms for long vowels and 240 ms for short vowels.

Second, experiments were conducted to train participants in the reception of haptic phonemes, words, and phrases.  The training sets are shown in Table 1.  The performance of 8 participants is shown in Figure 2, where phoneme identification scores averaged 92.4% correct.  Figure 3 shows  the equivalent number of words learned (ENWL) as a function of training set. When generalized to a 500-word vocabulary, the ENWL averaged roughly 50% correct.

Third, we conducted experiments on TAPS to determine the shortest possible durations for the time between phonemes when forming words (the inter-phoneme interval, IPI) and for the time between words when forming phrases and sentences (the inter-word interval, IWI).These were the minimum durations at which users of the device were able to maintain a criterion level of performance on 70% correct for the identification of isolated words or two-word phrases.  These values ranged from 35-150 ms for IPI and from 250-500 ms for IWI. We then tested the identification of two-word phrases using the customized inter-phoneme  and inter-word intervals for each participant, where scores averaged 83.5% correct.

Fourth, ideal transmission rates for the two-word phrases were computed by calculating the duration of the phrase (derived by adding together the durations of the haptic codes, IPI, and IWI) and converting to a rate in words per minute. The effective communication rate was defined as the ideal rate in words per minute multiplied by the percent-correct score on the two-word phrase test. Ideal and effective transmission rates for the two-word phrases are shown in Figure 4.  Over three days of training and testing, the effective transmission rate across participants increased from 37 to 53 words per minute, achieving our goal of rates in excess of 50 wpm.

This work has demonstrated the feasibility of tactile communication of speech with sufficient accuracy at presentation rates that are comparable to the slow speaking rates for auditory reception of speech. 

In addition to our primary objective of the development of a tactile device for the reception of speech through the tactile sense alone, this project also included work on the multi-modal perception of speech through the tactile and visual sensory modalities.  A pared-down version of the stand-alone tactile device (see Figure 5) was developed for use as a tactile aid to lipreading for use by persons with severe to profound hearing impairment.  Studies of the reception of consonant and vowel speech sounds were conducted in persons with both normal and impaired hearing. The tactile aid provided substantial benefits to the lipreading of consonant and vowel speech segments, with larger benefits obtained for consonants compared to vowels.

In summary, the work conducted here provides evidence-based proof of the capability of the tactile sense for the communication of speech and language, both when used alone and in a multimodal setting.

award.abstractText:
Technology continues to make great strides at the nanoscale, resulting in unprecedented capabilities.  Currently, thermal fluctuations have not driven nano systems outside their linear regime where their dynamics are well understood.  However, as mechanical systems are made smaller for next-generation technologies, their performance is becoming limited by the random thermal movements of the molecules that make up the device and surrounding medium as the thermal fluctuations are becoming sufficient to drive the mechanical system into a nonlinear regime.  Developing an understanding of the fluctuations of nano mechanical systems in this nonlinear regime is the focus of this work.  Three-dimensional nanoprinting will be employed to create structures designed to study nonlinear behavior when driven by the temperature alone.  A theoretical understanding of the nonlinear behavior will be created by utilizing the fundamental relationship between the fluctuations and the dissipation present in the system.  Our findings will provide the insights necessary to realize the next generation of nanotechnology where performance is anticipated to be well beyond the current state-of-the art.

The stochastic dynamics of nanoscale systems are at the heart of many important phenomena.  Currently, there is a good understanding of stochastic dynamics when a mechanical system remains in the linear regime.  However, many important challenges remain in understanding nonlinear fluctuations of nanomechanical systems.  In order to build this understanding, state-of-the-art nanofabrication and measurement approaches, coupled with the development of analytical and numerical methods to describe and predict these dynamics, will be utilized.  A direct laser write system will be used to fabricate structures tailored to exhibit highly nonlinear stochastic dynamics when driven by temperature alone.  The nonlinear stochastic dynamics of structures constructed from soft polymeric materials will be experimentally studied using measurements from a heterodyne interferometer.  A physical understanding of the system dynamics will be built using the powerful fluctuation-dissipation theorem.  The dynamics will be probed perturbatively and a factorization approach will be used to create a deterministic approach to describe the dynamics of strongly nonlinear systems.  After developing an understanding of the nonlinear fluctuations of a single mode of oscillation, the coupling between the different modes of oscillation of a complex structure will be investigated.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The exciting push forward of nanoscale technologies towards smaller mechanical devices continues to yield unprecedented capabilities. In this project, we investigated micro and nanoscale technologies whose ultimate sensitivity is limited by the thermal fluctuations in the displacement of elastic mechanical structures. Significant progress has been made in understanding the fluctuating, or externally driven, dynamics of the fundamental mode of oscillation for systems that remain in the small deflection limit where a linear description of the dynamics is possible. However, much less is understood for the multimodal response of small elastic mechanical structures when driven by thermal fluctuations, or an external drive, where the linear dynamics becomes nonlinear as the amplitude of oscillation increases. This project developed a fundamental understanding of the multimodal and nonlinear dynamics of small elastic mechanical oscillators when driven externally or by thermal fluctuations alone. We used theory, numerical simulations, and experiment to gain new physical insights into the stochastic and driven dynamics of small elastic mechanical systems when either placed in a vacuum or when immersed in a viscous fluid such as air or water.  Theoretically, we developed analytical descriptions capable of quantifying the multimodal dynamics of linear and nonlinear oscillators for a wide range of parameters. Computationally, we developed numerical approaches to quantify the multimodal dynamics for ideal and complex geometries including the precise, and often complex, conditions of experiment. The theoretical, computational, and experimental efforts of this project were tightly integrated and focused in order to build new physical insights.  The project provided support for graduate and undergraduate research. The PI used ideas and findings from this project in a multidisciplinary graduate course on the modeling of micro and nanoscale systems at Virginia Tech.

award.abstractText:
This project will study how data visualizations may help university faculty recognize their implicit biases and promote equitable participation in their classrooms. Participation is a key part of learning, but implicit biases can result in different opportunities for different groups of students to participate in STEM classrooms. Such differences can cause inequities in learning outcomes that may lead to underrepresentation of women, students of color, and other groups in the STEM workforce. By studying how to provide STEM faculty with meaningful data about the differential impact of their teaching on student participation, this project has the potential to improve teaching and learning in STEM at scale. This project aims to generate professional development methods and technologies that support equitable teaching across STEM fields. During the project, hundreds of faculty members will receive this professional development, which in turn will impact tens of thousands of students. The project will also develop supporting materials to enable university professional developers and teacher educators to effectively provide similar professional development to the educators they serve. Expected outcomes of this work include new knowledge about equitable teaching in STEM, effective methods for helping instructors teach more equitably, and widespread dissemination of these methods.
 
This project will directly support over 100 faculty to address implicit bias, by utilizing (and further enhancing) the classroom observation tool, Electronic Quality of Instruction Protocol (EQUIP). EQUIP is a free, web-based classroom observation tool that provides visual representations of classroom participation by different social marker groups. The research plan includes a longitudinal study of a subset of faculty members as they engage in sustained professional development through three interventions: (1) systematic design of data visualizations; (2) a summer institute; and (3) faculty learning communities. Through a mixed-methods research design, this project will address fundamental research topics around how STEM faculty interpret data visualizations, how professional development may leverage visualizations to reduce bias and improve teaching, and the nature of the resulting impacts on student outcomes. The methods will utilize a combination of within- and between-subject comparisons, triangulating data from: classroom observations, data analytics, student outcomes, surveys, and interviews. The major theoretical contributions of this project are to develop knowledge about how data visualizations may improve equitable teaching practices, and to longitudinally study the process through which faculty members go as they learn to recognize and address implicit bias in their teaching. This project can contribute significantly to broadening participation in STEM, because it addresses implicit bias, which is a pervasive problem that limits the participation of women, students of color, people with differing abilities, and other underrepresented groups in STEM. Helping the faculty who participate in the study address their biases is expected to directly produce more equitable learning environments in undergraduate STEM. Moreover, this project will contribute broadly to educator professional development efforts, by documenting and disseminating a suite of tools and best practices for addressing bias and improving equity.  The Faculty Early Career Development (CAREER) Program is a National Science Foundation (NSF)-wide activity that supports early-career faculty who have the potential to serve as academic role models in research and education. This CAREER project is supported by NSF's Education & Human Resources Directorate Core Research Program and its Improving Undergraduate STEM Education Program.

This CAREER project investigated how data can be used to help college instructors create more equitable learning environments in STEM education. The project focused on understanding how faculty interpret information about student participation in classroom discussions and how data analytics can support instructors in recognizing and addressing inequities related to race, gender, disability, and other social identities.

A major outcome of the project was the development and study of EQUIP, a classroom observation and analytics system that helps instructors examine patterns of participation in their courses. Unlike many teaching tools that focus only on overall classroom activity, EQUIP provides disaggregated data that make inequities visible across different groups of students. The project generated new knowledge about how instructors make sense of equity-focused data and how those data can support long-term changes in teaching practice.

The project also developed and studied faculty learning communities that used classroom data as a foundation for professional learning. Findings demonstrated that participation data can help instructors recognize previously unnoticed patterns of inequity and implement concrete instructional strategies that promote broader student engagement. This work has contributed to a deeper understanding of how data can be used to support equitable teaching and organizational change in higher education.

The project produced substantial scholarly and educational outcomes, including numerous peer-reviewed publications, two books, and professional development resources for educators. The books Equitable and Engaging Mathematics Teaching and Equity Learning Communities synthesize lessons learned from the project and provide practical guidance for instructors, instructional leaders, and faculty developers seeking to improve equity in their classrooms.

The project also expanded the reach of EQUIP beyond higher education. New methods were developed to capture multimodal forms of participation, including gestures, sign language, and the use of physical materials, making it possible to better study and support inclusive learning environments for students with disabilities. These innovations have informed new collaborations and additional externally funded research.

Broader impacts include the preparation of graduate students and faculty leaders, the development of professional learning opportunities for educators, and the creation of more equitable STEM learning environments. Over the course of the project, the number of EQUIP users grew from approximately 400 to more than 3,000 educators and researchers. An international EQUIP Network was established to support collaboration and dissemination, helping educators use data to improve teaching and student participation across a wide range of disciplines and educational settings.

Overall, this project advanced knowledge about equity, teaching, and professional learning while providing practical tools and resources that support more inclusive and effective STEM education.
