award.abstractText:
Neuromorphic computing is an inspiring and ambitious problem because by understanding how the human nervous system is able to work efficiently using less than 20-Watts of power,  we should be able to design intelligent computing systems that can solve complex problems like humans. While there have been significant advancements in the accuracy of artificial neural networks (ANNs), the quest for power efficiencies akin to biological systems remains elusive. Consequently, there has been significant interest in an approach called spiking neural networks (SNNs) which uses biologically-inspired event-driven spike communication. However, SNN design is still in its infancy, with need for exploring different neuromorphic computing models, learning algorithms, hardware substrates and designing a communication fabric that can scale to meet a strict power budget. This  research seeks to explore the design space of scalable, low-power SNNs. The outcomes of this research could be highly valuable and will pave the way for an array of related research in designing intelligent machines. On the educational front, plans include the involvement of undergraduate and graduate students in this emerging research, where they will get exposure to cross-cutting topics in computer architecture, electronic devices, circuits, and applications.  Female and minority students will be recruited to work in the project. Several Broadening Participation in Computing (BPC) activities such as summer camp for girls and collaboration with the Education Department to expose K-12 students to many areas of computer science will be pursued.

The project seeks to take a comprehensive approach spanning device/circuit level innovations for designing extremely low-power spiking neurons and synapses, architectural level solutions for designing hierarchical communication networks, algorithm level optimizations to improve the accuracy of SNN models, and evaluation of the designs with different classes of applications.   The proposed research consists of four research tasks. First, the team plans to investigate the design of neuron device primitives  using Magnetic Tunnel Junction (MTJ)-based spintronic devices that are orders of magnitude more power efficient than existing technologies.  Second, using these MTJ-based neuron tiles, the design space of a scalable on-chip interconnection fabric will be explored. Third, the research focuses on developing algorithmic solutions to enhance the accuracy of SNNs, and a hybrid solution to leverage the benefits of both SNNs and ANNs. Finally, the plan includes to develop a simulation platform to evaluate the performance and energy efficiency of different designs using diverse applications.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Understanding human brain, broadly known as brain science and mimicking its functionality in hardware, known as neuromorphic computing, is an inspiring and open problem that has eluded researchers for decades. Consequently, there has been significant interest in spiking neural networks (SNNs) that use biologically inspired event-driven spike communication. This project has made advances in the algorithmic, software and hardware domains of SNN design.

Intellectual Merit: The project developed a low power architecture called NEBULA that has the flexibility to be deployed for inference of SNNs, ANNs (Artificial Neural Networks) as well as a combination of SNN-ANN hybrid networks.  At the device level, a spin-based ultra-low-power device, called Domain Wall Magnetic Tunnel Junction (DW-MTJ) was employed for the architecture. Our evaluations show that NEBULA, in the ANN mode, was up to 7.9× more energy efficient than a state-of-the-art ANN accelerator, ISAAC. In the SNN mode, it was `45× more energy efficient than a contemporary SNN architecture, INXS. We also developed a Sparse Vector-Matrix Vector (SpMV) Accelerator using Diode-Selected Crossbars. Our architecture combines both computing in-memory and computing near-memory approaches to independently perform the entire SpMV operation.  It achieves 7.7× speed up and 4.9× energy-savings compared to a contemporary state-of-the-art design.

When paired with biologically inspired asynchronous event sensors, SNN hardware can create particularly energy-efficient near-sensor systems that are ideal for mobile, resource-constrained and embedded-computing scenarios. A key contribution to our work involved a new training approach for the SNN that results in our best-performing model being 38% more accurate with 35% lower energy and 55% lower Energy Delay Product compared to its traditional SNN counterpart. We extended SNN learning model for adoption in collaborative resource constrained devices. Specifically, a federated learning framework for Spiking neural networks was developed. The project further extended the SNN architecture to support fusion of multimodal datastreams and mapped them on commercial embedded system platforms to demonstrate energy efficiency.

Concurrently, the project made foundational advances to the models used for biologically inspired learning. An automated framework was developed for neuroevolution guided hybrid spiking neural network training. Our analysis reveals 53.8, 28.8, and 28.2% latency improvement for the neuroevolution-based SNN training strategy on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet datasets, respectively in contrast to state-of-the-art conversion-based approaches.  The project was the first time to deploy a Hopfield network with a convergent Recurrent Neural Network model and show that the attention mechanism of the Hopfield network can be used to solve complex sequence classification problems using Equilibrium Propogation. 

Our exploration also revealed strengths of SNN based architectures for adversarial attacks.

Broader Impacts: The project has provided training for several graduate students, some of whom have graduated and are contributing to US-based commercial companies. The research results have been shared with the community at conferences and through invited talks. Further, we have open-sourced code to facilitate further innovation. The innovations resulting from energy-efficient learning systems advance the ability to deploy SNN based systems in a wide range of edge devices.

award.abstractText:
Effective teachers of mathematics attend to and respond to the substance of students’ thinking in supporting classroom learning. Teacher professional development programs have supported teachers in learning to notice students’ mathematical thinking and using that noticing to make instructional decisions in the classroom.  This project investigates and expands teachers’ learning to notice in two important ways.  First, the research expands beyond teachers’ noticing of written and verbal thinking to attend to gesture and other aspects of embodied and multimodal thinking. Second, the project focuses on algebraic thinking and seeks specifically to understand how teacher noticing relates to the content of algebra. Bringing together multimodal thinking and the mathematical ideas in algebra has the potential to support teachers in providing broader access to algebraic thinking for more students.

To study teacher noticing of multimodal algebraic thinking, this project will facilitate video club sessions in which teachers examine and annotate classroom video.  The video will allow text-based and visual annotation of the videos to obtain rich portraits of the thinking that teachers notice as they examine algebra-related middle school practice. The research team will create a video library focused on three main algebraic thinking areas: equality, functional thinking, and proportional reasoning.  Clips will be chosen that feature multimodal student thinking about these content areas, and provide moments that would be fruitful for advancing student thinking.  Two cohorts of preservice teachers will engage in year-long video clubs using this video library, annotate videos using an advanced technological tool, and engage in reflective interviews about their noticing practices. Follow-up classroom observations will be conducted to see how teachers then notice multimodal algebraic thinking in their classrooms. Materials to conduct the video clubs in other contexts and the curated video library will be made available, along with analyses of the teacher learning that resulted from their implementation.

This is a Faculty Early Career Development Program (CAREER) proposal awarded under the Discovery Research PreK-12 (DRK-12) program. The Discovery Research PreK-12 (DRK-12) program seeks to significantly enhance the learning and teaching of science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) by preK-12 students and teachers, through research and development of innovative resources, models and tools. Projects in the DRK-12 program build on fundamental research in STEM education and prior research and development efforts that provide theoretical and empirical justification for proposed projects.

award.abstractText:
The broader impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will result from targeting pain points in the K-16 math and physical science curriculum to improve participation and sustained achievement in these subjects. Despite investments in education technology, curriculum overhaul, and teacher development, STEM education in the US continues to struggle to improve student proficiency, democratize access, and meet global changes in workforce demand. Current methodologies continue to promote 2D tools to teach concepts that are inherently 3D in nature, which have led to gaps in spatial reasoning and the ability to conceptualize abstractions - critical skills for success in STEM. The company seeks to develop an immersive virtual reality (VR) platform that closes these gaps in STEM proficiency, particularly for non-selective and historically underserved student populations. The aim is to shape the next generation of STEM practitioners by providing students the opportunity to creatively solve high impact real world problems in state-of-the-art interactive virtual learning environments. Ultimately, it is hoped the proposed platform will become the standard in advanced STEM learning solutions, utilizing multiple platforms (VR, AR, Mobile) and data analytics to ensure students of all backgrounds are equipped to succeed in STEM fields. 

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will address a key question for VR in education today - how can VR be used for the purpose of cognitive advancement in competencies and skills that serve as gate-keepers to success in postsecondary STEM? There is evidence that learning via VR increases activity, brain arousal, and engagement, but more lasting impacts on conceptual understanding and transfer have yet to be realized. The primary objective of this project is to define how core VR functionalities and multimodal interactions can be designed and implemented within a rich, problem-driven pedagogical framework to enable 3D sense making of abstract topics.  The company will conduct rigorous research and iterative user testing to identify the most effective VR modalities and kinesthetic interactions that support enduring content mastery and cognitive flexibility. In addition, data analytics will be developed to enhance interactivity, provide crucial real-time formative assessment of student progress, and predictive learning insights to teachers and parents. The technology will also enable networked interactions on the platform to promote collaborative learning.  In doing so, the project will not only transform the STEM learning experience, but also provide a model of how progressive pedagogical practices can be actualized through VR to drive student learning outcomes.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Despite ever-growing advances in multimedia technology and learning science, the delivery and instructional design of STEM learning tools have so far evolved little beyond the digitization of traditional learning mechanisms that have proved ineffective for the vast majority of students. Through our NSF Phase I project, we designed, built and implemented an experiential learning platform that leverages Immersive Virtual Reality (IVR) to foster enduring Algebraic skills that are often at the root of fragile understandings. Our goal is to situate students in compelling real-world contexts that promote deep emotional resonance & inspire 21st century problem-solving. We discuss the primary outcomes of our project below: 

 1. A game-based & problem driven pedagogical framework for immersive learning. 

We designed, modularized, and tested a research-based pedagogical framework that realizes best practice pedagogy using multimodal IVR. Students begin by physically experiencing everyday activities through which a virus spreads before joining the mayor’s task force to solve the challenge: “How long will it take for the outbreak to overwhelm hospital capacities given various levels of containment?” Through a strategic sequence of tasks, students create and interpret exponential models to solve this challenge.

 2. Interactive 3D Sense-making Tools. 

Our primary challenge in creating our pedagogical framework was the selection and design of novel interaction designs that result in greater fluency with exponential growth. Through rigorous user testing and iteration, we developed math reasoning tools that facilitate intuitive movements and visualizations to create strong associations between physical and graphical representations of the viral outbreak’s multiplicative growth. In designing these 3D visualizations, we ensured that they were not just interactive and fun, but also capable of elucidating the structural properties of exponential growth to yield immediate transfer on the post-module formative assessment.

3. Novel Formative Assessments in VR. 

As learning environments evolve, so too should the instruments that we use to assess their efficacy. Therefore, we created and monitored the impact of a new generation of formative assessments and checks for understanding in VR. In addition to conventional, 2D schemes like drag/drop, multiple choice questions, and prompts, we implemented 3D interactions with various sense-making tools that deepen learning and expand our evaluation of student thinking. 

 4. Virtual Learning Assistant. 

Early user testing indicated the need for external, in-the-moment guidance on how to navigate the module environment and learning tasks. To address this, we have incorporated a virtual learning assistant that allows us to exploit the unique affordances of VR and game engines in general. Our Virtual Assistant can do things that a human character could not (like floating around the learning environment) which provides easier viewing angles and improves comfort. It can also play videos to guide the user and give fun audio/visual feedback on their progress.

5. Cloud-based Data Infrastructure. 

The backend of our platform collects multimodal data relevant to student thinking and engagement. To provide real-time access to the data collected and learning insights extracted by our system’s backend, we have implemented a web-based prototype of the dashboard, and rigorously tested its ability to accurately capture and display key learning metrics. In addition to allowing teachers to monitor student learning and performance within the our immersive module, the dashboard also allows them to stage individualized interventions to mitigate moments of conceptual difficulty. 

 6. Instructional Support Materials. 

We provide teachers with a full scope and sequence as well as offline materials that have been carefully designed to solidify the conceptual foundations developed within the VR module and extend student understanding to additional, standards-aligned topics for long-lasting fluency. Our comprehensive facilitation guide ensures that teachers have all the necessary tools to implement our learning module, standards aligned pre/post assessments, conceptual reflection materials, and resources for follow up student fluency practice based on formative assessment data from the module.

7. Learning Analysis & Feedback

We designed an analytic framework to efficiently collect multimodal data logs on: 1) formative assessment data as students complete tasks within the IVR module, 2) information on how students use 3D learning tools while learning, and 3) data on what students are paying attention to within the module at any given time. Analysis of student engagement and learning behaviors using our logging system has enabled us to create a rule-based, authored hint system that provides students with helpful feedback during moments of confusion.

As a result we were able to demonstrate that students can successfully engage with and seamlessly navigate through our immersive modules to achieve the intended learning outcomes. The majority of students that tested our prototype were able to complete the module with little to no intervention. Our analysis of pre/post-module assessment results shows average learning gains of 20%. Though not yet statistically significant due to our limited sample size, this offers significant promise that our pedagogical and assessment design supports enhancements in student understanding.

award.abstractText:
This RAPID project plans to investigate visual-based physiological sensing technologies to facilitate remote triage and rehabilitation during pandemics, by using low-cost consumer-grade cameras to track such physiological conditions as respiration rate, heart rate, and blood oxygen saturation levels from videos.  The physiological data can be visualized and archived, and shared by users with medical practitioners to understand and support remote triage and rehabilitation.

The proposed research can enhance the interaction between medical providers and patients, and help address a projected surge in telehealth needs due to COVID-19.  The PI team plans to conduct the first-of-a-kind data collection, by incorporating the novel contact-free video sensing into a biomedical cohort study that is being rolled out by a public-health collaboration team. This cross-disciplinary opportunity of multimodal data collection will offer insights on the relationship of multiple biosensing modalities, and the data collected would facilitate the research on early detection of COVID-19 and related diseases. The visual-based physiological sensing will also help enhance the remote interaction between rehabilitation therapists and patients during pandemics.

The intellectual merit of this effort lies in advancing promising engineering techniques of video-based contact-free physiological monitoring to support the rising needs of remote triage and rehabilitation during pandemics. The research findings and techniques developed address an important missing component in telehealth, which simultaneously achieves social-distancing, avoids hospital overcrowding, and prioritizes personal protective equipment in response to pandemics. By collaborating with another cohort study, an unprecedented multitude of data collected by the joint effort will provide key insights toward understanding and managing COVID-19 diseases and remote triage for future outbreaks. The timeliness of this opportunity cannot be met by any regular NSF programs other than the RAPID.

The project’s broader impact lies in two aspects. The multidisciplinary effort will provide important new knowledge and insights toward understanding and developing technology capabilities for remote triage and rehabilitation, which will contribute to the early detection, spread control, and effective management and prevention of future epidemics. The techniques developed through the project to support tele-rehabilitation will have a strong potential to improve the adverse conditions and quality of life of the affected citizens.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The objective of this project is to investigate visual-based physiological sensing technologies to facilitate remote triage and rehabilitation, by using low-cost consumer-grade cameras to track such physiological conditions as heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, breathing, and more from videos.  The physiological data can be visualized and archived, and shared by users with medical practitioners to understand and support remote triage and rehabilitation.


Under the support from NSF, we have carried out research activities aiming at advancing the understandings and methods on video based physiological sensing. Recognizing that heartbeat signal plays a critical role in many physiological sensing tasks (such as breathing and blood oxygen estimation), we have investigated robust analysis and denoising of heart rate and heartbeat signal from video.  Motivated by the clinical significance of monitoring blood oxygen level from the early stages of the COVID pandemic, we have investigated contact-free privacy-respected sensing of blood oxygen using hand video. Compared to face video, the use of hand video enables easy compliance with social distancing and mask-wearing during the pandemic, and protects privacy of the person involved.  We have explored two types of approaches for measuring blood oxygen saturation from hand videos, namely, a principled approach by modeling the signal analytics pipeline and developing techniques grounded from signal processing and data science; and a primarily data-driven approach employing neural networks.  


Meanwhile, we have made a parallel effort to address the privacy sensitivity of facial video in physiological sensing, since both a person?s identity and his/her general health conditions are revealed at the same time.  We have developed an anonymization transform that removes sensitive visual information identifying an individual, while in the meantime, preserving the subtle color and movement changes that contain relevant physiological information. This can help both address the privacy concerns and provide technical support to the technical community?s collaborations and benchmarking to advance this emerging area.  Such proactive effort can contribute to promoting as balanced performances of the technology as possible for different racial, ethnic, or gender groups.


We have also made a significant progress toward transferring cutting-edge research into education and outreach.  The research outcome on video-based contact-free physiological sensing and the related physiological forensic aspects formed a primary basis for two tutorials that our PI team has given at leading international conferences on computer vision and information forensics.  We also showcased the new capabilities and high-level approaches achieved by this project in lecture material at the corresponding appropriate level at freshman level, undergraduate senior level, and graduate level as well as in talks and seminars for broader audiences to raise the public?s awareness of the new technology advancement and nurture interests and appreciation among students.  


Overall, in terms of intellectual merit, the project has explored this emerging research area of video-based contact-free physiological sensing by drawing synergy across multiple disciplines including signal processing, computer vision, machine learning, biomedical engineering, medicine, and information security and privacy.  Through publications, talks, and related resources developed, our effort in this project contributed new algorithms, systematic understandings, and data collection and protection that the research community at large can learn and benefit from.  The broader impacts are two folds:  through engaging graduate and undergraduate students, the project?s integration of research with education and outreach has contributed to the preparation of the future generation of engineering workforce with interdisciplinary strength, and stimulated their interests to pursue engineering R&D careers. Meanwhile, through new technologies and tools developed, the research outcome of the project can benefit public health and achieve global and societal impact in a long run.

award.abstractText:
Developing correct impressions of others is critical in many situations, including medical, legal, and interpersonal. It is sometimes hard to get past one’s initial positive or negative impressions of other people, even when new information is learned about them. Psychological science has shown that people pay a lot of attention to other’s initial behaviors and draw conclusions about those individuals based on those initial behaviors. For example, meeting someone who is being rude to another person may quickly lead to forming a negative impression. Even if people behave differently later on, and in different circumstances, it can be hard to move past those original feelings. Often, the first information people learn about another person might be false to begin with. This can happen through mistaken interpretations of someone’s behavior, false news or misinformation, learning information out of context, or through gossip or rumors. These issues are of particular importance when making important decisions regarding activities such as college admissions, hiring, promotion, and assessing patients and clients in medicine and law. These kinds of impressions have the potential to influence behavior, and so it is important to understand how these kinds of impressions can be corrected. This project examines people’s ability to accurately learn about the world around them, and when and how new information changes pre-existing impressions and beliefs. Understanding when and how people change their minds about other people is critically important for understanding how to correct biased assumptions. The information gained from this research will help illuminate how decision-makers integrate new information about individuals, such as patients, criminal suspects, clients, and job applicants, into their overall impressions.
 
This project focuses on two main theoretical questions about how people correct their impressions of other people. One question is whether updating of impressions occurs through “reconsolidation” versus “contextualization”. Reconsolidation occurs when new information that contradicts a first impression is integrated into the original information, such that the original memory is changed and is no longer recalled (i.e., a long-lasting change occurs). For example, when a public health official tries to correct misinformation about a current health policy, the ideal case would be that the false initial belief is completely replaced with the correct one. Contextualization, on the other hand, is when new memories are added to the original memory, and are tied to the situation in which the information was encountered. As a result, the first impression can still be activated from memory in that same situation.  That is,  the original memories are still retained, along with the new memories.  However, they are tied to specific circumstances (e.g., she is rude at work, but polite when socializing). The second question concerns the durability of, and the time course over which, updating occurs. It is expected that updating that occurs through reconsolidation will last longer than updating that occurs through contextualization. This research tests how these processes influence person perception decisions over time. The studies examine these questions using behavioral, neuroimaging, and computational approaches. Results will have implications for models of person memory, impression formation, and persuasion.  The project will contribute to a base of knowledge concerning how decision makers integrate new information about other people, with relevance to interactions with patients, criminal suspects, clients, and job applicants.  This project is co-funded by the Social Psychology and the Perception, Action, and Cognition Programs.

award.abstractText:
Nowadays, the availability of massive data is continuously increasing, primarily due to the continued advancement of technology. As a consequence, massive high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in many scientific and engineering disciplines, such as bioinformatics, computer vision, neuroimaging, and signal processing. The nonsmooth manifold-based learning with high-dimensional and multidimensional data is in general complicated due to its intrinsic non-convexity and non-smoothness. This project will address both statistical and computational issues of nonsmooth manifold-based learning and explore its new applications. 

It is known that statistical modeling of high-dimensional data may include the non-smooth regularization in the objective function, and some may even involve non-convex manifold constraints such as orthogonality constraints. The manifold-based learning offers a powerful framework for dimension reduction and signal processing. The combination of non-smooth regularization and non-convex manifold constraints brings new opportunities and challenges for designing optimization algorithms with convergence guarantees and also for developing new statistical methods and theory. The research outcomes of this project will provide new powerful analytic tools in nonsmooth manifold-based learning with theoretical guarantees. Software packages will be developed to make the research outcomes readily available to other researchers and practitioners.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Manifold optimization finds many applications in various fields of data science, including machine learning, statistics, bioinformatics, genomics, information science, and so on. For example, Sparse principal component analysis (PCA), sparse canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and sparse spectral clustering all end up with solving manifold optimization problems with nonsmooth objectives. These tools have been widely used to analyze data from genetic studies, microbiome studies, neuroscience, and social science. 
In this project, new optimization methods and theory have been developed to study several important questions in data science, including the Alternating Manifold Proximal Gradient (AManPG) method, the Manifold Proximal Linear (ManPL) method, and the stochastic Manifold Gradient Descent (stManPG) method. These new optimization algorithms have direct applications on high-dimenisonal statistical methods such as sparse PCA, sparse CCA, sparse spectral clutering, online sparse PCA, and so on. 

In this project, we have also leveraged the recent development of optimization tools and developed new statistical learning methods and theory for non-smooth manifold learning, high-dimensional statistics, statistical network analysis, microbiome compositional data analysis, high-dimensional regression with imaging data, nonparametric forecasting for large panel data, and many others.
Moreover, software packages have been developed to make the research outcomes readily available to other researchers and practitioners.

award.abstractText:
Developing correct impressions of others is critical in many situations, including medical, legal, and interpersonal. It is sometimes hard to get past one’s initial positive or negative impressions of other people, even when new information is learned about them. Psychological science has shown that people pay a lot of attention to other’s initial behaviors and draw conclusions about those individuals based on those initial behaviors. For example, meeting someone who is being rude to another person may quickly lead to forming a negative impression. Even if people behave differently later on, and in different circumstances, it can be hard to move past those original feelings. Often, the first information people learn about another person might be false to begin with. This can happen through mistaken interpretations of someone’s behavior, false news or misinformation, learning information out of context, or through gossip or rumors. These issues are of particular importance when making important decisions regarding activities such as college admissions, hiring, promotion, and assessing patients and clients in medicine and law. These kinds of impressions have the potential to influence behavior, and so it is important to understand how these kinds of impressions can be corrected. This project examines people’s ability to accurately learn about the world around them, and when and how new information changes pre-existing impressions and beliefs. Understanding when and how people change their minds about other people is critically important for understanding how to correct biased assumptions. The information gained from this research will help illuminate how decision-makers integrate new information about individuals, such as patients, criminal suspects, clients, and job applicants, into their overall impressions.
 
This project focuses on two main theoretical questions about how people correct their impressions of other people. One question is whether updating of impressions occurs through “reconsolidation” versus “contextualization”. Reconsolidation occurs when new information that contradicts a first impression is integrated into the original information, such that the original memory is changed and is no longer recalled (i.e., a long-lasting change occurs). For example, when a public health official tries to correct misinformation about a current health policy, the ideal case would be that the false initial belief is completely replaced with the correct one. Contextualization, on the other hand, is when new memories are added to the original memory, and are tied to the situation in which the information was encountered. As a result, the first impression can still be activated from memory in that same situation.  That is,  the original memories are still retained, along with the new memories.  However, they are tied to specific circumstances (e.g., she is rude at work, but polite when socializing). The second question concerns the durability of, and the time course over which, updating occurs. It is expected that updating that occurs through reconsolidation will last longer than updating that occurs through contextualization. This research tests how these processes influence person perception decisions over time. The studies examine these questions using behavioral, neuroimaging, and computational approaches. Results will have implications for models of person memory, impression formation, and persuasion.  The project will contribute to a base of knowledge concerning how decision makers integrate new information about other people, with relevance to interactions with patients, criminal suspects, clients, and job applicants.  This project is co-funded by the Social Psychology and the Perception, Action, and Cognition Programs.

award.projectOutComesReport:
When you learn information, you sometimes later learn that this information was false, and any inferences or judgments or attitudes you had formed based on that information would also be wrong. The initial information may have been a lie deliberately meant to deceive you (misinformation), or it may have been thought to be true by the person providing that information, but that person was simply, unknowingly, wrong. For different reasons, each of these scenarios describe circumstances where you learn something thought to be true, but later learn it was wrong. When new information contradicts the initial information, is your initial attitude/impression capable of being changed? Does it matter if the attitude/impression was formed consciously versus without your awareness (an implicit attitude)?

Whether the updating of an initial attitude or impression occurs may depend on whether you feel the new information is true only in specific contexts. For example, if you learn that your colleague Don was kind to his work colleagues at a dinner party he hosted, but later learn that Don was extremely rude to work colleagues during an important meeting at work, what attitude would you hold in the end? The initial attitude that he is positive (based on his kind behavior at Time 1) might not change if you believed his rude behavior at Time 2 was tied to the context -- that he is only rude during meetings at work, but is otherwise a kind person. In this case, one where the new information is contextualized, the attitude/impression might not update or change. On the other hand, if the new information was not seen as tied to the context you would likely see it as generally true of Don's character and capabilities, and you would update the attitude/impression from positive to negative in a context-free manner. Traditionally, implicit attitudes are assumed to be generally resistant to change because they are strongly context-dependent. We predicted that attitudes/impressions would be capable of being changed, and the effects of misinformation undone (updated) more easily than traditional approaches suggested. We hypothesized that this greater amount of updating would occur because the new information would not necessarily be contextualized.

In this research we explored whether implicit attitudes are updated when we learn something new about a person that is surprising and counter to what we had already believed about that person. It explores if first impressions stick versus change, and it explores factors moderating such change. This research further explored how the context in which new information is learned shapes such attitude/impression updating. In five experiments conducted with the support of this NSF grant (N = 2024), we investigated whether positive implicit attitudes about someone update after people learn negative, counter-attitudinal information about them. We tested whether implicit attitude updating depends on the similarity of the context of the initial learning versus the new (counter-attitudinal) learning.

In our experiments, participants perform a task at Time 1 where they form positive implicit attitudes about a person who is performing a positive behavior in a specific context (e.g., an office setting). Participants next learned negative counter-attitudinal information about the same person in a specific context that either matched (e.g., an office setting) or did not match (e.g., a home setting) the context in which the initial learning had occurred. The results consistently showed that the research participants updated their implicit attitudes from being positive to being negative, regardless of whether the new information was learned to have occurred in a different context. This pattern held across various types of contexts and was not moderated by how negative the counter-attitudinal information was or whether the context where people learned positive information only was present during testing as a memory cue. However, in the fifth study, we showed that learning about a contradictory behavior occurring in a new context does at times limit updating. The context can diminish updating when that context implies situational causes for the behavior that occurred and allows for one to attribute that behavior to the context rather than the person’s character. For example, participants learn a person is kind at Time 1, but counter-attitudinal negative information at Time 2 suggests the person is mean (physically harmed someone). However, the context at Time 2 is manipulated so that for some people it qualifies the negative behavior (it occurred during a boxing match) while other people learn the negative behavior occurred in a context that does not qualify it (it occurred on the subway platform). The positive first impression is updated, consistent with the first four experiments, when the context is irrelevant to the behavior (subway). However, if the behavior occurs in a context that provides a rationale for the behavior (boxing), the initial attitude is unchanged.

Together, these findings highlight that implicit attitude/impression updating is more common than previously believed.

award.abstractText:
Proteins are working molecules, playing crucial roles in almost all activities of a living cell. Therefore, elucidating the biological function of proteins is fundamental in any modern molecular biology, biochemistry, medical science, and drug development. In the post-genomics era, when a vast quantity of genomics and proteomics data are awaiting biological interpretation, substantial improvement of computational function prediction methods is essential to achieve the scale and reliability required for practical use by experimental biologists. Computational prediction is crucially useful in biological studies for designing experiments and for interpreting experimental data. In this project, a comprehensive framework for protein function prediction will be built that effectively integrates various aspects of protein features that are indicative of function. Moreover, a web-based portal will be developed, which will provide biologists with easy-to-access function prediction, visualization, and analysis tools as well as pre-computed genome function annotation. The project will train next generation interdisciplinary students through course work and direct involvement with research. Interdisciplinary proteomics approaches will be learned through local and national workshops. 

The framework will integrate several different types of state-of-the-art deep neural networks. Multiple relationships of proteins, including physical similarities and proteomics data similarities, will be represented as similarity graphs centered at the target proteins, where the functional inference will be performed using deep convolutional neural networks. Among the protein features to be considered, we incorporate three-dimensional structure similarity of proteins, which will be measured through encoded local protein structures detected from protein sequence information using deep convolutional neural network. The developed methods will be used for functional analysis of photosynthesis and nitrogen fixation pathways of photosynthetic cyanobacteria, Cyanothece ATCC51142, which provides promising platforms for light-driven biofuel production. Proteins involved in photosynthesis and nitrogen fixation cycles will be experimentally identified using a new protein complex profiling method that combines chromatography separation techniques with quantitative mass spectrometry. Then, we will apply the developed prediction methods to determine their function and validate the predicted functions with the expressed proteome. All project outputs will be available at http://kiharalab.org/software.php

award.projectOutComesReport:
Elucidating the biological functions of proteins is fundamental to modern biology. Biologists often generate hypotheses of protein function from circumstantial evidence, where computational prediction can play an important role. Building on our successful function prediction frameworks, we developed three new methods that pioneer the incorporation of novel ideas into protein function prediction. The first approach we developed, Contact-PFP, leverages predicted residue–residue contact information, a critical structural feature of a query protein, to identify distantly related proteins through database searches. This method was among the first to pioneer the integration of protein structure prediction into function prediction. At the time of its development, deep learning approaches were becoming widespread in the protein structure prediction community, yielding substantial improvements in residue contact prediction, though not yet in full 3D structure modeling. Contact-PFP capitalized on this progress by utilizing the increasingly reliable contact predictions available at that time. The second method, Domain-PFP, applies deep learning to represent domains within a query protein. These representations capture correlations between domains and their associated functions, particularly with respect to Gene Ontology (GO) terms. The third method, GO2Sum, introduces a novel type of tool that generates human-readable summaries in free text from lists of GO terms predicted for a protein by function prediction methods. GO2Sum leverages large language models (LLMs), the powerful AI techniques underlying ChatGPT and similar tools. Together, Domain-PFP and GO2Sum demonstrate new directions for applying deep learning to protein function prediction. We developed a web server for each of the three methods we developed, to provide easy access to users. The source code of the methods is also made available on GitHub.

Using function prediction tools we developed, we participated in real-life application of function annotation to three newly sequenced genomes, Nile rat, Etruscan shrew Suncus etruscus, and blue whale. Also, we investigated the function of proteins in photosynthesis and nitrogen fixation pathways of photosynthetic cyanobacteria, Cyanothece ATCC51142. Cyanobacteria are tiny aquatic organisms that can both capture energy from sunlight (photosynthesis) and turn nitrogen from the air into ammonium, a form that living things can use, which makes them important organisms for studying carbon and nitrogen cycles and promising platform for producing renewable energy. To learn more about how they do this, we grew cyanobacterium Crocosphaera subtropica (formerly known as Cyanothece ATCC51142) under day/night conditions with and without an added source of nitrogen to create nitrogen non-fixing or nitrogen fixing growth condition, respectively.

By comparing protein, the cells express during the day and at night under these growth conditions,  we discovered major changes in how Crocosphaera cells produce energy and manage cellular processes. By integrating proteomics experiments with our function prediction methods, we identified different alternative pathways and revealed that Crocosphaera coordinates its energy use very carefully, tapping alternative metabolic routes to generate extra energy and support nighttime nitrogen fixation which is highly energy expensive process.

Intellectual Merit: Our key innovations include (1) use of reliable residue contact prediction results to represent a protein structure and to perform a structure database search using the contact information; (2) use of deep learning-based representation (embedding) for capturing the correlation of protein domains and their functions; (3) use of LLMs to produce human-readable function description from a list of GO terms, which brings GO term-based function prediction paradigm back to free text; (4) advances fundamental understanding of how the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium Crocosphaera subtropica coordinates energy production, protein turnover, and nitrogen fixation under varying light and nutrient conditions, providing new mechanistic insights into microbial carbon and nitrogen cycling.

Broader Impacts: Through the development of function prediction methods, new approaches including use of deep learning techniques for analyzing protein function data were established, which have broad applications for analyzing biological data in proteomics and genomics. Developed function analysis web servers help the broad biology community with more accurate and comprehensive functional analysis of proteins. Taking advantage of the PI Kihara’s joint appointment between Biology and Computer Science, as well as the co-PI Aryal’s appointment at the Purdue Proteomics Facility and the Department of Comparative Pathobiology, one postdoc researcher, four graduate students and eight undergraduate students from four different departments, Computer Science, Biological Sciences, Comparative Pathobiology, and Agricultural and Biological Engineering were trained through direct involvement with the project. High school senior student from West Lafayette Junior/Senior High School was also trained in proteomics sample preparation and data analysis and results were presented in Indiana regional high school science fair. Moreover, computational analysis of protein function was taught in two courses the PI offered. Interdisciplinary proteomics approaches were delivered through workshops organized by Aryal and attended by graduate students, post-docs, research scientists and Purdue professors.

award.abstractText:
Calcification of soft tissues (e.g. arteries) is a hallmark of several cardiovascular diseases like aortic aneurysms and atherosclerosis. Calcific deposits lead to adverse consequences such as stiffening of arteries and disruption of normal blood flow, often leading to morbidity and mortality. The goal of this project is to understand where calcific deposits are formed in soft tissues. In particular, the investigators will examine how collagen fibrils (present in the extracellular matrix surrounding the cells in the arterial wall) can facilitate pathological calcification. The insights gained will advance our understanding of the fundamental mechanisms governing soft-tissue calcification especially in its early stages. This can help improve cardiovascular outcomes by designing new strategies for early diagnosis and treatment and aid biomaterials development for cardiovascular bioprostheses. In addition to advancing the field of extracellular matrix and vascular biology, the project will help train the next generation of scientists and engineers by providing graduate and undergraduate student(s) with multidisciplinary hands-on research experiences and under-privileged K-8 students with enrichment activities. Furthermore, new education materials and microscopy approaches will be developed to enhance education and research infrastructure for the broader scientific community.

The goal of this project is to understand the role of the collagen fibril in mediating vascular calcification.  While it is accepted that pathological calcification is mediated by phenotypic switching of vascular smooth muscle cells into a ‘bone-like’ osteogenic phenotype, there is also evidence indicating that in abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA), a subpopulation of collagen fibrils in the extracellular matrix undergoes a structural change as compared to the native (normal) fibrils. The project’s overall hypothesis is that structurally altered (abnormal) collagen fibrils in AAA serve as the major substrates for calcific deposits due to perturbations in their surface-charge distribution. To test this hypothesis, studies will be conducted at the single fibril level on human AAA tissue, beginning with mapping the micro and macro-calcifications in the excised AAA tissue using micro-computed tomography. The Research Plan is organized under two aims.  The FIRST Aim is to test the hypothesis that structurally altered collagen fibrils in AAA are “hot-spots” for negative charges in the ECM.  Surface potential and surface charge mapping of collagen fibrils in ambient air will be accomplished using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM), a technique available on most commercial AFMs (Atomic Force Microscopes) that has been used for mapping surface potential and surface charge on metals and semiconductors, but is being uniquely applied in this project to the analysis of normal and abnormal fibrils in situ in tissue sections.  Surface charge distribution of collagen fibrils in a fluid environment will be measured using another AFM based approach based on recording force-distance curves, which can map both surface charge and sample topography at high resolution in physiologically relevant fluid environments (e.g. different salt concentrations).  The SECOND AIM is to test the hypothesis that both natural as well as bio-mimetically induced calcific deposits in AAA are localized on structurally altered fibrils. A biomimetic approach will be used to determine if abnormal fibrils can be a cause as well as an effect of vascular calcification. Biomimetic mineralization will be induced in a cell free manner (in mineral-poor regions) using ionic solutions (e.g. dental fluid) that mimic the native ion concentrations in plasma without its biological components and by incubating extracellular vesicles (EV) isolated from cultured cells with decellularized AAA tissue.  Spatial distribution and characterization of calcific deposits will be determined using analytical transmission electron microscopy (TEM) approaches to characterize the size, composition and location of minerals with respect to the collagen fibril at the ultrastructural level.  Abnormal fibrils are expected to be more prone to calcific deposits as compared to normal fibrils both with respect to percent of fibrils mineralized as well as number and size of calcific deposits present per fibril, and a similar trend is expected to be observed for biomimetic and naturally induced calcific deposits.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Intellectual Merit: The blood vessel wall is a highly structured tissue comprising layers of protein fibers made up of elastin and collagen. These layers have a highly specific function and are responsible for the mechanical strength of the underlying tissue as well as cell function. In vascular diseases such as abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), the structure of the vessel wall is disturbed. In this disease, the normally present elastin fibers in the aorta are degraded, excess collagen fibrils are deposited, and there are regions with calcific deposits in the soft aortic tissue. In our previous studies, we had shown how a subset of collagen fibrils in AAA has an abnormal structure. In this project, we investigated the functional importance of these abnormal collagen fibrils in human AAA tissue obtained from patients undergoing surgery. We found that abnormal fibrils resist platelet adhesion as compared to normal collagen fibrils. Further, the abnormal (but not normal) collagen fibrils served as regions of micro-calcific deposits which increased the local stiffness of AAA tissue. The surface properties of abnormal fibrils were significantly different from that of normal collagen fibrils.  

As a technological advancement, we employed a high-throughput nanoscale imaging technique, namely atomic force microscopy (AFM), to simultaneously assess the structure and stiffness of AAA tissue and achieve multimodal AFM and fluorescence microscopy to analyze collagen fibril structure.  We also developed a method to map the surface adhesion and estimate the surface charge of individual collagen fibrils in AAA tissue.   

Broader impacts: Structural abnormality in collagen fibrils can also occur in other diseases. Our results highlight how not just the quantity but also the quality of collagen can be important for pathogenesis of diseases. The AFM approaches developed via this research can be adopted to analyze collagen fibrils in other tissues in health and disease. This project involved three PhD graduate students, four undergraduates, and a high school student in hands-on research. Two graduate students were also provided with non-academic research experience via the NSF-INTERN program. New teaching materials on AFM analysis and collagen remodeling were developed for graduate courses.

award.abstractText:
Coronary artery disease (CAD) has been influencing a market over $2.8 billion with roughly 1,000,000 treatment procedures performed annually. Existing guidance for CAD treatment suffers from limited spatial resolution and lacks real-time detailed pathological identification. This project is to investigate novel computational techniques for pathological, super-resolution visualization of coronary images. The project, if successful, will contribute towards a new generation of clinical guidance for the treatment of cardiovascular disease, which is currently the leading cause of human deaths in the United States. Technically, the method of encoding multi-domain image representations into a single-domain image acquisition could benefit other fields, such as multi-camera surveillance monitoring, multimodal biomedical imaging, etc., in terms of greatly reducing hardware cost and medical labor. The educational plan in this project emphasizes activities designed to guide senior designs, enrich curriculum in deep learning courses, and facilitate outreach for minority students in multicultural engineering programs.

This project aims to develop a data-driven approach to use off-line data and training process, without any hardware modifications, to generatively produce new information that could not be acquired previously or can only be obtained ex vivo. This project will develop generative deep learning algorithms to produce additional information for low-resolution optical coherence tomography (OCT) images by aggregating image information from high-resolution OCT images and histological microscopic images during off-line training. This project will investigate on improving the resolution of OCT while maintaining fast scanning rate via a volumetric generative adversarial network (GAN) for super-resolution. This project will develop a novel unpaired training scheme to map OCT image to a histopathology image by using a GAN-based image translation framework. The approach will be validated using both objective and subjective analysis on OCT images and histopathology images. This project is expected to generate academic outcomes in both computer science and biomedical informatics. This project will provide a deep learning solution for cross-platform volumetric super-resolution and a generative learning approach to address cross-modality image translation.

award.abstractText:
Emotions color and shape the way people perceive the world and thus how they make decisions and form memories; and those emotional impacts in turn can depend upon specific brain structures and functions. These effects are especially consequential in the context of the emotionally charged decisions and actions needed to respond effectively to the COVID-19 pandemic. To address these issues, in combination with data on pre-pandemic behavior and brain architecture, this project will measure how emotional state during the COVID-19 pandemic alters decision-making, and how that varies with the structure of the brain's dopamine system. Improved understanding of decision making in the context of the pandemic may enable us to design new interventions and information formats that will increase preparedness and resilience. 

The effects of emotions on decisions and memory have both been posited to depend on the brain’s dopamine system, which is involved in processing emotions and rewards. The project will determine the extent to which dopamine system anatomy and function predict changes in decision-making and memory in the current context of the pandemic. This project leverages a recently completed neuroimaging study that includes structural, functional, and diffusion-weighted data, which characterized the dopamine system in a group of 50 participants who completed a series of cognitive and behavioral tasks assessing impulsivity, inhibitory control, and value-directed memory formation. To assess the emotional impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on decision-making, these same cognitive and behavioral tasks will be made available online to the same group of participants from the previous study. The degree to which emotional state, and pre-existing dopamine system anatomy, predicts differences in decision-making and memory formation relative to baseline will be tested. Dopamine system anatomy is predicted to moderate the relationship among emotions, cognition, and behavior. Overall, the project will contribute to an understanding of how brain and emotion combine to impact behavioral responses to COVID-19.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Emotions shape our behavior by prioritizing relevant information to guide our behavior to resolve the problem that triggered the emotion initially. In the brain, these effects are believed to be mediated, at least in part, by the action of a number of neurotransmitter systems. In prior research funded by the NSF, we collected data to characterize the structure and function of the dopamine system. We compared measures of the integrity of this system with several decision-making assessments. The onset of the COVID-19 pandemic presented an opportunity to leverage these brain and behavior measures. This RAPID project re-contacted the subjects from our previous study. Participants reported the emotional and behavioral responses to COVID. We also had participants complete the battery of decision-making assessments that they completed previously. Our goal was to determine whether COVID caused changes in behavior that were predicted by our neural measures of the structure and function of the dopamine system.


We had two primary findings from this RAPID project. Behaviorally, measures of impulsivity changed in our subject pool during the COVID pandemic. This effect was correlated with the extent of the behavioral precautions that people took during the pandemic. Moreover, our neural measures of the integrity of the dopamine system was related to these COVID-related changes. Ultimately, while promising, these results were not robust enough to warrant publication. However, they will guide our future research on emotions and impulsivity.


Second, we collected behavioral measures on how people prioritize memory based on how valuable it is to recall specific events. In order to investigate the neural basis of the memory-enhancing effects, we developed a method to characterize the projections between the dopamine system and the hippocampus – a critical brain structure for memory. While value-directed memory did not change in our subject group as a function of COVID, the RAPID funding did allow us to demonstrate that dopamine-hippocampus projects predict value-based memory benefits. These results have been submitted for publication and are currently under review at the Journal of Neuroscience.

award.abstractText:
The proposed project seeks to examine and understand individual differences underlying the occurrence of false memories, which is defined as remembering an event incorrectly or differently than how it originally occurred. The investigation of individual differences underlying both cognitive and neural variability in memory performance will be a critical factor in understanding the sources of false memories across the lifespan. By understanding the mechanisms that lead to these memory errors, we can better understand how to avoid these errors. The project will examine the benefits of a cognitive training strategy aimed at reducing false memories in older individuals. The research will use both behavioral and neuroimaging (fMRI) methods to understand the basis of false memories. Neuroimaging analyses will include univariate, functional connectivity, and multivariate analyses to uncover the neural mechanism underlying both true and false memories. This will expand understanding of factors that contribute to false memories across the lifespan. The research will train undergraduate and graduate students on cognitive neuroscience of memory and cognitive aging and will educate the public about memory and cognitive processes that change with age. 

Memory research typically aims to identify how memories are represented in the brain. Aging research typically aims to identify sources of age-related deficits in memory. The current proposal combines these goals to reveal the cognitive and neural processes underlying a significant source of error in cognitive aging, that of false memories. The long-term goal is to identify domain-general and domain-specific sources of variance associated with false memories across the lifespan and identify effective, evidence-based strategies for reducing memory errors. This project aims to identify the cognitive and neural markers of such variance as well as individual differences factors that contribute to false memories. The research will also examine the effects of cognitive training in older adults to successfully reduce the incidence of false memories. To do so, the work will utilize behavioral methods examining individual differences in false memories in older adults, as well as advanced neuroimaging methods to investigate how neural information is processed, and represented, throughout the brain. By understanding both common and unique influences associated with the susceptibility to false memories across difference sources, the project can identify strategies for effectively reducing false memories, thereby ameliorating age-related memory decline.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The research provided valuable insight into the ways in which the brain processes false memories. The research provided additional insight into individual differences related to understanding the underlying cognitive and neural mechanisms accounting for false memories. Finally, the research identified a simple strategy intervention that was able to reduce false memories in older adults, highlighting the fact that memory impairments in aging are not ubiquitous, and that they are modifiable.  

Study 1 showed that, in younger and older adults, false memory in both semantic (i.e., words) and perceptual (i.e., pictures) tasks can be explained by a more generalized construct, rather than by two distinct constructs specific to each domain (i.e., one for semantic and one for perceptual). This generalized construct consists of three cognitive factors: frontal functioning, semantic discrimination, and perceptual discrimination, all of which were negatively associated with false memories in both younger and older adults. In other words, irrespective of age, false memory susceptibility was associated with overall lower frontal functioning, semantic discrimination, and perceptual discrimination abilities.  

Study 2 followed up these findings investigating the neural overlap of perceptual and semantic false memories. Significant neural overlap across both types of false memories was identified in frontal and parietal processing areas in both younger and older adults. Specifically,  domain-general false memory activity was found in the medial prefrontal cortex and inferior parietal cortex--brain regions implicated in memory-related monitoring. Of significance, the research showed that older adults were more likely than younger adults to produce semantic and perceptual false memories. Study results showed that this behavioral difference was associated with age differences in brain activity. Specifically, older adults, relative to younger adults, exhibited reduced neural activity in sensory regions when correctly recognizing similar, yet novel items in a memory test, and increased activity in frontoparietal regions when falsely remembering similar items. Taken together, these results suggest that older adults have a reduced ability to retrieve critical sensory details used to reduce false memories.  

Study 3 saw the development and testing of a three-day cognitive training for older adults aimed at reducing false memories. During this training, participants learned to identify item-specific details related to the studied items and use these details to distinguish previously studied items from new, yet related items at test. Importantly, the same study intervention was applied with success to both perceptual and semantic stimuli. Specifically, the strategy intervention resulted in reduced false memories both within the training domain as well as evidence of transfer to the untrained domain. Data supporting the investigation into the neural benefits of training have been collected and will be analyzed within the next six months.  

Collectively, the findings have made significant contributions to the fields of memory, aging, and false memory research. With a clearer understanding of the cognitive and neural bases of false memories, we can further refine strategies that support the veracity of older adults’ memories, ultimately promoting better quality of life and independence within the growing, aging population. 

At the time of this report, five manuscripts describing the results have been published in peer-reviewed journals. Numerous presentations of the data have been shown at conferences, including the Cognitive Neuroscience Society Annual Meeting and the Psychonomics Society Annual Meeting. Additionally, our lab has shared our research within the local community, including at lectures focused on healthy aging and memory at local senior centers and the Osher Lifelong Learning Institute at Penn State, and through articles written in local newspapers and newsletters sent out to the aging community. The investigators have also participated in community events (e.g., the Walk To End Alzheimer’s, health fairs, community lectures on aging), during which we have shared the implications of our research with older adults.  

Importantly, this grant was also instrumental in supporting the training of lab managers, graduate students, and post-doctoral fellows alike. Two of three lab managers leveraged their experience provided by this grant to gain acceptance into doctoral programs, and the third lab manager will utilize her experience in her application to graduate school this year. The graduate students supported on the grant have all benefitted with publishing of articles (first author included), conference travel and data presentations, as well as numerous advances in professional development as they apply for post-graduate work. Relatedly, a post-doctoral fellow who was able to utilize the data obtained in the grant, obtained a professorship position from this opportunity.

award.abstractText:
This study seeks to understand biodiversity by focusing on animal weapons and courtship displays, which often diversify more rapidly than other traits. Male rhinoceros beetles wield a giant, pitchfork-shaped horn on their head that they use in battles between rival males over feeding territories visited by females. Males with the longest horns win, in part because horn length accurately reflects body size and fighting ability of males - it is an honest signal of male quality. Prior work by the investigators revealed that winning fights is not enough, however. Even after battling to hold a territory, males must still spend hours each night "singing" to females using a novel file on their wing covers that they rub against a plate on their abdomen, and they produce blends of scents in their waxy outer cuticle that appear to communicate male body size and nutritional state. This study will explore the link between male condition and both song and scent signals, examine female preferences for these signals, and characterize the diversification of this suite of courtship signals across the range of the species. How do females discriminate among males, and why do they ignore the obvious signal of male quality (the horn)? The investigators will also work with the Gonzaga department of dance to design performances inspired by animal behavior, develop an interactive exhibit on insect songs for the Missoula Insectarium, and design interactive online curricula for K-16 students through the University of Denver to share information about beetles with the public.   

Prior work on the Japanese rhinoceros beetle, Trypoxylus dichotomus, a heavily weaponed species characterized by a textbook resource defense mating system, led the investigators to suspect that these beetles show elements of lekking behavior. Females are reluctant to mate with resident males guarding feeding territories despite those males consistently being among the largest, longest-horned individuals in the population. Using a combination of laboratory manipulation experiments and field observation and perturbations, this study will rigorously characterize stridulatory song and cuticular hydrocarbon (CHC) profile signals in rhinoceros beetles (Aim 1), and evaluate their importance to female mate choice (Aim 2) and male rival assessment during contests (Aim 3). In addition, this study will compare song dialects and CHC profiles across the range of this species (Aim 4), to contrast the relative rates of evolution of agonistic and mate-choice signals. Finally, they will perform a quantitative trait locus mapping study of adjacent, genetically similar but phenotypically divergent populations, combining the resulting linkage maps with a re-sequenced reference genome, and FST 'outlier' results from a prior PoolSeq study of the same populations, to delve into the genetic architecture of this suite of multimodal signal traits.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This study sought to understand biodiversity by focusing on animal weapons and courtship displays, which often diversify more spectacularly and rapidly than other traits. Male rhinoceros beetles wield a giant, pitchfork-shaped horn on their head that they use in battles between rival males over feeding territories visited by females. Males with the longest horns win, in part because horn length accurately reveals the body size and fighting ability of each male - it is an honest signal of male quality. Prior work by the PIs revealed that winning fights is not enough, however. Even after battling to hold a territory, males must still spend hours each night "singing" to females using a novel file on their wing covers that they rub against a plate on their abdomen, and performing trembling, rocking “dances” on their backs. These beetles also produce blends of smells (cuticular hydrocarbons) in their waxy outer cuticle that appear to communicate male body size and nutritional state. This study explored the link between male body condition and song, dance, and smell signals, examining female preferences for these signals, and characterizing the diversification of this suite of courtship signals across a range of related species. This involved a large experiment in the lab (during the pandemic when foreign travel was prohibited) and then several summers of fieldwork observing beetles in Japan (summers of 2023, 2025; see figure below). Our findings revealed unexpected nuance and complexity to the communication systems of insects, particularly beetles, and also showed exciting parallels in the signaling systems of insects (beetles) and vertebrates, especially deer and elk. 

Giant rhinoceros beetles and elk are charismatic species of great interest to the public, and we leverage the excitement they generate in every way that we can. Everyone connected to this project engaged routinely with myriad audiences, including audiences outside of academia, during this award period. The lab hosted a dance choreographer and a music composer for an extended residency that has now been turned into an hour-long documentary film on the intersection of science and art, told around the behavior of the rhino beetles (‘Scarabic Serenades’). The lab partnered closely with a new family-focused science museum, the Missoula Butterfly House & Insectarium, contributing to several permanent exhibits, providing opportunities for students to get hands-on practice as ambassadors of science, and sharing beetles from this research with the public. The PI used the intuitive parallels between animal and military weapons to give outreach talks across the country, to share the excitement and relevance of basic research. This past year he served as a Phi Beta Kappa visiting scholar, visiting seven campuses to meet with students and faculty and to talk about the state of science in the US. This study produced mentored ‘out of classroom’ research experiences for more than twenty undergraduates, many of whom went on to pursue careers in research, teaching, and human and veterinary medicine.

award.abstractText:
Massive high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in many scientific and engineering disciplines, such as bioinformatics, computer vision, neuroimaging, and signal processing. This proposal is motivated by emerging tools for analyzing data from these disciplines, such as nonsmooth, manifold-based learning with high-dimensional and multidimensional data. Building on the synergy among statistics, machine learning, and optimization, this research will focus on the development of new optimization algorithms and theory for nonsmooth manifold optimization. The project will also build on existing optimization strengths to develop new methods and theory in statistics and machine learning. Software packages will be developed to make the research outcomes readily available to other researchers and practitioners. In addition, the project will enhance the future technical workforce through the training of graduate students. 

It is known that statistical modeling of high-dimensional data may include the non-smooth regularization in the objective function, and some may even involve non-convex manifold constraints such as orthogonality constraints. The manifold-based learning offers a powerful framework for dimension reduction and signal processing. The combination of non-smooth regularization and non-convex manifold constraints brings new opportunities and challenges for designing optimization algorithms with convergence guarantees and also for developing new statistical methods and theory. The research outcomes of this project will provide new powerful analytic tools in nonsmooth manifold-based learning with theoretical guarantees. Software packages will be developed to make the research outcomes readily available to other researchers and practitioners.
